statement: The follow-up survey was administered 2.5 months post-injury, by which time many injured patients, including those with mild traumatic brain injury, have already recovered from cognitive symptoms.

Respondents were not representative of the patients registered in the surveillance system because severe and less common injuries were deliberately oversampled and young males were less likely to respond.
The EQ VAS was used as a proxy for health-related quality of life and is subject to end-of-scale bias.

The cognition question was placed immediately after the EQ-5D and before the EQ VAS on the same page, so responses to the original EQ-5D items may have been influenced by the added question and its sequence.
Some subgroup analyses of EQ VAS by cognition level were not significant, probably because of small sample sizes for specific profiles.

The study recruited outpatients because cognitively demanding valuation tasks were difficult to conduct with hospitalized patients; prior hospitalization was required to enrich the sample for severe health experience.
The literacy requirement could have selectively excluded otherwise eligible participants, especially older patients.
The preferences came from patients in Singapore and can differ across countries because of cultural and healthcare-system differences; suitability should be evaluated before use elsewhere.
The study did not assess how heart-disease type, comorbidities, disease duration, treatment, or socioeconomic characteristics affected preferences for health states of different severity.
A Singapore general-population EQ-5D-5L value set was not available for comparison at the time of this study.
The study did not collect discrete-choice experiment preferences even though the cited EQ-5D-5L valuation protocol requires them.
Single-centre recruitment in Shanghai and the sample's high education and socioeconomic status can limit generalisability.
The 2- to 3-week retest interval may have allowed true health changes, which can affect reliability estimates.
The stable-health reliability sample included only 65 carers, which can limit generalisability and underestimate true reliability.
Unmeasured health conditions and financial or social challenges may have confounded the results.
Vaccination status was not recorded for children or parents, and most children were unvaccinated, so its effect could not be assessed.
The EQ-HWB-S was scored with a United Kingdom value set because no Chinese value set was available, which may disadvantage comparison with EQ-5D-5L scored with a Chinese value set.
The experimental EQ-HWB-S may be modified in the future.
When the same caregiver reports the child's health and their own HRQoL, caregiver emotion and burden may bias proxy assessments and spillover estimates.
The number of participants was limited, although the authors judged it sufficient for statistically significant coefficients.
The sample represented the Russian population only by age and sex; rural residents were underrepresented, and education, employment, and income quotas were not controlled.
Only regions in European Russia were included, which limited geographical representativeness.
The Van Hout crosswalk sample included no Russian respondents, so differences in EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L response patterns could bias the mapped value set.
Because the topic was specialized, the authors used a targeted citation search based on four seed papers and did not conduct a broader systematic review.
Much early EQ VAS research was not formally published, and identification of relevant grey literature depended on communications with researchers involved in early EQ-5D development.
Recruitment through Prolific, an online survey company, may limit representativeness.

The cognitive-debrief interview itself may have influenced participant behavior; interviewers sometimes intervened to prevent prolonged struggles, so it is unclear whether participants would have resolved confusion independently.
The sample was small, which limited the presentation and interpretation of quantitative results, including age-group differences.
Participant views about using OPUF for decision-making were not analyzed because responses had limited depth, possibly because prompts came late in a long interview or were too open-ended.

The reused dataset did not contain wording equivalent to the current experimental EQ-HWB-S for three of nine items. The mobility and concentrating/thinking items had to be constructed from item pairs, and only the Australian sample permitted a combined sad/depressed analysis.
Only English-language EQ-HWB-S data were analyzed, although the source psychometric study included other languages.
The source dataset was not collected for the known-group comparisons, which limited those analyses.
Because the source survey sampled particular conditions and population groups, its composition could have contributed to the strong scalability and might not generalize to other patient populations.
The instrument is conceptually multidimensional, and an analysis with additional well-being items would provide more clarity about scalability.
Automated item selection can identify the wrong number of dimensions when factors are strongly correlated; therefore, its two-scale result requires cautious interpretation.
Data on subclinical myocarditis and pericarditis after COVID-19 in the general population were lacking.
The pathophysiological mechanisms of myocarditis and pericarditis after COVID-19 vaccination were not completely understood.
Long-term outcomes after vaccine-associated myocarditis and the safety of a subsequent mRNA vaccine dose remained uncertain and required prospective study.
The Slovenian translation of the most severe pain/discomfort level as unbearable rather than extreme pain may have exaggerated the disutility attached to that level.
No modelling strategy is agreed for value-set estimation, and using cTTO data alone can deliver logically inconsistent estimates, although it did not do so here.
DCE data were collected under the EuroQol protocol but were not used, because the current EuroQol DCE design and protocol do not allow a value set to be estimated from DCE data alone.
No exclusions were made on data-quality grounds, and interviews failing the quality-control criteria were retained when the interviewer judged that the respondent understood the cTTO task.

The sample is too small for discrete choice modelling and estimation of coefficients needed to produce EQ-5D-Y-5L health-state utility values; the authors state that this would require about 1000 participants.
Snowball recruitment through community organisations may introduce selection bias and may under-represent eligible youth affected by socioeconomic disparities or access barriers.

The study did not use the existing Chinese EQ-5D-5L value set; it estimated core coefficients from newly collected data produced with the same design and interview team, which could favor compatibility and predictive performance.
The standalone bolt-on models used relatively small samples of about 200 respondents per arm, which limited power and could contribute to nonsignificant or nonmonotonic additive coefficients.
The comparison was not a definitive test of model superiority because constrained scaling factor models borrow information from the core EQ-5D-5L data and trade model flexibility for consistency.
Random-intercept Tobit models accounted for baseline preference heterogeneity but not individual variation in sensitivity to health-state severity or heteroscedasticity in cTTO responses.
The by-state cross-validation was an internal validation and did not use a fully independent sample.
The scaling factor model was tested only with cTTO data; the study did not evaluate DCE data or a hybrid cTTO-DCE approach.
Index values were based on an interim value set derived by crosswalk rather than on directly measured Polish EQ-5D-5L preferences, which the authors describe as a major limitation.
The cross-country comparison was qualitative only, with no formal statistical analysis.
The generic criteria may not be appropriate in all circumstances because health experiences are complex, so developers may need to adapt them to the context and health area.
Some psychometric criteria may not be assessable with available data: construct validity needs valid comparator measures, and test-retest reliability and responsiveness need longitudinal data.
The framework did not explicitly specify valuation criteria, although amenability to valuation informed several criteria; further research is needed on how bolt-ons should be valued.

Internal consistency and item response theory methods were excluded because bolt-ons are single-item dimensions and comparison with overlapping multi-item domains would be difficult to interpret as generic guidance.
The simplified, self-reported severity screening question used for recruitment quotas often did not align with interview accounts or validated severity scores.

Atopic dermatitis and chronic urticaria diagnoses were self-reported, so some participants might not have had a formal diagnosis; the recruitment and screening process reduced but did not remove this risk.
The chronic urticaria sample was imbalanced by subtype: 12 participants had chronic spontaneous urticaria and three had chronic inducible urticaria.
The study was conducted with English-speaking participants in the United Kingdom; the authors stated that other geographical and cultural contexts require further research.
Feasibility assessment included only missing responses. The study did not collect completion time, qualitative assessment, or participant preference data.
The responsiveness results have limited generalizability because the heterogeneous group included non-elective management and the study did not collect data before and after the intervention.
Recall bias could affect repeated responses if participants selected their best, worst, or average health state differently across assessments.
A recalibration response shift could bias the results if a participant's point of view changed during recovery.
The COVID-19 pandemic prevented completion of the original face-to-face collection and caused a delay of approximately two and a half years before collection resumed.

The resumed study used video conferencing and new interviewers, but the revised protocol did not assess administration-mode or interviewer effects; values could therefore differ between the two collections.

The analyzed sample underrepresented people from the Southern region and people with lower education, although the final value set used population weighting and weighted and unweighted results differed only slightly.
The single-center sample included only female patients with breast cancer in one country, so findings may not generalize to other cancers, male patients, or poorer settings with less access to care.

Caregivers and core family members were not included. Because most patients were female homemakers and men are often household providers in Indonesia, the study may not have captured financial toxicity comprehensively.
Nearly all patients had treatment insurance, and limited response variability may have weakened associations for some sociodemographic covariates.
FACIT-COST was developed in the United States and may not be the most suitable measure of financial well-being in the Indonesian context.
EQ-HWB-S index values used the United Kingdom pilot value set, which does not fully represent Indonesian population preferences.
The baseline cross-sectional analysis cannot establish causality; longitudinal research is needed, including assessment of possible mediators such as social support.
The pragmatic design accepts necessary variation in how the intervention is implemented across renal programs, which limits the rigour of the evaluation of the efficacy of PROM interventions.

To maintain anonymity of patient-reported experience data and because of drop-in and drop-out of dialysis patients, individual CAT surveys are anonymous, so the primary analysis compares unit-level mean CAT scores rather than individual change scores.

No optimal sample size was calculated for adequate power; the sample was determined by unit eligibility, and the available sample gives 80% power only for a small effect size of 0.23 on the primary outcome.
Blinding is not feasible, so the trial is open label and research staff, clinicians and patients are aware of group allocation.

The instruments and delivery differ between programs (ESAS-r: Renal in AKC-North and Ontario, IPOS-Renal in AKC-South; report cards only in Alberta), so the intervention is not identical across sites.
The QC process is probably not the only cause of the observed differences, because protocol version 1.1 also introduced practice states and a confirmatory pop-up screen.
Improved interviewer training in Spain may have affected the data, impeding conclusions about causality and about how much improvement is attributable to the QC process.
Differences between respondents, including the shift from panel quota sampling to convenience samples, may affect the distribution of values by interviewer.
Further studies are needed to clarify which parts of the QC process are most helpful.
A generic measure cannot include every relevant domain.
Available valuation approaches constrain how many domains the classification system can contain.
The measure was designed mainly for self-completion; proxy completion needs further work to determine which aspects an observer can meaningfully report.
Focusing on health-, social care-, and carer-related quality of life may limit relevance to sectors such as housing, prisons, and community interventions.
Using service users and carers as the main source of domains may overlook concerns held by the general public.
Framing interviews around impacts of conditions, disability, care, and caring can emphasize deficits rather than positive human capacity and flourishing.
Expectations, adaptation, and response shift can affect both a respondent's assessment of functioning and outcomes and the self-report of that assessment.
The EQ-5D-3L was always presented after the EQ-5D-5L and the order was not randomised, so sequence effects cannot be excluded.
Baseline EQ-5D-5L was completed electronically while the retest was paper and pencil, which may have confounded test-retest results; actual health change was not measured at retest.
Quota and convenience sampling may cause selection bias and yielded few severe health responses; random household sampling might have included more frail respondents.
Cognitive ability was assessed only informally by interviewers, and no data on exclusions or true response rate were kept.
The candidate explanations cannot be empirically disentangled with existing evidence, so interpretation of the child effect on values remains ambiguous.

The utility function for life-years is not observed and is perfectly confounded with the utility function for HRQoL, so stated preference tasks do not allow the underlying preferences to be identified.
It is unknown whether enough respondents hold the view that children are more resilient to drive the difference in the value scale of most EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets.

There is no consensus on whose preferences should be sought for valuing child HRQoL, and the theoretical foundations of cost-effectiveness analysis give little guidance on age-specific versus age-invariant value sets.
The authors recognise the risk that raising these issues appears to undermine the progress made in developing EQ-5D-Y-3L and other pediatric value sets.
The sample included only female patients with one type of cancer.
The study took place at one public referral hospital, and 99.7% of participants had insurance; this setting can limit generalizability and can help explain the absence of worst possible scores.
Some subgroup analyses may have had insufficient statistical power because subgroup sample sizes were small.
The diversity of teams, services, and contexts prevented one standardized provincial implementation approach, and some teams had difficulty integrating the survey into workflow.
Some clinicians found the EQ-5D-5L insufficiently specific or clinically valuable for their patient group, including wheelchair users for whom the mobility wording was not relevant.
The current data system did not give clinicians individual patient results or an accessible view of change over time, which limited clinical decision-making and care planning.
The available sample size did not yet permit comparisons of rehabilitation performance across sites and health zones.
Data were collected online, so the authors had no control over the environment in which respondents completed the survey.
The online panel sample reported generally mild health impairments, so generalising the comparison to more severe health problems requires careful consideration.
The study compared only health-related quality of life measures and did not include broader quality of life or social care measures such as ASCOT or EQ-HWB.
PROPr cognitive function scores had to be imputed with the DeWitt regression approach because only PROMIS-29 was administered, although the reported error of that imputation is small.
The low variation in EQ-5D-5L self-care responses confounds the interpretation of the weak correlations between self-care and the PROMIS-29 domains and PROPr.
Twenty-four respondents provided incomplete EQ-5D-5L or PROMIS-29 data and no sensitivity analysis including them was conducted.
EQ-5D-Y has no value set, which limits its use as a preference-based single index measure in cost-utility analysis.
The instrument's sensitivity to small changes in health-related quality of life is limited, possibly owing to high ceiling effects.
Published counts of paediatric preference-based measures should be treated with caution, because under a narrow definition only three instruments were developed specifically for younger age groups.
No self-reported EQ-5D-Y exists for the youngest children, so proxy versions must be used below age 8, and proxy reports can be biased.
The review used a targeted selection of reviews for common medical conditions because all conditions could not be covered; rarer conditions can therefore be less well represented.
Known-group testing included limited assessment of severity and no assessment of change over time, so responsiveness requires further validation.
The groupings used for known-group validity were very limited for social care users and carers.
Psychometric testing must be repeated on the final 25-item and nine-item versions, including equivalence between direct EQ-HWB-S administration and the same items embedded in EQ-HWB.

The study could not recruit every population group, such as people with long-term conditions and carers, in all six countries except the United Kingdom; China results and the lack of African work show the need for broader cultural validation.
The pragmatic seven-day recall period can be difficult for conditions with less frequent episodes, and format or presentation changes will require testing.

The valuation evidence came from a small qualitative pilot; a full TTO and DCE valuation is required to test feasibility across the large health-and-wellbeing classification and determine whether all items matter in valuation.

Designs were tested using VAS data, whereas most EQ-5D valuation studies use time trade-off; VAS values theoretically lack ratio properties, so caution is needed when applying the results to other valuation methods.
Rescaling the VAS values on two extreme states assumed interval scale properties and produced a more compressed valuation space than raw VAS or time trade-off data.
The analysis was restricted to a main-effects model, because previous work found that interaction terms increased the likelihood of misspecification.
The secondary data were collected from 2011 to 2013.
The sample included only patients with intermediate burns and no more than 20% total body surface area burned, which limits application to severe burns.
Only adults were included, so the findings do not address children or proxy assessment.
Responders differed from non-responders, which could overestimate the HRQL impact.
The study used EQ-5D-3L rather than the newer, more sensitive EQ-5D-5L.
The arbitrary conversion of the POSAS 2.0 ten-level itching scale to three levels could cause measurement bias through ceiling effects, loss of refinement, and overestimation of reported problems.
No local respiratory bolt-on value set was available; the study used experimental Dutch value sets that may not represent preferences in the multi-ethnic Asian population.
The Dutch value sets contained non-monotonic coefficients. Rule-based replacements produced a logical structure, but their accuracy cannot be established and may differ from reality.
Differences between known clinical groups might partly reflect the larger possible utility-index range of bolt-on systems rather than true differences.
The exploratory study had no sample-size calculation, so its conservative design may have caused type II error.
No value set existed for EQ-5D-5L plus both R1 and R2, so the study used a level-sum score and could not assess the combined version utility index.
Mental fatigue could cause participants to misinterpret instrument timeframes or headings despite interviewer administration, which could produce reporting errors.
The three-month SGRQ recall period overlapped the mean 2.8-month reassessment interval, which could reduce the accuracy of SGRQ-based change groups for patients with shorter follow-up.
Self-reported data and simulated palliative contexts might not capture the complexity and emotional depth of real-life palliative-care needs.
The study did not specifically address cultural diversity within each country, which limits generalizability to all national subpopulations.
The design assumed that all participants interpreted the context vignettes uniformly, but individual perceptions and valuations can differ.
The review did not include nonmalignant hematologic conditions such as anemia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia or hemophilia, in order to maintain transparency and specificity.
Conference abstracts and presentations were excluded because their form usually does not allow extraction of meaningful HSUV details such as the value set used.
Results of the EQ-5D descriptive system and EQ VAS were not reported, being deferred to a separate publication.
A meta-analysis of the identified HSUVs could not be performed because of high heterogeneity in the subgroup definitions used by the authors of the individual articles.
Some included clinical trials do not reflect current clinical practice or were made obsolete by more recent trials, so at least some of the catalogued HSUVs may be inapplicable in further analyses.

Some subgroups are of questionable value because of their definition (for example specific EORTC QLQ categories) or limited sample size, but were retained to stay consistent with the inclusion and exclusion criteria.
No study limited solely to minors was included, partly because EQ-5D is not a standard instrument in that age group and methods of estimating utilities from the EQ-5D-Y are still developmental.
Important clinical areas such as Hodgkin lymphoma were covered by relatively few studies, patients and identified HSUVs.

The limited evidence base, especially the evidence gaps in Africa and South Asia, limits generalizability. Differences in language versions, design factors, and sample health status could not be analyzed because data were unavailable or insufficient.
Fifteen articles used both EQ-5D versions but did not report administration order, so order effects could not be considered.
EQ-5D-5L studies were generally more recent than EQ-5D-3L studies; unaddressed cultural changes over time could create temporal bias.
The restriction to English-language publications can cause language bias, omit relevant studies, and limit generalizability to non-English-speaking populations.
The search had no time restriction, so the evidence combined methods used across decades in which patient-reported outcome analysis practice changed.

Clinical trial reports often gave little space to statistical methods and nonprimary EQ-5D results; missing details about covariates, correlation structures, baseline adjustment, and imputation could make the reported frequencies underestimates.
EQ-5D was often absent from titles, abstracts, and keywords, which could reduce database-search sensitivity, and nonsignificant exploratory EQ-5D results could be subject to publication bias.
COVID-19 related recruitment barriers and facilities' tendency to recommend residents without cognitive impairment produced uneven numbers in the two cognition sub-groups.
Some participants clearly struggled with the think-aloud process, which may have caused loss of focus and less careful attention to their responses.
Administering the SMMSE immediately before the think-aloud interview may have added cognitive load and fatigue, and the think-aloud protocol itself adds cognitive burden.

Data were not collected on the use of mobility aids, personal care assistance and treatments or medications, so these factors could not be controlled when examining response issue patterns across cognition sub-groups.
The high completion rate cannot be taken as evidence of self-report feasibility of the EQ-5D-5L in this population, because interviewers were involved in the completion process.

A saturated VAS dataset was used as a proxy for TTO valuation; TTO data show more heteroscedasticity between states and more heterogeneity between respondents, so more states or observations may be needed in a TTO valuation study.
A blocking effect may exist because the 3125 states were divided into 16 blocks, but the analysis assumed no such effect rather than using a two-level model.
University students were used as respondents; their limited experience of health problems and more homogeneous preferences may have produced smaller RMSE than a general population sample would.
The models did not account for possible censoring of mild-state values or heteroskedasticity, and the main effects model did not capture all effects on valuations.
The general-population sample contained younger and more highly educated people than the national adult population.
The validity sample was not contextually neutral because it came only from an urban megacity in South Vietnam.
The absence of HRQoL measurements from other instruments prevented convergent-validity testing.
The absence of measurements at different time points prevented tests of reliability and sensitivity, so the study covered only a limited part of EQ-5D-5L psychometric performance.

The quality control report covers only formal objective indicators such as consistency and duration, and does not capture what was actually said or the nonverbal interaction between interviewer and respondent.
Recruiting through interviewers' personal networks may have introduced bias and interdependent data collection, so part of the sample may reflect interviewer networks.
Problems of the 20 people who declined participation are unknown.
The urban-rural classification followed administrative definitions and had to be corrected for two areas that did not resemble rural areas.
The analysis used only 266 respondents, 25% of the target, who were mainly young, well-educated and urban, so the problems found may not represent the complete sample.
All interviews were conducted in three cities on Java, so problems such as language barriers in the home regions of other ethnicities are unknown.
Interviewers were questioned by the researchers who hired and evaluated them, which may have led to more positive answers.
The retrospective questionnaire may have caused recall bias and omission of information.
The review excluded non-peer-reviewed sources such as registry reports, although these can contain important information about PROM use for quality improvement.
A meta-analysis and effect-size estimation were not possible because study designs and outcomes were heterogeneous.
PROM scores were reported inconsistently as total scores, dimension scores, or both, which limited synthesis by outcome dimension.
Most included studies did not measure intervention compliance, so the reviewers could not determine the extent to which patients or providers used the PROM interventions.
PROMs were often one component of a complex intervention, which made it impossible to isolate the contribution of the PROM.
Videoconference administration, required during the COVID-19 pandemic, may have suppressed subtle interactions or changed their frequency relative to in-person interviews.
The pattern list was developed from a subsample of 24 interviews conducted by only two interviewers, so it may not be exhaustive.
Only 42 interviews were scored rather than all interviews in each batch, which prevents exact matching with quantitative quality-control indicators and permits random-sampling effects.
For most interviewers, recordings were available only from the first two batches, so later improvements could not be detected.
The study did not analyze non-verbal communication such as facial expression, gesture, voice, and posture.
The exploratory sample was too limited to support firm conclusions about the usefulness of the quality-control process.
The DCE design excluded duration as an attribute and death as an alternative, so latent DCE coefficients could not be anchored without cTTO data.
The best conversion method cannot be determined from these data because the true DCE-based value is unknown, and best fit to observed cTTO data does not prove a model is better.
Model selection by information criteria is meaningless here because the models use different data sets (cTTO, DCE, or both).
The hybrid model is sensitive to the ratio of cTTO to DCE responses, and the larger, more informative cTTO data strongly influence its results.
The conditional logit model assumes identical coefficients for all people, cannot account for the panel structure, and assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives.
The sample size was not based on a formal statistical calculation, and the study design, including the ranking task before cTTO and the order of tasks, may have influenced the results.
The study could not determine whether the fit difference arose from sample composition, face-to-face versus online administration, interviewer support, permission to skip items, or other factors.
All new participants came from Guizhou Province; validation in multiple regions of China is needed for broader generalizability and applicability.

The tested factor structure does not exclude other structures that may fit the Chinese population better, and the EQ-HWB still requires further refinement and validation at item and instrument levels.
The condition samples were not optimal; a student cohort was used to represent a healthy population, whereas an age- and education-matched general population sample would have been more suitable.
Inter-country differences in the descriptive data cannot be excluded, since condition groups came from different countries (Italian liver disease, Polish students, Dutch personality disorder).
The F statistic assumes normality, but the 3L and 5L utility distributions were often non-normal because of ceiling effects and clusters.
The conclusion that 3L overestimates health problems may be challenged for the first three dimensions, where 3L level 2 ('some problems') is not identical to 5L level 3 ('moderate problems').
The study used cross-sectional data, so firm conclusions about the impact of 3L versus 5L on QALYs cannot be drawn.

Respondents were recruited through local contact persons and were not chosen completely at random, having already been deemed suitable for participation, so non-completion rates could be higher under a more random sampling and recruitment strategy.

Data collection was stopped abruptly by COVID-19, so some interviewers had completed substantially more interviews than others, and interviewer effects in handling situations such as dropping out were inevitable despite training and an interview guide.

The EQ-PVT software did not easily allow collection of partially completed interviews, so partial TTO responses were not saved and information on where respondents dropped out or how their earlier responses differed was unavailable.
Because the data were collected primarily to value the EQ-5D-5L, other potentially relevant measures such as respondent or interviewer evaluations of the interview were not collected.

The three respondent characteristics were crude proxy variables for unmeasured phenomena; in particular immigrant background is a presumptive proxy for language barriers, since proficiency also depends on duration of stay and education.
The study was conducted in a single population.

Respondents were younger and more educated than the general Emirati population of Abu Dhabi and the other six emirates were not represented, so findings cannot be generalised to all Emiratis or to other Muslim Arab populations.

The assessment of the impact of spiritual or religious views relied on a single open-ended question in a self-administered survey, which limits the validity of results and the strength of conclusions.
The design is subject to interviewer and response bias and to bias from the experience and judgement of the researchers analysing and interpreting the data.
The United Arab Emirates is a high-income Middle East country with a very specific set of social characteristics, so findings can only be interpreted within that context.
The sample did not reflect the San Joaquin Valley racial and ethnic composition, especially its large Latino population and other disadvantaged or underserved communities.
The sample size was limited because the study had no funding, which restricted representation of the region's diverse population and the ability to validate subgroup findings.
The air pollution policy measurements require replication in regional studies to test whether they validly represent the reported orthogonal constructs.
Pre-infection EQ-5D-5L scores were unavailable, so pre-existing differences in health-related quality of life could not be assessed.
Hospitalised patients were overrepresented relative to people who remained at home during acute infection; the authors addressed this by reporting stratified results.
Some controls may have had unidentified or asymptomatic COVID-19 because testing was scarce when they were recruited, which could misclassify controls.
The study could not distinguish post-intensive-care syndrome from post-COVID condition in ICU survivors because their presentations can be similar.

Selection bias could not be ruled out because people with no burden and people for whom severe symptoms made questionnaires too burdensome may have participated at different rates; this could underestimate severe complaints.
Vaccination status relative to each follow-up questionnaire was unavailable, so the study could not distinguish possible vaccination effects on post-COVID symptoms.
Quota sampling used region, age, and gender but did not stratify by employment, education, or marital status.
The source valuation study was not designed to test predictors; the authors called for a focused study with a larger sample.
The exercise question was general and did not distinguish gym activity from other physical activity such as walking.
The study did not collect household size or number of children, although prior studies reported these as predictors.
The subgroup with more than one comorbidity was small, and its p-value was close to 0.05, so the authors advised caution.

There was clustering of TTO values at 1 (nontrading for mild health states) despite interviewer performance assessment, suggesting respondents were unwilling to trade time for states they considered mild.
The distribution of background variables in the sample differed from National Bureau of Statistics data, although differences were small and limited to residence and religion.
Relying on supervisors as mediators between interviewers and respondents through personal networks may have introduced bias, and further investigation of its effect on data quality is needed.
Data were collected only in Addis Ababa city and the Butajira rural area of the Gurage zone, which may raise questions about the representativeness of the sample.
The lite protocol valued only 91 health states and was designed for a 20-parameter main-effects model; this may have limited detection of significant interactions.
Interaction construction treated main effects as continuous, which may have constrained the model's ability to capture interaction effects fully.

Representativeness was suboptimal because recruitment relied mainly on active members of a chronic-disease risk-factor cohort, and less educated and ethnic minority groups were slightly underrepresented despite quota sampling.
Participants selected either in-person or Zoom interviews. The two modes could have introduced systematic differences, although the study found no evidence of mode differences.
The study used summated dimension scores as proxies for EQ-5D-Y index scores because no EQ-5D-Y value sets were available at the time.
The Y-5L was not an official version and future modifications could change its measurement properties.
All pupils completed Y-5L first, which could cause an order effect and loss of patience during later Y-3L completion.
Only vision and BMI information were available, and the overweight subgroup was very small.
The cross-sectional design did not permit assessment of reliability or responsiveness; longitudinal studies are needed.
Early trial termination caused variation in the timing of the final visit.
The planned 2-year interval between routine HRQoL measurements was too long to capture the trajectory of quality of life over time and could miss changes during the first year.
About 24% of patients in each group did not complete the EQ-5D at final visit, and some characteristics differed between participants with and without final EQ-5D data.
Most value-set studies considered at the workshop were not yet published, so the authors could not report their quantitative results.
The exploratory study was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the variant groups were small and may have lacked power to detect significant differences.

Participants may have processed recall periods, instructions, and response scales differently despite interviewer training; cognitive biases and heuristics could attenuate differences between time frames.
The 3-month SGRQ was used as a comparative reference because no true HRQoL gold standard exists, which may favor EQ-5D-5L variants with longer recall periods.
Resource and burden constraints prevented real-time symptom tracking and standardization of follow-up intervals, which limited benchmarking of exacerbations and change status.
Interviewer administration may not generalize to self-administration in busy routine clinics.
Results may not generalize to milder obstructive airway disease managed in the community or to other fluctuating health conditions.
The multiethnic Asian setting may limit transferability because cultural concepts of time and well-being could affect responses.
The conceptual framework and checklist items reflect the experiences, opinions, subjectivity, and judgment of the authors and expert reviewers, who were health economists.

The authors note a difficult balance between comprehensive reporting and a checklist that is concise enough for different users; the preferred depth may differ for researchers, trial designers, and decision makers.
RETRIEVE does not cover mapping from disease-specific to generic instruments or methods other than direct stated-preference elicitation for assigning values to disease-specific states.
The authors caution that the geographic locations of the development team and reviewers can leave country- or jurisdiction-specific requirements outside the checklist.
The application test covered only four selected studies, and the authors report feasibility rather than full validation.
The checklist does not establish a gold standard or settle criteria for judging the validity of child HRQoL values.

Respondent group and valuation perspective differed together: adults valued an unspecified 10-year-old child, while adolescents valued their own health. The study therefore cannot separate sample effects from framing effects.
The adult task did not define who the 10-year-old child was, so respondents could have used different cognitive frames; the reference age also did not match any adolescent respondent.
The DCE omitted dead and health-state duration and collected no anchoring data. The latent estimates cannot be used to calculate QALYs, and comparisons are limited to relative importance.
Online collection can have data-quality problems, especially for adolescents, although face validity and logic checks were generally good.
Exclusion of participants with multiple illogical responses or indifference in anchoring can overestimate agreement between tests.
OPUF uses visual analogue scales that can be affected by response-spreading and related biases, which the analysis could not account for.
Online recruitment can preferentially include participants with better digital literacy, despite attempts to obtain a representative sample.
Use of a German sample can limit generalisability.
OPUF reliability was assessed across several component tasks and levels, so the results are not directly comparable with conventional reliability assessments of TTO and DCE.
The secondary data analysis could not examine reliability, convergent validity, or responsiveness to change because the required data were unavailable.
Forced-choice online survey responses prevented analysis of missing values and the practicality of EQ-5D-5L completion.
The researchers could not independently confirm that respondents were caregivers.
Care-recipient dementia severity was reported by caregivers, and no further clinical severity information was available.
Personality traits that could affect caregiver health-related quality-of-life ratings were not assessed.
Convenience recruitment and unequal distributions of age, sex, and other characteristics limited generalizability.
The analyzed sample of 212 participants was relatively small.
Backward selection applies multiple testing, easily produces significant results, and yields biased regression estimates and confidence intervals.

Subgroups were created only from self-reported EQ-5D-5L health because no medical diagnoses were collected in the German valuation study, so results cannot be generalised to patients with a diagnosis.
The same health impairment can be reported differently across respondents, so conclusions are limited to differences by subjective self-reported impairment.
Most participants reported no or mild impairment (only about 30% had severity level 8 or worse), so the results cannot say whether severely impaired people differ from the general population.
The recommended sample size of 1000 participants for generating a value set could not be reached for the subgroup-based value sets.
The study values hypothetical health states only, so results may not generalise to experience-based values preferred in countries such as Sweden.
Values were reported on a pits scale, not a QALY scale, because the study included no time trade-off or preference evidence about dying immediately.
The analysis was exploratory rather than confirmatory, which complicates interpretation of p-values and statistical inference.
Taste and scale remain partly confounded in choice analysis, so scale adjustment might not fully separate scale from preference coefficients.
The constant paired-comparison comparator and relatively small sample prevented exploration of more extensive heterogeneity structures; the SALC model was limited to two taste and two scale classes.
Income and task-completion time were absent, although they could have informed class membership.
Results depend on the selected SALC parameterization and require a justified theoretical basis.
The online sample was not fully representative and was smaller than the sample used for the original Dutch value set.
The age group proportions differed significantly between the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L samples.

Values from choice models are not cardinal: full health is dominant and cannot anchor the model, and death was not included, so the scale had to be rescaled using published Dutch valuation studies rather than an internal anchor.
Using the same number of 240 choice pairs for both versions gives broader coverage of the smaller EQ-5D-3L state space, so estimates may be somewhat more precise for the 3L than for the 5L.
Participation was limited to caregivers who could answer in English and access the questionnaire online.
Down syndrome, autism spectrum disorder, and cerebral palsy were overrepresented relative to the Australian intellectual-disability population, and not all very rare diagnoses were included.
Population heterogeneity and the moderate sample size can limit generalizability.
Caregiver proxy reports can introduce subjectivity, especially for pain/discomfort and worry/sadness/unhappiness, which require appraisal of the child's internal state.
The test-retest sample was small, and the interval varied from 9 to 32 days instead of a uniform 14 days.
The study did not provide longitudinal evidence on responsiveness to age, comorbidity exacerbations, or other HRQoL factors.
Findings come from a single English-speaking country (Australia) and from a primary study that purposively sampled people with specific characteristics.
As a secondary analysis, all analyses relied on the pain and discomfort items as collected in the EQ-HWB psychometric study, so comparisons with studies using differently worded items need caution.
Some EQ-HWB items underwent slight wording modification after the psychometric study, so the items analysed are not identical to the final EQ-HWB items.
The EQ-5D-5L used a "today" recall period while the pain and discomfort items used "the last 7 days", and the extent to which this explains response differences is unclear.
Few respondents reported extreme pain/discomfort on the EQ-5D-5L, limiting applicability to more severe samples.
The sampling approach of the primary study was not informed by the aims of this analysis.
Breakout rooms allowed more participants to speak but limited general debate and consensus.
Identity protection allowed quotations to be attributed only to participant numbers, without country or work-setting information.
A longer, more general introductory session might have improved the consultations despite provision of preparatory reading.
Experts differed in their knowledge of outcome measures and EQ-TIPS, which limited discussion and debate in some instances.
The study did not collect details about experts’ parenting, caregiving, or lived experience of caring for a child with a health condition.
Experts were recruited from people known to the research team or extended networks, which may have biased results.
Hospital treatment made health improvement expected, which limits interpretation of the responsiveness results.
Formal inter-data-collector reliability was not assessed, although all data collectors received protocol training.
The study did not conduct cognitive interviews to assess younger children's understanding of EQ-5D-Y-3L items.
Children with developmental disabilities were not included, which limits generalizability to the broader pediatric population.
The Zimbabwean EQ-5D-3L value set was used because no Ethiopian value set was available, and cultural or contextual differences can limit the utility estimates.
Selection bias is possible because patients with more severe illness or lower HRQoL may have been less likely to complete both assessments, which can overestimate improvement.
Hospital-based collection can introduce social desirability bias or effects of acute emotional states in self- and proxy-reported responses.
The impact of the value sets was not tested on clinical trial data, so QALY estimates could not be directly compared; this is the next planned stage of the programme.
The psychometric performance and cost-utility impact of the EQ-5D-5L were not compared with other generic preference-based measures such as the SF-6Dv2.
Some patients gave apparently inconsistent responses across the two descriptive systems, producing a wide range of individual value differences.
Condition ranking evidence is based on a limited set of conditions, several with small samples, and requires exploration across a larger range of conditions.

The data covered only survey respondents discharged from inpatient care or emergency departments. Respondents can differ from nonrespondents, and reliance on survey data could worsen inequity because only responders could benefit.
The analysis excluded people with no patient-reported data and imputed partial missing data, which could introduce bias.
Only a modest set of available sociodemographic predictors was used; important social determinants such as poverty and housing insecurity were unavailable.
Predictor operationalization choices, such as comorbidity counts instead of individual condition indicators, could change predictive performance and importance estimates.
Results for these specific PROMs and PREMs may not generalize to other measures or care settings.
The small sample size limits the generalizability of the utility values.
Snowball sampling did not produce representative Polish-migrant or native-Irish samples, so the results should not be treated as representative of these populations in Ireland.
Only 30 EQ-5D-5L health states were valued, which could reduce econometric precision and population representativeness.
The empirical example did not permit exploration of the full range of differences between national value sets.
Low response rate and a sample limited to well-educated, Caucasian, older retired teachers limits generalizability to other arthritis populations.
A Canadian value set was used for the EQ-5D-5L index while a UK value set was used for the SF-6D index, so index scores may reflect different general population valuations.
All data were self-reported and may be under- or over-reported.
No data on type, location or severity of arthritis were available, preventing subgroup analyses of discriminative validity.
The study used secondary data and was therefore subject to possible registration bias.
Prevalence data came from highly populated areas, no regional disaggregation was done, and the analysis applied national estimates.
Classifying low back pain as a rheumatic disease was a limitation, although the study used the same classification as GBD.
The assessed diseases could not be ungrouped, which made it difficult to obtain high-quality data for each topic.
The caregiver's proxy rating of the child's VAS could have been influenced by the caregiver's own health-related quality of life, creating an artificial correlation.

The proxy rating may have been clouded by the caregiver's expectations of the child, their definition of health-related quality of life and their understanding of the child's illness and its sequelae.
Selection or completion bias is possible because general population caregivers who returned the research pack may have been more motivated than those who did not.
The reasons for caregivers reporting problems in each EQ-5D-3L dimension were not sought, so it is unclear whether those problems were due to the child's health.
South Africa has no locally derived value set, so United Kingdom time trade-off values were used for the caregiver index scores.
Caregivers unable to read or write English were excluded because the TANDI existed only as an English prototype awaiting translation.
Recruitment from specialist clinics may limit generalizability to the wider pediatric asthma population managed in primary care.
Chinese value sets were used because Singapore-specific value sets were unavailable, and these may not fully represent preferences in Singapore’s multiethnic population.
EQ-5D-Y-5L was summarized with a level sum score because no value set was available, which may limit comparability with utility-scored instruments.
The PROMIS asthma measure used as a convergent-validity comparator had not been validated in this study population, and no gold-standard or other validated measure was available.
The long and variable interval between baseline and follow-up was not ideal for responsiveness assessment with a retrospective health-transition question, especially for children.
Only five patients reported worsened health, which limited responsiveness assessment in this group.
Samples differed across countries in sample size, administration mode, purpose and time of data collection, which may limit comparability despite adjustment for sample structure.
Some archived surveys were old, and population norms may change over time in some countries.
Non-response may bias results towards underestimation of self-reported health problems, and only some countries applied a sampling design.
Differences between country language versions of the EQ-5D may add variability.
Age standardization used the European population structure, which may not be justified for non-European countries, especially China.
Reporting behaviour heterogeneity, for example by education, may affect variability in reported health problems between countries.
The patient sample is relatively small and covers a narrow age range (all participants below 34 years), so generalization beyond this age range should be made with care.

Characteristics and problems of SUD patients may vary between countries and welfare systems; Norway is wealthy with low inequality and universal health care, so generalization beyond wealthy northern European countries is not supported and studies elsewhere are needed.
The higher HRQoL reported by cocaine users remains unexplained, and socio-economic markers that might account for systematic differences were not included in the study.
No Norwegian EQ-5D-3L value set exists, so the UK tariff was applied to both samples by convention.
Sensitivity of the EQ-5D to change in HRQoL among SUD patients was not established, because only responses at the start of treatment were available.
The response rate was low (26.5% at T1), so respondents may be a self-selected sample with higher consistency, affecting internal validity and generalisability to the Dutch trauma population.

A stand-alone paper-and-pencil questionnaire was used, so comprehension of the HRQL questions could not be verified; half of respondents reporting full health on EQ-VAS also reported problems on EQ-5D.

The group interview protocol with a digital aid and limited interviewer support produced many states valued at zero and short completion times, which may have masked real differences between the TTO variants.
Minor imbalance in group sizes arose from technical problems with the EQ-VT during initial recruitment, though the authors judge this to have no bearing on the results.
The sample had a higher educational level than the general Argentinean population.
The analysis used pooled cross-sectional data, so it gives a snapshot of associations and cannot measure change over time or the effect of social care interventions.
The variables available for the regression models were constrained by the content of the Health Survey for England.

Only people aged 65 and over living in private households were included; those in care institutions or hospital, who are likely less healthy and less independent, were excluded, and social care applies to people of all ages.
The Barthel index was used as a proxy for social care needs, and the EQ-5D was not developed for social care so it may not capture the full range of social care outcomes.
The search for recommendations was restricted to health economics and PROM development or evaluation; a wider disciplinary or generic-guidance search could identify additional recommendations.
Each included recommendation record received equal weight, and the relative importance of recommendations for health state valuation was not evaluated.
The synthesized recommendations should be used only with consideration of existing engagement guidance, such as GRIPP checklists.
The review excluded qualitative research participation that informed health states when it did not represent peer-to-peer collaboration, which limited the evidence included.
Only English-language content was included, and the valuation-study search was restricted to contemporary studies published from 2019 onward.
Sparse observations prevented the planned subgroup analyses by age group and collaborator type.
The sample size was constrained.
Preventive-care use was based on subjective self-report and might not be wholly accurate.
Potentially relevant variables, including time preference, were missing and could have influenced the model results.
Some variables were measured crudely; the study could not capture the participant's health history or family health history.
Focus groups used a hybrid format because of COVID-19 travel restrictions. Data richness, articulation, and interaction might differ from a fully face-to-face format.
The interviewer focus groups used a convenience sample recruited through Nanjing CDC.

Interviewers were local primary health-care staff with medical or public-health backgrounds. The observer-assessment mindset and other findings might not generalize to surveys that use other interviewer types.
The study identified behaviours and plausible pathways but could not determine how much they changed ceiling effects or overall data quality.
Findings came from one municipal survey context and should be applied to other settings with caution.

The recordings concerned EQ-5D-3L administration in 2020, whereas focus-group participants discussed EQ-5D-5L experience from 2021. Similar behaviours were reported, but their nature and extent can differ because 5L has more response levels.

Differences from the 2011-2012 reference sample may reflect factors other than lockdown or the pandemic, including different administration modes, sample sizes, cohort effects, demographic changes, and the age of the reference data.
The full-lockdown QALY estimate assumed that average utilities observed in the four waves remained constant over the 99-day lockdown.
The lockdown sample was relatively small, which may have contributed to non-significant comparisons.
Recruitment through an online panel may have caused selection bias because panel members can have higher education and socioeconomic status than non-panel members.
The baseline used EQ-5D-Y-5L as a proxy for EQ-5D-5L, which may have biased results.
The three-week follow-up was short and may have missed larger later effects of lockdown.
Quota sampling was non-probability convenience sampling and may have biased representativeness.
Mean EQ-5D dimension level scores treated ordinal response levels as if they had parametric properties.
The baseline occurred shortly before formal lockdown, when anticipation and voluntary staying at home may already have affected health, which limits its use as an unexposed confinement reference.
The study could not determine how much QALY loss was attributable to quarantine, fear of COVID-19, effects on others, or economic anxiety.
Some critically ill patients cannot self-report, and proxy and patient HRQoL ratings can disagree.
Subjective EQ VAS ratings can differ from EQ-5D-5L algorithm scores, and general-population preference weights may be less generalizable to critically ill patients.
HRQoL components can move in different directions, and patients can value morbidity and mortality differently, which complicates interpretation of composite outcomes.
HRQoL measures are time-specific; baseline data can be unavailable because of incapacity or can have recall bias when patients or proxies report past health.
Mortality can skew QALY distributions, the correct follow-up horizon is uncertain, longer follow-up increases missing data, and methods for baseline imbalance and responsiveness remain uncertain.

Information was self-reported, so some participants may have answered in the way they believed the interviewer wanted to hear, although interviewers were experienced senior neurotrauma nurses with a standard operating procedure, study-specific training, and supervision.
The exploratory study tested only two poor EQ-5D-5L health states and one 2.5-year duration, so results may differ for other health contexts, states, or durations.
The study tested only whether EQ-5D-5L context affected ASCOT valuation; it did not test the reverse direction in which ASCOT defines the context for EQ-5D-5L valuation.
Only EQ-5D-5L and ASCOT represented health-related and social-care-related quality of life, and other instruments might produce different results.
General-population respondents imagined hypothetical health conditions, so their preferences may not represent people who live with those conditions.
The online sample was younger and more highly educated than the Australian population, and people with communication, cognitive, or some physical disabilities were probably underrepresented.
Online survey data quality was a concern, although the study used strict quality-control checks.

Participants reviewed the EQ-5D-5L displays without completing the full decision aid, and they usually reviewed Part 1 or Part 2 separately instead of in sequence. This loss of context could have changed their feedback.
The study used paper prototypes, although the decision aid will be online. The mode difference could have changed feedback, especially feedback about visual appeal.

Recruitment occurred after the surgical screening appointment, when some patients had already made a treatment decision. This timing could have reduced reported usefulness compared with intended use before screening.
There is no defined acceptable threshold for prediction accuracy; the maximum-sample 20-parameter TTO-only benchmark was a comparison threshold, not a proposed standard.
Mean RMSE obscured the larger variation and greater risk of high error in small samples.
The study did not assess prediction standard errors, parameter significance, or utility assumptions such as monotonicity, although these are relevant to final value-set model selection.

The three national data sets were selected by convenience and from populations considered comparable with Norway, so the findings may not transfer to countries or cultures with different response patterns.
Resampling did not account for respondent characteristics, so differences in sample composition could contribute additional error, especially at smaller sample sizes.

Repeated RMSE observations in the effect regression could underestimate standard errors; simulation suggested that independent samples would give slightly larger standard errors without changing the main findings.

The community-based, non-hospitalized cohort had relatively few respondents with severe breathing or cognitive problems, which limited the range available for validation and limits transfer to more severe clinical populations.
Pulmonary and CANTAB comparator tests were measured at 8-13 months, about 20 months before the 28-32-month bolt-on assessment, so change over time can weaken correlations.

EQ VAS is a single-item criterion measure of general health and has limitations for judging the additional contribution of specific bolt-on dimensions; multi-item global, physical, and mental health measures can be more suitable.
CANTAB reference values were from a United Kingdom population because Norwegian reference values were not available.
Twelve of the 45 responding countries had fewer than three responses, which limited country-level representativeness.

It was difficult to identify the most appropriate person within an HTA agency: senior personnel might lack detailed subject knowledge, while analysts might not represent the agency's official position.
Recruitment through EuroQol Group member networks could overrepresent HTA personnel who know or favor EuroQol instruments.
Recruitment was organized by country, respondents gave individual views, and agency identifiers were not collected. The researchers could therefore not reanalyze data with the HTA body as the unit.
The study was not powered for subgroup analyses, and respondents often worked across several technologies, therapeutic areas, and roles. Overlap and uneven category sizes would limit interpretation.
The researchers could not verify respondent eligibility because the anonymous survey collected no personal names or agency identifiers.
Only 4 of Canada's 13 provinces and territories were included in the valuation study.

The sample size was chosen to give adequate precision for the national algorithm, so the regional algorithms lack precision; the usual activities coefficient for British Columbia had the wrong sign and a large standard error.
The analysis did not investigate the reasons or determinants of regional variation in preferences.
Using the three WHO health dimensions as guiding questions to encourage fuller responses may have introduced leading bias.
The COVID-19 pandemic may have influenced participants' health perspectives, including emphasis on masks and hygiene.
The study did not perform a formal information-saturation analysis because the necessary data were not available.

About 24% of self-arm respondents were included in design updates despite failure of the inverse VAS traffic-light check; their responses remained embedded in the adaptive design even though exclusion produced similar final estimates.
The inverse VAS traffic-light check may not have been intuitive and may have been too strict.
Online-sample quality remained a concern because repeated reCAPTCHA checks may not have detected every bot, and the high exclusion rate showed substantial quality problems.
Parents and nonparents received different repeat-question quality checks, which could affect subgroup comparisons.
Because this was the first nonlinear valuation of a pediatric HRQoL instrument, the validity of the estimated discount rates could not be assessed against comparable pediatric studies.

The estimated discount rate may capture heteroskedasticity as well as time preference and may depend on survival-choice framing and the duration range; its relation to social discount rates used in health technology assessment is unclear.
The refugee-matched control group has a different demographic structure from the full Estonian population, so the results cannot be generalized directly to the Estonian general population.
Direct comparison was limited to variables available in both surveys; refugee-specific migration and living-condition indicators were absent from HBEP.
Declining response rates and the change in the male-to-female ratio from the refugee sample to the response data indicate possible non-response bias.
The included covariates were unlikely to explain all variation in EQ-5D-3L index values, so residual bias may remain.
All data were self-reported and could not be validated externally, which may cause under-reporting or over-reporting, especially for mental health symptoms and differential item reporting.
Stepwise removal of non-significant variables may bias coefficients and p-values.
Only one translation, the Chichewa version for Malawi, had piloted the method within a complete translation process; evaluation in other languages and cultural groups was still needed.
Only card ranking was taken forward to pilot testing, so other qualifier-ranking approaches might be preferred by children in some countries or populations.
The problems and benefits observed may not generalize to all multi-attribute utility instruments and may be more relevant to instruments that use ordinal or Likert-type scales.
Adding card ranking can increase the time required for translation and cognitive debriefing, especially if adapted for adults, and this time cost requires consideration.
The cross-sectional design did not permit assessment of sensitivity to change over time.
Interviewer-assisted administration could have influenced responses, and social desirability bias could have occurred.
The quota-recruited sample may not fully represent the diverse experiences of social care users and caregivers.
Chronic conditions, caregiver status, and social care use were self-reported without verification against medical records.
The caregiver and social care user subgroups were relatively small, which may affect the validity results.
EQ-HWB was completed at the end of the interview, so fatigue could have affected responses.
The United Kingdom pilot EQ-HWB-S value set may not represent Italian population preferences.
Correlations may be affected by shared method variance or measurement error.
EQ-HWB remained experimental, and its wording and response options could change during further validation.
The 3L and 5L were evaluated in different patient samples with different levels of mental health problems, so the comparison is not a head-to-head one.
Observed change on the PHQ-9 and GAD-2 in the PROACTIVE population was small and likely not clinically meaningful, which may have made the 3L anxiety/depression dimension appear less responsive.
The 5L sample was relatively small, giving inadequate numbers within each change category of the anxiety/depression dimension.
The EQ-5D and the anchor measures use different recall periods and different symptom characteristics, which may reduce correlations and limit the responsiveness assessment.
The anchor measures used are not gold standards for assessing depression and anxiety and have inherent limitations.

COVID-19 stopped data collection before the planned sixth state, Meghalaya, was sampled; the final value set therefore used data from five states. The authors reported that interim analysis supported a good-quality value set and that state-level sample-size calculations preserved study power.
The selected hybrid approach assumes a linear association between DCE and TTO utilities, an assumption that has been challenged.

Data collection occurred during the COVID-19 outbreak. DCE data spanned the Spanish lockdown, and C-TTO mode changed from face-to-face to video conference. The authors could not determine whether the pandemic, lockdown, or mode change affected population health preferences.

Online DCE administration can reduce respondent engagement through speeding or random responses. The study used completion-time and dominant-pair checks as proxy engagement measures to reduce this risk.
Clinical variables such as treatment duration and CD4 count were not collected because the electronic clinical system was under upgrade and paper records had little usable information.
Mandatory electronic items eliminated missing responses in the digital arm and could bias the data-completeness comparison with paper.
Recruitment was limited to people living with HIV, which limits external validity for other conditions and healthy populations.
The high proportion of women limits sex-specific inference, especially for men.
Paper-form completion time was not recorded, so completion-time feasibility could not be compared across modes.

The framework makes simplifications: uncertainty and discounting are discarded and allocative efficiency is assumed to be the only criterion for societal decisions, ignoring equity, non-health outcomes and regulation.
The strong assumptions underlying the QALY, including measurable, interpersonally comparable cardinal preferences over hypothetical health states, are taken as given and are not challenged.

The proposed majority voting system has large informational demands, needing detailed primary data on health outcomes and on individual health state preference functions, and is unlikely to be a viable alternative to the current system in the near future.

Majority voting is insensitive to preference intensity, so minuscule benefits to a small majority may outweigh large losses to a minority, and individual cost-effectiveness thresholds could in principle differ between people.
Informing participants about the policy purpose of a valuation survey may invoke strategic behaviour, with respondents exaggerating preferences to tilt the tariff.
Deriving local tariffs takes time and resources, and may only be worthwhile if preferences and resulting decisions differ significantly between communities.

Most of the 14 countries included are not resource-constrained, because resource-constrained countries did not report the standard deviations or standard errors of observed mean utilities needed as simulation inputs.

The approach assumes exchangeability across countries and normality of mean utilities within and between countries, which may not strictly hold since societal preferences and model functional forms differ across countries.
The work covers EQ-5D-3L only; performance of shrinkage estimators for EQ-5D-5L value sets remains to be evaluated.
The magnitude of error reduction was relatively small and, in rare cases, reversed, because between-country variation exceeded within-country sampling variation for EQ-5D-3L.
The BDS score comes from discrete items and is more appropriately ordinal than continuous; linear-model results need cautious interpretation, although ordinal analyses gave consistent results.
The cross-sectional design does not permit causal inference between food insecurity, psychological distress, and HRQoL.
Data collection ended early in September 2024 because of the Israeli war on Lebanon, so the final sample was below the target, although the demographic quota balance was reached.
Participants might not fully remember past experiences, which can produce recall bias.
Sensitive topics and self-reported data can produce reporting and social-desirability bias.
Non-probability sampling can limit sample representativeness and the generalizability of the findings, despite efforts to include rural areas and older adults.

No published minimally important difference estimates existed for the anchors in opioid use disorder, so distribution-based classification (half a standard deviation) was used, which makes no judgment about clinical meaningfulness.

The data-intensive requirement of complete responses at multiple time points excluded a large proportion of trial participants from the analysis, and caution is advised when generalizing beyond the study population.
Instruments were administered in a fixed order (EQ-5D-5L, HUI3, then EQ-5D-3L), although 60+ intervening questions were used to mitigate question-order bias.
As is typical with pragmatic trial data, the directionality of health change precluded separate examination of sensitivity to positive and negative change.
Brief Substance Craving Scale follow-up occurred at weeks 10 and 22 and was paired with week 12 and week 24 index scores, a misalignment that may weaken the observed sensitivity for that anchor.
The study modified the standard EQ-VT protocol (third-person C-TTO framing and coloured DCE cards), which may affect any cross-country comparison involving the Vietnam value set.
Use of the coloured DCE cards was not systematically recorded, which could potentially bias the study.

Interviewer bias remains possible; the C-TTO is a complicated exercise and interviewers may focus on younger respondents who find the task easier, although re-training, daily discussions, the quality-control tool and real-time electronic reporting were used to limit this.
The effect of the third-person approach on the elicited values is not clear and requires further research.

Attrition limited analysis to baseline and the first three follow-ups, so the study observed each participant for no more than four years even though observations were distributed across up to 26 years after onset.
The short individual follow-up did not permit a comprehensive analysis of intraindividual long-term trajectories.

The sample and analyses focused mainly on the first 26 years after onset and on SCA3 because of the participant distribution, which limits generalizability across subtypes with different progression rates.
Individual variability was substantial, especially for PHQ-9 scores, so estimates require cautious interpretation.
The cohorts may represent a mentally resilient sample because people with depression may have been less likely to participate or may have received treatment.
Medication, other treatments, sleep quality, and other psychosocial or protective factors were not available, which limited explanation of the depression and HRQoL trajectories.
Data covered only a six-month period.
Longitudinal data, especially parent-reported mental health problems, may be affected by recall bias.
No laboratory markers were included and medication use could not be controlled for.
Analyses were exploratory, the same sample was analysed with five longitudinal models, and some subgroups were small with unbalanced disease groups.
Some health complaints measured by the HBSC-SCL overlap with symptoms of the studied diseases.
The Kids-CAT study was observational without systematic intervention and prior treatment was not controlled, so change over time may partly reflect routine medical care.
Validation of the approach relied on state-based pairwise choice tasks of the very kind the authors argue are problematic.
Anchoring the PUF at dead still requires stipulating a duration (10 years here), since whether a state is worse than dead may depend on duration.
Current methods cannot construct PUFs for respondents who consider dead to lie below all health states in the descriptive system.
The tasks for examining interaction effects were difficult for respondents to understand and their data were not used in deriving the social utility function.
Interviewers were instructed to discuss inconsistencies with respondents and may therefore have strongly influenced responses, with limited means to detect such effects.
The Excel-based tool was rudimentary and could be improved in functionality and presentation.
Interviews were relatively long at about 45 minutes, suggesting a need for larger incentives and clearer disclosure of the time commitment.

Aggregating individual PUFs into a social utility function requires treating them as interpersonally comparable and choosing among alternative definitions of 'average' preferences, which is a normative choice.

The sample was small and only a simplified three-level version of the EQ-5D-5L was valued, so comparisons with existing value sets must be treated cautiously and feasibility for the full EQ-5D-5L remains untested.
EQ-HWB-S valuation data were collected during the COVID-19 pandemic, which may have affected subjective health-related quality of life and mental wellbeing.

EQ-5D-5L utilities were obtained by mapping to the EQ-5D-3L UK value set, which reduces dispersion and has an upper limit below 1; conclusions may need reassessment with the new UK EQ-5D-5L value set.
The analysis used an experimental EQ-HWB-S version, and a definitive EQ-HWB-S value set had not yet been produced.
The analysis used a general population sample rather than patient groups, so fewer problems may be reported and performance in specific diseases or conditions remains to be tested.
