The study combined two data sets that differed in long-term-condition question wording, instrument order, and administration mode; some differences may result from ordering or mode effects.
The survey did not include some PROGRESS-Plus variables, including religion, disability, sexual orientation, and vulnerable-group membership; household size was only a proxy for social capital.

Four of the five countries had no country-specific EQ-5D index value set, so Trinidad and Tobago crosswalk values were used for Barbados, Belize, Jamaica, and Trinidad and Tobago, and the Uruguayan value set was used for Colombia.
Health inequality may have changed since the 2012-2014 survey period.
The comparison with other countries should be interpreted cautiously because it mixed EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L indices and covered only 22 countries.

Patients with celiac disease and clinicians did not take part in current-study screening, face-validity assessment, dimension prioritization, or item refinement; all such decisions were made by the research team.
Only the deductive coding task was repeated with four additional LLMs; the full prompt sequence was not recreated across models, and the effects of different prompts were not assessed systematically.
The comparison with qualitative analysis and topic modeling used only 85 of 1977 entries because independent qualitative double-coding of the full dataset was not feasible.
The single disease, Dutch setting, and survey free-text source limit transferability and generalizability; the question framing may also have structured responses and made the LLM task easier.
Coauthor familiarity with the 85-entry subset could have influenced judgement-based screening and refinement of dimension labels and descriptions.
Prompt statement order could influence aggregation output; the reshuffling analysis found possible instability for self-efficacy, although not for the other 11 dimensions.

The UK general-population convenience sample may lack generalizability to clinical trial samples, and is probably not representative of participants with specific conditions or diseases, despite at least 50% having comorbid conditions.

The 30-minute interval between administrations may have introduced carryover or memory effects, and the brevity and sole inclusion of the EQ-5D-5L is a likely source of bias that inflated agreement among modes.
The magnitude of carryover effects cannot be estimated statistically, so the high ICCs were probably partly due to participants recalling their previous responses.

Administering the EQ-5D-5L at 30-minute intervals is not how it would be used in a clinical trial, so mean differences and ICC estimates would probably show greater variability and lower agreement across more distal time points.
The qualitative design limits generalizability, although it was intended to explore diverse personal experiences and perspectives.
The study was conducted in the Chicago area, so the findings may not represent experiences across the United States.
The sample reported relatively few problems with health-care bills and had high health-related quality of life on the EQ-5D-5L, which limited socioeconomic and health-status variation.
Passive flyer recruitment and self-selection through ResearchMatch may have introduced selection bias.
The interview mode could have produced social-desirability bias or interviewer effects related to interviewer behavior, appearance, or voice.
Because of issues with the characteristics and quality of the TTO data, TTO models could not be reliably estimated and compared between countries.
Given the pilot nature of the work, no formal sampling framework was used; respondents were only broadly representative by age and sex.

Values worse than dead are affected by the chosen lead-time to disease-time ratio, and some participants may want to trade more time than the composite TTO design allows, producing censored values that require further modelling research.

Unresolved issues remain for discrete choice methods, including possible use of decision heuristics that violate model assumptions and the perfect confounding of the scale factor and parameter estimates (variance heterogeneity), and DC values still need anchoring on the utility scale.
Whether the scales on which elicited utilities are placed are true interval scales, as required by the QALY model, remains under debate for TTO, standard gamble and discrete choice alike.
Recruitment relies on an online panel, which may not be generalisable to the US general population, particularly to less educated people and to those who do not take part in online surveys.

EQ-5D-Y-3L values on an experience scale (0 is being in a coma and 1 is full health for a week) may not be suitable for use in cost-utility analyses at present, because experience scaling does not convey the trade-off between quality and length of life.
The findings will only reflect US values for one-week episodes for a generic 10-year-old child, so other child ages, health problems and durations need further adaptation of the protocol.
Respondents may experience psychological distress from evaluating the hypothetical scenarios.

Mental-health concerns might have been discussed but not charted, or documented in paper records such as treatment run sheets, so chart-note analysis likely underrepresented identification and management.
The views of other dialysis clinicians could differ from the views of nurses.
All interviewed nurses were female and worked in smaller community units, so nurses in larger urban units could have described different resources.
Three of ten patient interviews occurred in the public dialysis setting, which might have affected what participants were willing to share.

The retest was offered only to respondents who had limited difficulty with the first interview, producing a more highly educated retest sample and probably biasing results toward favourable test-retest variation compared with real-life valuations.
Respondents' own health could have changed between the two measurements and influenced reliability indicators, although no significant association was found.

About 6.33% of C-TTO responses were highly inconsistent, likely reflecting interactions between health state severity, interviewer effects and respondent characteristics that may not be completely avoidable.
The available literature lacks empirical evidence about the relative importance of the different uncertainty sources.
The authors state that their list of valuation-study uncertainty sources is not exhaustive and that its order does not indicate importance.
The article focuses on uncertainty generated by valuation studies and does not analyze all possible uncertainty sources in the other study types in equal detail.

The Canadian valuation study was in the first wave of EuroQol EQ-5D-5L valuation studies and used an 11-parameter functional form that differs from common 21-parameter and newer 8-parameter CALE models; functional form can affect predictive performance.

The analysis followed the original Canadian study by censoring cTTO values at zero and leaving traditional TTO values uncensored; other censoring decisions can affect parameter uncertainty and were outside this study's scope.
The method is suitable for TTO or standard-gamble utilities but requires further development for DCE data and joint cTTO-DCE hybrid estimation.
The study addressed parameter uncertainty in the value set but did not quantify other uncertainty from data quality, valuation task, choice of population, or health states worse than dead.
The available data did not permit assessment of responsiveness to change.
Test-retest analysis was not possible for AQoL-8D because the two-week follow-up contained only EQ-5D-5L.
The dataset did not include a non-carer control group.
The dataset did not report whether informal carers had underlying health conditions, which limited isolation of health effects attributable to caregiving.
The best way to account for time preferences in a DCE with duration has not been identified, and discount rates can be computed in different ways.

Models that account for non-linear time preferences are complex and are not implemented in standard choice-modelling software, so preference heterogeneity and non-linear time preferences could not be accounted for at the same time.

The approach places high demands on the experimental design, requiring interim design updates with adequate priors, and results may depend on the data quality obtained along the way; speeders were excluded post-hoc rather than before the design updates.
The reliability of the estimated discount rates, which were high relative to rates used in economic evaluation, needs to be established in future research.
Samples were not fully representative: fewer respondents with lower education than the Dutch population, and a much larger share with college or higher education than Chinese norms.
Care should be taken when generalising the results to other countries.
A parent did most of the talking in one adolescent interview, which likely limited that adolescent's contribution.
The study did not capture younger children, fathers, or people who speak a language other than English.
The sampling prioritised clinics planned for later design work, including colorectal surgery, asthma, sleep, and encopresis clinics, so findings might not transfer beyond these clinics.
Only three adolescent patients participated, and a larger adolescent sample could strengthen further research.
The study presented EQ-5D-Y-5L for assessment rather than allowing stakeholders to choose from several P-PROMs because the scope was limited.
The skewed individual-level distribution of inconsistency forced the analysis into logistic modelling of categories rather than continuous measures.
The classification of inconsistency into slight and severe was arbitrary because no well-accepted definitions exist.
The moderate sample size prevented responsiveness analysis in patients whose health worsened, and the sample was skewed toward younger children, with limited evidence for ages 12-16.
All participants came from one high-socioeconomic-status hospital in Shanghai, which limits generalizability to other regions and countries.
EQ-5D-Y-5L was evaluated with an unweighted level sum score because no Chinese value set was available; this score can inflate reliability and reduce known-groups validity and responsiveness.
EQ-5D-Y-5L was always administered before EQ-5D-Y-3L, so an ordering effect could have influenced responses.

The GINA criterion covered the past four weeks, while EQ-5D-Y assessed health today; this recall-period mismatch could add response variability and overestimate perceived well-being in known-groups analyses.
The study included more DCE tasks per respondent than a standard EQ-5D-5L valuation study, which may cause respondent fatigue and reduced response efficiency.
Respondents' decision-making processes cannot be properly assessed with a simple retrospective feedback question, so it is unclear whether the context display encourages simplifying heuristics.
Differences between desktop and laptop users cannot be attributed to the device, as the environment and unobserved respondent characteristics may also explain them.
The context display did not work on smaller devices, limiting its applicability if valuation moves to smartphones or tablets.
Findings relate to the English language version only; extension to other languages with reported preference inversions, such as Brazilian Portuguese, is needed.
Only one option for the context display was tested, selected from informal piloting with a convenience sample of friends and family; alternatives such as animation or a visual cue were not evaluated.
The study was powered for equivalence of mild health states and may have been underpowered for moderate and severe states, which had much larger cTTO-value variance.
The appropriate equivalence limit for the Australian context was uncertain, so the authors cautioned against relying heavily on the equivalence tests.

The sample included more women than the general population and was highly educated; men without university degrees were especially difficult to recruit, and education-by-mode interactions appeared for four states.

Eligibility required willingness and ability to use both modes, including access to a suitable camera-enabled device, and market-research-panel recruitment selected people already interested in research; results might not generalize beyond this self-selected group.
Participants learned about the additional AUD 40 face-to-face compensation only after expressing interest and being randomized, which might have influenced participation decisions.
Reasons for refusal after randomization and for nonattendance were incomplete because these participants were difficult to follow up, so these data were excluded from the final analysis.
Selection bias cannot be ruled out because people with poorer physical or emotional well-being might have declined participation.
Recruitment from a weight-management clinic included only people compliant with follow-up visits and might have favored participants with better outcomes.
Asian populations have diverse ethnic and cultural contexts, so findings from this Singapore sample may not apply to other Asian populations.
The impact of obesity or MBS on physical intimacy might have been discussed inadequately because such topics are culturally sensitive and often avoided in Asian contexts.
A female interviewer could have affected comfort with sensitive topics, and three virtual participants joined from locations where other people were present, which might also have limited disclosure.
The cross-sectional design did not assess within-person change from preoperative to postoperative PROMs, so it could not test whether a preoperative lockdown effect persisted through recovery.
Privacy restrictions prevented analysis of regional differences in PROM response rates and responder representativeness.
PROM response rates in the LROI were relatively low, although they did not change during the lockdown.
Differences between the Dutch lockdown and measures in other countries can limit international generalizability.
Registry data could not distinguish clinician selection from patient self-selection, such as patients delaying surgery because of fear of infection.
Telemedicine physical therapy was not recorded, and some patients in short-term comparisons had surgery before the lockdown and could already have started therapy.
Each source study included at most 37 tasks because the components were designed for completion in under 30 minutes, so sequence effects beyond that number could not be examined.
Trends in the relative risk of a modal response may under-represent losses in TTO precision from rounding, because most modal TTO responses are themselves in 5-year units.

The reduction in half-year responses could reflect satisficing, reluctance to backtrack or overshoot, or genuine satisfaction with whole-year precision; the data cannot distinguish these explanations.
The absence of sequence effects in the discrete choice tasks may be due to their simplicity (two alternatives with two attributes).

The samples could not be matched on all factors that might influence results; only age and gender were controlled for, so differences in true health problems or other unobserved characteristics may explain the observed differences.
The EQ-5D-3L data were collected in the 1990s and may not represent current UK and Japanese populations, although the authors argue between-country comparison remains valid.

The EQ VAS regression models showed non-normal residuals, heteroscedasticity and non-linear functional form in several specifications, so P values are affected and coefficients could be biased by omitted correlated variables.
Only two European countries were available for comparison, so it is unclear whether the results extrapolate to other Western countries.
The 17 EQ-5D-3L states valued in Japan were a subset of the UK state set, and the mix of severity presented may itself influence TTO values.
For the Japanese EQ-5D-3L dataset only the valuation subsample (N = 543) was available, and EQ-5D dimensions had to be treated as continuous variables because severe levels had very small cell sizes.
The sample was small: 52 caregivers and only one health professional supplied ratings, which limited robustness and generalizability.
EQ-5D-3L was always completed before EQ-5D-5L, so order effects and overuse of levels two and four in EQ-5D-5L were possible.
Administration mode differed: caregiver ratings were interviewer-administered, while the care manager self-completed the instruments.
The care manager completed the EQ-5D instruments after interviewing the caregiver, so the caregiver response could have influenced the care-manager rating.
Different value sets and utility ranges were used for EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L, which could have affected agreement, discrimination, and convergent validity.
The review focused on generic HRQoL instruments and did not include condition-specific HRQoL measures.
The search used major bibliographic databases, so regional-database literature and grey literature could have been missed.
Restriction to English-language papers could have excluded relevant publications in other languages.
A single reviewer performed data extraction, which could have introduced extraction errors despite use of a standardized form.
The sample size within each known condition group was small, so known-group validity results should be interpreted with caution and require larger samples per group.
No data on race, home language or socioeconomic status were collected, so results cannot be generalised to the greater Western Cape region.

Only an English version of the EQ-5D-Y-3L IA was available at the time of data collection, so non-English-speaking children were excluded, creating selection bias in a country with 11 official languages.
Reasons for the level of reporting were not collected at retesting, and stable health across the 48-hour interval was assumed rather than verified.
There was a high proportion of non-responders in both age-groups and the reason for declining participation was not recorded.
Because of respondent burden in this young sample only one instrument, the EQ-5D-Y-3L, was investigated, and comparator instruments used recall periods different from the EQ-5D-Y-3L.
Only healthy participants took part in cognitive adaptation interviews, so the study did not test whether sick children understood the concepts differently.
COVID-19 restrictions limited data collection to one time point, so test-retest reliability and responsiveness could not be evaluated.

The study recruited only highly educated healthcare professionals or health-research experts; some participants who were unfamiliar with health utility found preference-elicitation methods technical, and lay public views were not included.
The interviews focused on child health valuation methods, and the potential effects on health policy were discussed only briefly because of time constraints.
The localised sample of 30 UK adults may lack breadth, so data saturation does not ensure that all possible themes were identified.
Paper-based individual exercises conducted in a group setting differ from the one-to-one computer-assisted personal interviews used in many valuation studies.
Perspectives were presented in a fixed order, so order effects cannot be excluded, especially for the quantitative results.

Researcher choices could have shaped themes, including the mental-versus-physical profile framing, no specified age for the other adult, and use of an abbreviated TTO exercise that did not present states worse than dead.
Discussion of child-versus-adult prioritisation did not systematically cover opportunity cost and cost-effectiveness arguments.
Focus groups can produce general discussion rather than a systematic point-by-point comparison of every perspective; think-aloud interviews could provide a different account.

The sample reported more pain or discomfort and worry, sadness, or unhappiness than problems on other EQ-5D-Y-3L dimensions, although the authors noted that this pattern is normal in representative samples.
A single interviewer collected all data, so the interviewer's attitude could have affected the depth and detail of some topics despite self-reflection, peer debriefing, and an audit trail.
The existing analytic framework helped reduce personal influence but might also have framed the analysis.

Data collection during the first wave of the COVID-19 pandemic could have affected participants' quality of life, wellbeing, and theme priorities; video conferencing could also have affected participant-interviewer interaction.
Resource and practical limits prevented coverage of all patient and informal-carer groups in which the generic instruments could be used, including older people receiving social care support.
The sample is not representative of children and adolescents living in Germany, although participants with different sociodemographic characteristics, age groups and educational levels were sought.
The study followed a mainly qualitative approach aimed at identifying suitable and understandable wording, and qualitative approaches never aim at full representativeness.

The psychometric properties of the new EQ-5D-Y-5L, including responsiveness and its comparison with the EQ-5D-Y-3L, were not tested and still have to be examined, also in larger populations and in specific patient groups.
No value set (preference weights) exists for the EQ-5D-Y-5L, so the questionnaire is not yet suitable for all fields of application.

The surveyed cohort was relatively small (N = 2002), so the regression analyses were likely underpowered to detect differences in QALE or life expectancy for participants in outer regional or remote/very remote areas.

To keep sufficient participants per stratum, the primary MAIHDA was limited to age, sex, and SEIFA quintile, omitting race and nonbinary gender; only 4.0% of participants were Indigenous Australians, so including race would not have been informative despite known Indigenous health disparities.
The data were self-reported and cross-sectional, so reporting bias in income, education, and health status is likely and transitions between intersectional strata could not be examined.

Data were collected during the COVID-19 pandemic, when Australian HRQoL was lower than prepandemic, which limits generalizability; the varying jurisdictional public health measures could not be disentangled.

Negative utility values representing states worse than death give negative QALE, which is a mathematical and methodologically controversial challenge when using EQ-5D utilities as a population health indicator.
The secondary MAIHDA with five social dimensions had 38 of 216 strata missing and reduced statistical power.
Because this was a secondary analysis, comparison instruments were limited to the K6.
The pilot UK preference weights were not specific to Australia or New Zealand, were developed to test the weighting method, and provide only indicative index values.
The level sum score assigns equal weight to every item, which is a known limitation.
The secondary dataset did not include detailed caregiving information such as caregiving time, intensity, or primary caregiver status.
High chronic-illness and mobility-problem rates in caregivers could confound known-group differences.
Online panels can over-represent younger, progressive, or survey-engaged people, so sample bias could have inflated the prevalence of informal caregiving and LGBTQIA+ identification.

The equality constrained latent class model assumes preference homogeneity, so respondents who simply place low importance on an attribute may be misclassified as non-attenders, and the estimates may represent an upper bound on attribute non-attendance.
Dimension order effects were not directly tested, so the differential findings for mobility and anxiety/depression cannot be separated from ordering.
Only zero-prior designs from four construction methods were analysed, so results do not cover designs constructed with informative priors or the other methods in the parent survey.
The sample was more highly educated than the overall Australian population.
The FEDEV data were repurposed and were not collected for this analysis; few respondents had serious health problems, and their distribution across the 12 choice blocks was imbalanced.
The interaction model did not necessarily improve goodness of fit over the baseline model.
Matching used age, gender, education, and marital status, but residual confounding can remain, including comorbidity with serious problems in other EQ-5D-5L dimensions.

Self-reported health referred to today, so the analysis could not distinguish acute from long-term problems or identify prior exposure among respondents who reported no current problem; this can underestimate preference effects.
The study covered current personal health experience only and did not assess knowledge gained from past or anticipated illness or from knowing another person with the condition.
The study did not explain why serious anxiety/depression affected pain/discomfort preferences; the authors stated that qualitative research would be needed.
Respondents completed the three versions of the EQ-5D before the paired comparisons, which biases the design downward against the prevalence of preference inversions.
Only English-language EQ-5D labels were tested and no alternative labels or translations were explored, limiting generalizability across translations and English-speaking cultures.
The online sample over-represented White, older, and more highly educated postpartum adults, and vaccination rates were higher than in other national surveys, which limits generalizability.
There was no gold-standard measure of vaccine hesitancy, so criterion validity could not be evaluated.
The retrospective study used self-reported vaccine uptake as an imperfect proxy for acceptance; uptake could not be verified and can also reflect access and awareness.
The survey response rate was not captured.
The cross-sectional design does not support causal inference, and unmeasured confounders can affect socioeconomic position and self-assessed health.
Online-panel recruitment can cause selection bias because internet users can differ from the general population in socioeconomic status and health-reporting patterns.
Subjective income adequacy and EQ VAS can share psychological determinants, such as optimism, which can inflate their association.
EQ VAS can be affected by socioeconomic response styles, and the design cannot distinguish reporting differences from genuine health differences.
The restriction to eight high-income countries limits generalizability to low- and middle-income settings.
Some country-stratified estimates had limited precision, especially for profile 11121.
The analysis used predefined EQ VAS consistency thresholds. Although few cases were excluded, the thresholds can affect within-profile means and estimated gradients.
The study did not collect a broad set of demographic characteristics, including ethnicity, education, and employment, which limited detailed interpretation and formal subgroup analysis.
People with lived experience in the community were not involved in conceptualization, design, implementation, evaluation, or dissemination.
The study was conducted in one district where Nepali was widely spoken, so interpretations may differ in other settings and the guide may need additional adaptation.
The study did not make quantitative comparisons between alternative translations or between the water-glass scale and standard administration.
The sample was too small to evaluate category functioning, threshold ordering, or differential item functioning by gender and age.

The study did not compare recall periods, so it could not determine how today versus longer periods changes outcomes; the authors note that today may underestimate health impacts, especially for variable anxiety and depression symptoms.
The convenience sample was not purposive. Although family and staff roles varied, the study did not provide detailed analysis by proxy relationship, age, or gender.
The study examined proxy reports only and could not compare them with residents’ own assessments.
The interviews and analysis sought problems with EQ-HWB use, which may have produced views that did not give enough weight to positive comments.
The study examined only the EQ-HWB. It did not make head-to-head qualitative or quantitative comparisons with other generic or older-person-specific measures.
The study did not evaluate other psychometric properties of the EQ-HWB in residential aged care, including agreement between self-reported and proxy-reported scores.
Patients and caregivers were not separated during questionnaire completion, so they could have consulted each other despite instructions not to do so.
The very short follow-up did not permit an adequate assessment of responsiveness to improvement.
Responsiveness to chemotherapy initiation was assessed in a very small subgroup.
No EQ-5D-Y-5L value set was available, so a level sum score was used as a proxy for a preference-based index; its measurement properties might not generalize to an index score.
Evidence that validates the proxy version of the Overall Health Assessment is scarce.
Interviewees were mainly from Western countries, especially Switzerland and Germany, so generalization to other countries requires caution.
User interviewees were mostly specialists, and the study did not control for years of professional experience.
The design components were discussed in interviews but were not built into and evaluated as a dashboard in a real-world clinical setting.
The parental questionnaire return rate was low (about 20-28%), although post-hoc analysis found no difference in VAS score or disability between defaulters and other children.

The exact relationship of the adult respondent to the child was not recorded, so female and male respondents were only assumed to be mother and father, and reasons for missing adult responses are unclear.
The regression model fitted the data poorly, explaining only 13% of variance, with 22 participants whose predicted scores were more than two standard deviations from observed scores.
Numbers in Grades 1 and 7 at the special school were small and gender distribution differed between the two school samples.
No Australian EQ-5D-Y-3L value set was available. The primary analysis used Australian adult EQ-5D-3L weights, which can weight dimensions differently and can mask or amplify agreement differences.
Proxy version 2 always followed proxy version 1. An ordering effect or an effort by parents to keep responses consistent cannot be ruled out.
The study did not record whether the participating parent was the primary caregiver.
Fathers were under-represented, and the sample was too small for a parent-sex subgroup analysis.

The community sample was generally healthy. EQ-5D-Y-3L can have limited discrimination in this population and can exaggerate agreement, so the results need confirmation in clinical paediatric samples.
The validity of child self-report responses in this sample requires further investigation.
The use of a limited set of databases and exclusion of non-English studies may have caused relevant articles to be missed.

The small number of head-to-head studies and heterogeneity in convergent-validity measures, known groups, test-retest intervals, and responsiveness criteria prevented selection of the most appropriate generic preference-based measure.
Excluding respondents with inconsistent EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L responses from model estimation could have caused selection bias.
The ordinal logistic models assume proportional odds, but the authors could not test this assumption for their de novo model implementation.
The real-world program-evaluation applications lacked a control arm, which limited comparative research and causal interpretation.
The absence of cohesive and compatible data-capture technology limited data fidelity, storage, export, display, sharing, and analysis.
Short-term program participation and the administrative burden of repeated follow-up made long-term outcome collection difficult.
Implementation and reporting varied across PCNs, and network size and analytical capacity limited standardized comparison and provincial-level use.
The report presented four examples and discussed benefits and challenges broadly; it did not provide an in-depth examination of implementation across all PCNs.
The worse-than-dead part of the composite TTO adds the assumption of additive independence on top of constant proportional trade-off.
Two different elicitation modes are used for better-than-dead and worse-than-dead states within one task.
Sequence effects may affect lead-time TTO outcomes because the 10 years in full health always come first, although comparisons of lead- and lag-time suggest a negligible impact.
The ratio of lead time to disease time censors values for respondents who would trade more than the maximum available time, and further research on modelling these censored values is needed.
Dependence on interviewers might introduce interviewer bias.

Only cost-utility analyses published in English were included; including non-English literature such as Chinese publications was judged technically difficult and resource-demanding, although a parallel review of Chinese-language studies showed similar trends.

The poor reporting quality of the reviewed studies means only a small portion of studies reported health-state utility characteristics, so the findings may not reflect the true status of Asian cost-utility analyses; many cost-utility analyses are also unpublished and may be of lower quality.

The review did not investigate the extent to which literature-derived health-state utilities were used appropriately in the cost-utility analyses, for example whether original values were modified without justification.

The relatively healthy general-population sample came from one country and included few participants with problems in some EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB-9 domains, which limits generalization to patients, caregivers, and social-care users.

Preceding items and ordering could influence VAS responses. The study did not record presentation order in the database, so it could not analyze order effects, and results after the full EQ-HWB form remain unknown.
EQ-HWB-9 and PROPr utilities used nonlocal value sets, which might not represent Hong Kong cultural or regional preferences and could introduce bias.

Traditional Chinese translated health and well-being as physical and mental health because there is no direct equivalent. Although cognitively debriefed, this wording can limit generalization to the United Kingdom English source and other languages.
Non-responders, patients with only preoperative or only 12-month data, and patients with missing values were excluded, although sensitivity analyses gave similar findings.

Socio-economic status was measured with area-based postal-code information, which may not accurately reflect individual socio-economic status, although area-based measures generally underestimate associations.
Hospital-level data were not available, so the role of region, hospital or physician group in the observed inequalities could not be analysed.
The LROI does not collect ethnicity, an important determinant of health inequality that may be associated with the observed socio-economic differences.

EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L data came from different time periods and different patients, so changes in practice, patient characteristics, or other time-varying factors could affect the comparison; within-person completion of both versions would have been preferable.

Retrospective registry data limited control over registration and may overestimate complete response rates if nonresponses were not recorded; information was also limited for language skills, assistance, comorbidities, support, and prior disease experience.
Known-groups analyses used different scoring products for EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L, which added methodological variation, although the 5L crosswalk was based on the 3L value set.

Generalizability is limited because the sample mainly included people with unilateral dysvascular amputation who had entered prosthetic rehabilitation, and not all SwedeAmp patients had an EQ-5D follow-up; the findings may not apply to bilateral amputations or less healthy groups.
The sample was smaller than many comparator population studies, which had 2000–4000 respondents.

Advance knowledge that the interview would take more than one hour could have selected participants who were healthier or more positive about their health than nonparticipants or people who were not invited.
People with higher education were slightly overrepresented relative to the Danish general population.
The COVID-19 pandemic reduced recruitment and delayed data collection.
There were not enough data to estimate the extent or cost of deprescribing for either profession, so deprescribing was not included in the model.
The small waiting-time sample did not support reliable estimates, so waiting time was excluded from the model.
The heterogeneous patient sample covered two professions and different health conditions. The analysis could therefore use only a generic QALY outcome and not condition-specific health outcomes.
Prior studies used different outcomes, cost ranges, comparators, conditions, professions, and settings. This limited generalizability and comparison with this study.
Doctor perceived-ease-of-use and perceived-usefulness results could be biased because 665 patients were not equally allocated among the 49 doctors.
Patients who were more annoyed by repeated assessments may have been less likely to agree to a qualitative interview.
The study did not assess the feasibility of training existing clinical staff to introduce and administer the assessment in real practice.
Findings from Chinese patients with knee or back problems may not generalize to non-Chinese populations or to patients with other musculoskeletal problems.
The HSE sampling frame excluded institutionalized people, including hospital patients and people in retirement homes, and excluded people who were unhoused.
The latest EQ-5D-3L data were already more than ten years old, while more recent HSE waves used EQ-5D-5L.
Changes to local government boundaries made some geographical areas not strictly comparable over time.

In 2011, health and lifestyle attitude questions appeared before EQ-5D-3L, unlike previous waves; the authors note that this order change could have influenced responses but could not explain the earlier trend.

Changes in HSE questionnaires caused discontinuity in individual and household variables across years; socioeconomic class was not collected from 2010 onward, and the deprivation index was absent in 1996.
EQ VAS was available only for 2010-2012 and 2014, which restricted conclusions about its temporal variation.
Sampling weights were available only from 2003 onward.
MEDLINE and PubMed had no established MeSH terms for gender inclusiveness, so the search probably missed some eligible articles.

Although the search allowed articles in three languages in addition to English, all included articles were in English; the review therefore could not explore the complexities of inclusive wording in other languages or language families.
Most data were self-reported, so recall bias was possible.
Only a small number of countries had both published EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L value sets, which limits the reliability of cross-country and instrument comparisons.
The authors adapted criteria developed for EQ-5D-5L to identify EQ-5D-Y-3L aggregate preference patterns, which reduced comparability with the earlier Olsen et al. study.
EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-5L have different descriptive systems, dimension wording, and severity labels, so differences in values cannot be attributed only to child versus adult preferences.
Dimension importance was ranked only with coefficients for the worst level of each dimension, which may not represent the importance of the full dimension.
The sample of 26 participants did not cover all health conditions, minority ethnic groups, or all intended populations.
Saturation was not formally assessed during data collection.
Verbal probing can cause participants to overthink items and can create order effects in which probing about earlier items affects later responses.
Recruitment through an online research panel produced a sample with high educational attainment and limited generalizability.
Instrument developers helped to verify coding and interpret findings, which is a potential source of bias.
Time limits meant that comprehensiveness was discussed in only 11 interviews and that the protocol was amended after four interviews to remove completion of the EQ-HWB-9.
Online panel-based non-probability sampling may have introduced selection bias and limited participation to people with internet access and digital literacy who were willing to take health surveys.
People with the most severe health impairment were underrepresented, which limited evaluation across the full range of severity.
The EQ-5D-5L and bolt-ons were given in a fixed order, which could have caused context or order effects.
Most bolt-on translations used forward translation without cognitive debriefing; only the Dutch self-confidence item had forward-backward translation and cognitive debriefing.
The cognition/memory wording differed between countries and could have reduced conceptual equivalence and cross-country comparability.
The cross-sectional design did not permit evaluation of test-retest reliability or responsiveness.
Some chronic-condition subgroups were small, which produced wide confidence intervals.
The study could not disentangle cultural, linguistic, methodological, and epidemiological explanations for country differences.
Web-based surveys can exclude people with poor or no internet access and can therefore bias the samples.
Use of online research panels can introduce additional population-representativeness bias.
Cultural differences in how measures are interpreted and function can reduce comparability between countries.
A single cross-sectional data-collection period limits the questions that can be addressed and does not show population-health change over time or instrument reliability.
Candidate-item selection depended on prior reviews and qualitative studies and may have inherited limitations from those sources.

All non-expert respondents were recruited in Shanghai, which limited regional diversity and the ability to observe regional influences on HRQoL perceptions, although some were migrants and experts came from different regions.
Translation of the candidate dimension wording from Mandarin into English may have caused semantic changes and may limit generalizability.

The sample was not fully representative of the French general population: women were overrepresented, respondents aged 25-34 and 55-74 years were in excess and women aged 75 years and over were in deficit, despite an extra quota of 20 older women, because acceptance of interviews was lower in that age group.

Geographical distribution was not a stratification criterion, and Paris and its adjacent departments plus residential units above 100,000 inhabitants were overrepresented, while units of 2,000-100,000 inhabitants were underrepresented.
Comparison between the 3L and 5L value sets is limited by different wording of dimension levels between the two versions.
Three coefficients remained non-significant in the preferred hybrid models (level 3 terms for mobility, self-care and usual activities).

The sample mostly comprised relatively healthy children, with only 7.5% having a Cobb angle above 40 degrees and up to 71.3% under observation only, which may affect generalizability, although the authors argue this reflects the general AIS population.
Patients were aged 10 to 18 years by the AIS definition while the EQ-5D-3L-Y is designed for ages 8 to 15 years; 12.6% of patients were above the upper age limit.
The lack of a child-specific value set for the EQ-5D-3L-Y made it impossible to compare patient-proxy agreement in a utility measure needed for quality-adjusted life years.
Without test-retest data the results cannot be generalized to agreement over time or to agreement in the magnitude of change in HRQoL after treatment.
The cTTO comparator data came from a different study that used different interviewers and a different number and set structure of valued health states.
All interviewers completed CGTTO interviews before LTTO interviews, which could have caused an ordering effect.
Only 10 health states were valued, so the study could not examine method effects on individual EQ-5D dimensions.
Because TTO values for EQ-5D-Y-3L can differ by culture, especially between Asian and non-Asian countries, the findings may not generalize to other populations.

Construct validity and responsiveness were judged against hypotheses defined by the included studies rather than hypotheses specified a priori by the review team, which reduced comparability across studies.
Substantial heterogeneity in populations, settings, administration modes, study designs, follow-up periods, and comparator measures prevented pooled quantitative analysis.
The eligibility criteria excluded studies that supplied only indirect psychometric evidence without an explicit measurement-property focus.
The search may have missed work in progress presented at conferences other than the EuroQol proceedings.
Age-group analyses used study-level mean age, which can misclassify samples; studies without a reported mean age were excluded from those analyses.
Restriction to English-language publications may have contributed to the predominance of Western studies and the limited evidence from low- and middle-income countries.

Participants received the decision aid after their surgical screening appointment rather than before it, as intended for routine implementation; this timing could have affected their experience and feedback.

Participants came from only one of Alberta's 12 surgical clinics, which raises a concern about generalizability even though the authors considered the clinic demographics similar to those elsewhere in the province.
The sample was English-speaking and computer literate, so the findings might not apply to non-English-speaking or less technologically proficient patients.
The accuracy of the post COVID-19 condition group cannot be guaranteed because the questionnaire was self-reported and "probable" COVID-19 infections were included.

Chronic conditions were self-reported, included an open "other" option, were not verified by health practitioners, and were diverse and subjective, which challenges generalisability to the post COVID-19 condition population.

The authors did not test for differences between the post COVID-19 condition and chronic condition(s) groups in the number and types of chronic conditions or other influencing indicators, so the attribution of worse outcomes to post COVID-19 condition rather than comorbidity is cautious.
Respondents lost to follow-up at T2 were significantly younger and more often reported chronic conditions, which may have caused higher attrition of persons with post COVID-19 condition.

The T1 COVID-19 questions differed from the improved T2 questions because of limited knowledge and testing capacity in 2020, so no exclusive post COVID-19 condition group existed at T1, the non-response analysis could not be applied to disease status, and comparison of disease-status classification is less accurate.
Very low negative utilities, especially for severe states, lacked face validity and can reflect task misunderstanding; methods without censoring need careful procedures for extreme values.
Low values for mild and moderate states in arms B and C also lacked face validity and may reflect erratic respondent behavior.
Modified tasks used nonconstant health profiles, were cognitively more demanding, and produced more inconsistencies.
Arm C had very coarse response granularity and reached very negative values in few steps.
The convenience sample was young, educated, and not representative of the general population; modified arms can be more difficult in less educated samples.
The online format can have contributed to task difficulty.
The sample was largely surveyed in the Netherlands, nationality was not collected, and Dutch samples can trade more than other samples.
The experiment focused on mild and severe health states, so evidence for performance in the middle of the scale was limited.
The project was not designed to compare tele-TTO with personal TTO; it aimed to replicate and extend earlier work, so the comparison is post hoc.
The data types were fixed before the switch to tele-TTO, so no information was collected on sign-ups, response rates, cancellations or respondents’ interview experiences.
Evidence on the interview process rests only on the single interviewer’s subjective recollection of events, with no records kept of dropped video connections.

Mode of administration was not assigned randomly; tele-TTO interviews were conducted later in time, so the developing COVID-19 crisis, growing interviewer experience and growing respondent familiarity with videotelephony may confound the comparison.
No measures were taken to control for selection effects between the two modes of administration.
No UAE-specific English EQ-5D-5L version was available, so the United Kingdom English version was used; this could influence direct responses and introduces a possible language effect.
The requirement that expatriates had lived in the UAE for at least 5 years was not supported by conclusive evidence, so its sufficiency for local preference formation remains uncertain.
Sixty-eight percent of participants contributed repeated observations, so the base-case data contained within-person dependencies that limit generalizability.
EQ-5D-3L was always administered before EQ-5D-5L, so order effects could have affected level use and missing responses; the authors recommend randomized administration order in future studies.
The study did not assess important measurement properties such as responsiveness and reliability.
The sample was small for a validation study, which limits generalizability and especially affects comparisons between cognitive-severity groups.
Censoring of data at -1 is inherent to the cTTO task, so observed values cannot express preferences below the design floor.

The study used EQ-VT version 1.0 in the first wave, before improvements such as warm-up questions, confirmation pop-ups and feedback on inconsistencies were introduced; clustering of values and inconsistent responses were observed.
Interviewers could differ in engagement and ability to support respondents in performing the task well.
The design and sample size were optimised for main effects only, so no interaction terms capturing diminishing marginal utility could be estimated.
The sample under-represented respondents aged 80 to 90, lower educated respondents in the aggregated categories, and inhabitants of Noord-Holland province.
Additional research is required to assess the responsiveness over time and the discriminative properties of the Dutch tariff in patient samples.
Choice-based models produce only relative values on an undefined scale, without meaningful anchors such as dead and full health.
Interaction terms were not modelled because the design was generated for main effects only, although other studies suggest moderate interaction effects exist.
Older individuals and people with low education were under-represented, limiting generalizability.
The paired comparisons did not specify duration, so respondents may have imposed their own diverse assumptions about the duration of the states, potentially biasing values.
Level labels in the Dutch and French versions may not correspond exactly to the English version, so observed country differences may reflect translation rather than preference differences.
A programming error meant block 11 of pairs was not assessed in The Netherlands, and country sample sizes were modest.

Pilot and actual samples differed in background characteristics: pilot participants were more often highly educated, employed, urban, and located in Cairo, and the effect of these differences on the results was unclear.
The small purposive sample of 14 stakeholders might not capture the full range of views among interested parties or the general public.
The selection did not account for geographic or regional differences in the United States.
Participants had experience beyond their stated roles, so some expertise and perspectives were probably overrepresented despite an intended balance.

The study did not use a consensus method such as Delphi or a more structured qualitative analysis; these methods could have prioritized decisions or identified additional themes but would need more resources.
The prompts focused on QALY estimation and cost-effectiveness analysis and did not explicitly consider other EQ-5D-Y-3L uses, such as profile scores.

Participants had different baseline knowledge, and pre-meeting materials plus a 30-minute introduction did not prevent misconceptions; more education could improve understanding but would increase burden and might influence views.

The EQ-5D-5L was explored in greater thematic depth than the EQ-5D-Y-3L. Children and adolescents provided fewer details, which reduced evidence density and could weaken conclusions for the youth instrument.
Web-based interviews were the only data-collection mode. People unfamiliar with this mode might have been excluded, which could cause selection bias.
Adult participants were 18-32 years old, so the study did not include the views of older adults with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. This limits generalisability.
Both valuation methods used the perspective of a 10-year-old child, so it is uncertain whether the preferences represent the full EQ-5D-Y-3L target age range of 8-15 years.
Preference data were collected during the COVID-19 pandemic. The effect of pandemic conditions on preferences and their post-pandemic stability is unknown.
The cTTO task used only one block of 10 health states, which limited the available modelling options.

The online DCE survey may have selection bias because participation required internet access and digital literacy. The exclusion of 255 respondents for speeding or inconsistent dominant-pair responses may also have been too strict for fast decision makers or people making random errors.
The DCE and cTTO samples used different recruitment and incentive strategies despite generally similar sociodemographic characteristics.

Perspective comparisons also differed by country because value sets with both perspectives were not available within one country, so the effects of perspective and country could not be separated fully.
The value sets were developed at different times, from UK data collected in 1993 through Swedish and German data from the late 2000s and early 2010s.
The Swedish and German VAS value sets were not anchored on dead in their development and were therefore not rescaled in this analysis.
The pandemic caused interviewer turnover and changes from face-to-face to distanced and online interviews, although the analyses found no clear interviewer or administration-mode effect.
The COVID-19 pandemic could itself have changed how people valued health, and the study could not separate all pandemic effects from the collected EQ-VT data.

The analyzed sample of 775 was below the EuroQol recommendation of at least 1,000 because the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted recruitment; the smaller sample reduced statistical power and could contribute to nonsignificant coefficients.
Direct comparison with the Swedish experience-based value set was restricted because the hypothetical and experience-based values came from different valuation tasks and methods.
The 5L blocks were balanced for health state severity but the 3L blocks were not necessarily balanced.
Each respondent valued only three 3L health states, giving few observations underpinning the 3L value set.
The 5L tasks were always completed before the 3L tasks rather than randomised, so order or learning effects may have influenced the 3L values.
Interviewers did not explicitly orient respondents to the 3L descriptive system before the 3L tasks.
Findings concern descriptive system differences under a common protocol and should not be generalised to existing published value sets.
A broader combined measure can still omit relevant quality-of-life constructs and can have limited applicability to some populations or interventions.
Overlap between source instruments can cause double counting or redundant dimensions, while removing dimensions changes the original instruments and can prevent use of their original value sets.
Many dimensions, different item formats and response scales, and mixed positive and negative wording can make the combined descriptive system difficult to value and increase respondent burden.
Changes that simplify dimension wording must preserve the original meaning and require discussion and approval under the source developers' intellectual-property and adaptation policies.
Participants were recruited by nonrandom quota sampling from a few preselected geographic areas rather than by rigorous random sampling.
Adults may have found it difficult to imagine the effect of health problems on a hypothetical 10-year-old child, adding complexity to the cTTO task.
The results depend on a specific set of priors derived from a single data set that was itself collected with a design not optimized for any of the included discount functions.

The prior data set had more than 500 respondents and hence produced relatively precise conditional logit estimates, so a sensitivity analysis with substantially inflated prior standard errors was needed (and gave closely corresponding results).
The design optimization relies on informative priors for severity stratification, health-state selection, and duration values, so the software is not intended for use with uninformative priors.
The 5L was always administered first, so an order effect may be present; this could account for the slightly higher proportion of missing values for the 3L.
The study was mainly conducted in patient population settings, so sampling weights could not be calculated and applied.
Not all measurement properties were tested; reliability for language versions other than Korean and responsiveness to health change were not assessed.
The study sampled the general population only and did not include patient samples, so content potentially specific to patient groups was not explored.

Face-to-face interviews were the sole data collection method; health can be a sensitive topic for some Asians in one-to-one conversation, and combining in-depth interviews with focus groups might have elicited more, for example sexual function, which was raised in an earlier Singapore study but not here.
Because of manpower constraints, Malay and Indian participants who did not speak English were excluded, so views of older Malay and Indian people with lower education were not represented.
Only participants aged 40 years and above were invited, so health concepts important to younger people may have been missed.
Participants were recruited by convenience and snowball sampling from selected residential areas, which limits representativeness.
No formal experimental design guided the selection of health states, so a utility function could not be generated and power to detect adult-adolescent differences was limited.
Scenarios mostly involved health states with at least one extreme dimension, which may have made the switch easier to detect and lowered the observed choice-blindness rate.
Interviewer status was not held constant because peer or near-peer interviewers were used, so results may be confounded by interviewer effects.

The reduced three-dimension descriptive system based on the EQ-5D omits usual activities and self-care, so findings do not generalise to the full EQ-5D classifier, and certain personality traits may relate to omitted dimensions.

The sample was small, drawn from a single US city, and included few older adults, limiting generalisability and precluding conclusions about older people with cognitive decline or adults with intellectual disabilities.
IQ and education level were not examined and could be considered alongside personality in future studies.
The analysis estimates population-level associations rather than individual risks and includes only patients hospitalized with COVID-19.

Withholding hospitalization or life-sustaining treatment from frail patients, including those with severe heart failure, could have overestimated associations; more intensive treatment of younger patients could have underestimated them.
The low prevalence of heart disease among patients younger than 65 years limited power for age-specific conclusions.

Selection into critical care differed by age, comorbidity, resources, patient preference, and cultural clinical decision-making, so associations with critical care admission could not be assessed reliably.
The study assessed only in-hospital mortality and did not include deaths in community or nursing-home settings.
Neither registry used central adjudication of events.
Echocardiographic data on baseline heart-failure aetiology and systolic or diastolic dysfunction were not available.
Caregivers used only the proxy-proxy perspective; discrepancies may be smaller for a proxy-person perspective, and a direct comparison of the two proxy perspectives was not available.
EQ-5D-5L uses a today recall period, but dementia-related health can vary from day to day and respondents may have referred to different periods despite simultaneous assessment.
EQ-5D-5L does not cover dementia-specific features such as cognitive functioning, and its broad dimensions can be understood differently by people with dementia and caregivers.
The authors state that EQ-5D can be less responsive to health changes, which can bias conclusions in intervention studies and requires critical interpretation.
Recruitment of the large hospital sample during the COVID-19 pandemic may be difficult because planned face-to-face recruitment can be disrupted.
The survey will obtain minimal child-level clinical information, so instrument performance cannot be assessed by factors such as disease severity.
Responsiveness analysis depends on recruiting enough children whose health changes, but the number who will change during follow-up is unknown.
There is no single gold standard for self-reported health-status change, and it is unknown whether the planned change questions will adequately identify change.
The number and condition balance of children recruited through the hospital are unknown despite strategies to target more seriously ill children.
One follow-up period cannot be optimal for every condition: a short period can limit observable change, a long period can reduce completion, and actual completion times will vary.
No accepted general method exists for psychometric-study sample-size calculation, and specific calculations were not completed for item response theory, factor analysis, or each subgroup analysis.
No external sample was available for external validation.
The sample was likely too small for the adjusted limited dependent variable mixture model.
Few participants reported a lot of problems in the EQ-5D-Y-3L mobility domain, which limited representation of severe health states.
Sample size precluded subgroup analyses by age, condition, or report type, and application to samples with different characteristics can produce mismatched estimates.
The study mainly considered additive predictor functional forms; other functional forms could perform differently.
Interviewer administration, chosen because patients had major vision problems, could be associated with more positive outcomes and lower responsiveness, although it applied equally to all measures.

SF-6D and HUI3 were collected using their short descriptive systems rather than the recommended SF-36 and HUI questionnaires, and the SF-6D descriptive system is likely to generate less responsive utilities than the full SF-36.

Generalizability may be limited by the study sample and location: the sample reported much better health than US cataract patients, possibly because Asians underreport health problems and because of family care in Singapore, and cataract surgery in Singapore is usually performed when the cataract is mature.

The series of two-way repeated measures ANOVAs comparing change between pairs of utility measures was not sufficiently powered and was not adjusted for multiplicity, so those results should be interpreted with caution.
The data sets were mostly from developed Western countries and did not represent all diseases, so EQ-5D items may be interrelated differently in other populations.

Many data sets came from country-specific valuation studies whose respondents were relatively healthy, giving less variation in health states; modelling on this narrow health range may not fully inform the structure for the broad range of EQ-5D-5L applications.
Internal MIMIC models cannot themselves generate usable scoring weights; they only clarify the internal structure, which must then be harnessed with other structural equation modelling methods.
Only the MIC data set could support the full range of external MIMIC specifications, so models 2a-2 and 2b-2 could not be fitted elsewhere.
Relatively healthier valuation samples sometimes had no endorsements of level 4 or level 5 on EQ-5D-5L dimensions.
The recommendations are based on the informed perspectives of a single research team, are not definitive, and should be treated as a starting point for further debate and iterative refinement.
The set of recommendations is not exhaustive; other issues such as equity concerns and cross-cultural adaptation are also likely to be important.

The focus is on single questionnaire-based assessments, whereas comprehensive assessment of infant and toddler HRQoL may require a multimethod approach combining caregiver reports, direct observation and interviews.
Randomization was not feasible. The groups differed at baseline in comorbidity, dependency, caregiver support, and caregiver burden, which created selection bias despite multivariable adjustment.
Comparison of two care models at different primary-care centres could produce an unavoidable Hawthorne effect.

The recruited sample was small and the intermediate analysis had low statistical power. Recruitment was limited by the small home-care population, severe frailty, advanced illness, refusal, and mortality.
First-year losses were high, at 42.6% in the functional-model group and 22.4% in the integrated-model group, because of transfers and deaths.
Both centres were in densely populated urban areas, so the authors questioned whether the findings would apply to suburban or rural settings.

The general population quota sample was recruited from an online panel and may be subject to selection bias, because digital literacy and internet access are required for panel registration; random sampling and paper-based questionnaires are recommended for future studies.
Data on severity within condition groups were not available, so the study could not assess how well the two measures discriminate across severity groups.
Data collection took place during the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, which might have affected health status and consequently the measurement properties of the instruments.
The order of the three health status measures within the survey was not randomized, which might have affected responses.
The community-recruited and PureProfile samples could differ, although recruitment source was not significant in the regression models.
A larger sample would have been preferable in this difficult-to-recruit population, although the analyzed sample exceeded the stated minimum for this type of analysis.
Approximately 300 bot responses arrived during one night and were removed; the researchers then added more data-quality controls.
The United Kingdom-specific EQ-HWB-S value set may not represent Australian population preferences.
The missing responses for EQ-HWB item 22 indicate that unclear item layout can cause respondents to skip a question.
The study does not evaluate other caregiver populations or responsiveness to change over time, for which evidence remains limited.

The group had to remain small so that all participants could contribute, and scheduling allowed only two online workshops with all stakeholder groups; much feedback was obtained individually and could differ from group feedback.
Some participants were unfamiliar with the online technology, which could have limited engagement with creative activities.
Power imbalance between patients, caregivers, and service providers remained possible despite steps to reduce it.
Participating service providers could have been early adopters who were more open to clinical paediatric PROM use.
The study did not include non-English-speaking participants.
The generalisability of the design to other age groups, clinical settings, and geographic contexts is unknown.
No gold standard for health state valuation exists, so some protocol design decisions, such as the fixed 10-year time horizon, were not based on empirical evidence.
The authors are not aware of any empirical research comparing the relative merits of the Paris and MVH protocols.
The protocols cover only TTO data collection and exclude sampling frames, experimental design for health state selection and modelling of the collected data.

Both conventional and composite TTO can be criticized for eliciting better-than-death and worse-than-death values through different procedures, and the available methods for handling worse-than-death values have limited theoretical underpinning.

The source valuation data used purposive, non-probability convenience quota sampling. The authors stated that this design can introduce bias and limit generalizability, although quotas were used to approximate the population distribution.

The EQ-5D-5L outcome had many observations at 1, which the authors stated made beta regression perform poorly; they therefore preferred censored Tobit models and used beta regression only for robustness checks.
The samples in the national value sets were not entirely representative of their corresponding general populations.
Some national value sets were old, so changes in population structure may limit how well they represent current preferences.

Societal, demographic, linguistic, methodological, modelling, and data-quality differences across national studies may have affected the pooled valuations; some source value sets contain questionable values or inconsistencies.
The study did not test more advanced finite-mixture specifications; the population-weighted finite-mixture model did not converge, and further model research is needed.

Question types I to V used partial corner-state descriptions rather than whole EQ-5D-5L states, so respondents may have filled in the unstated dimensions with their own assumptions, which limits the sensitivity and wider applicability of the findings and affects the assumed values used in the time preference analysis.

The V values used (0.8 and 0.9 for mild states, 0.4 and 0.6 for severe states) appear to have been set too low, since the great majority of respondents chose the full-health option, and only a small range of V values could be used.
Respondents in stages 1 to 3 were limited to those aged under 65 years, a restriction arising from the online panel and carried over to the interview stages.

The design of the stage 1 binary-choice questions was not the most efficient: collinearities reduced the number of comparable scenario combinations, and the wording of the satisfaction levels and their combination with health states was potentially problematic.
Minimum completion times of 5 minutes for PRET and 3 minutes for PRET-AS were chosen fairly arbitrarily after piloting, and the effect of using shorter cut-offs could not be assessed.
Because of limited funds and time, stages 3 and 4 covered a narrower range of topics than the earlier stages.

The stage 4 think-aloud study used a convenience sample of non-academic university staff who were younger, better educated, more female and healthier than the general population, so additional themes might emerge from a wider sample.

Think-aloud methods may not fully replicate the thought processes respondents use, respondents may not verbalise everything, and follow-up questions are limited to what respondents can and will recall and report.
Only 18 of the 120 DCE-with-duration pairs had differing durations, so the duration coefficient, by which all attribute coefficients are divided, had a comparatively wide confidence interval.
EQ-5D state 11111 was assumed equivalent to full health, so upper-end censoring was not addressed, and duration was treated as continuous rather than categorical.

The binary-choice lead-time TTO design used only five whole EQ-5D-3L states, so individual dimensions and levels could not be modelled, and the analysis assumed zero time preference and a logistic cumulative distribution despite the asymmetric density of valuation data.

The time preference analysis is at group rather than individual level and required assuming that respondents facing a given choice had a median health-state value equal to the corresponding PRET-AS DCETTO value, so apparent differences between states could reflect that assumption.
The response rate for the CAPI arm is unknown because the survey company did not record it, and characteristics of non-responders in face-to-face interviews are typically unavailable.
Even with quota screening, the online and CAPI samples may differ in unobserved characteristics arising from the different selection mechanisms, and results may vary across internet panels.

The stage 3 follow-up probing questions were multiple choice and designed by the research team, so important factors may not have been captured and the reasons behind responses could not be explored in depth during the interview.
No gold standard was available, so construct validity had to be assessed with indirect methods.
EQ-HWB-9 items were embedded in the full EQ-HWB and were not administered as a stand-alone measure.
Although the total sample was large, condition-specific subgroup samples limited analysis and prevented comparison of standardized response means by condition.
The study used crude known-group definitions instead of clinical severity measures because only these measures were feasible to collect.
Online data collection required an answer to every question, so the study could not assess missing responses, feasibility, or acceptability.
Participants received no study intervention, and stability for the reliability analysis was self-reported and could not be verified.

The block design produced different recruitment-source and special-healthcare-needs mixes across adapted and original instrument samples; subsampling by special healthcare needs reduced but did not remove this concern.
The newly developed adapted instrument still needs evaluation in other countries, settings, samples, and disease groups.
Level sum scores weight dimensions equally and collapse different health profiles to the same score; profile ordering by level sum score can also differ from utility ordering.
Proxy reporting can be biased for unobservable aspects of young children's HRQoL, and parent-child agreement cannot be assessed plausibly in this very young age group.

Some condition-specific known-group analyses and especially the worse-health responsiveness analyses had small samples, so those results require caution and adapted-versus-original responsiveness could not be formally compared.

No EQ-5D-Y-5L or adapted-version value sets were available. Applying the Netherlands original EQ-5D-Y-3L value set to the adapted instrument assumes that wording changes and the younger target age do not change preferences.
The authors state that very little evidence shows which factors adults consider when they value health states in very young children.
Evidence about differences between parents' and non-parents' preferences for health states in children aged 0 to 3 years is limited.
It is unclear whether instructions can make all respondents exclude caregiver spillovers and future developmental consequences from child health-state valuations.
A proposed EQ-TIPS crosswalk would depend on the untested assumption that EQ-5D-Y values elicited for an older child are relevant to infant and toddler health states.
The study relied on conveniently available EQ-5D data and dialysis models, which limits generalizability of the findings.
Only one type of EQ-5D data was collected and the other was generated by crosswalk, which is bound to suffer from bias, so the impact of switching from 3L to 5L cannot be assessed accurately.
Data collection was online and unsupervised. Interviewer support might have prevented some data-quality problems, especially for the complex frame F task.
The study did not include a lag-time TTO frame despite its possible advantages, including for youth instrument valuation.

The proportion of worse-than-dead classifications was unexpectedly high. Prolific users may differ from the general population, or repeated exposure to severe states and immediate-death comparisons may have influenced responses.

The think aloud technique depends on the participant being able to articulate thoughts, and one interview was stopped after the EQ VAS assessment because the participant seemed uncomfortable thinking aloud.
All participants had a moderate to high level of education, although the sample was otherwise relatively diverse.

The broad age inclusion criterion of 18-70 years led to additional sampling, and the upper age limit was not respected in one interview, which was still included because the limit had no theoretical justification.

Most participants reported no or slight problems on the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system although 13 stated other health problems, and no other health measure was available, so it is uncertain whether they were in good health, had adapted, or had problems not captured by the instrument; health status was not part of the assessment of information power.

The fixed sequence of the assessments, the introductory questions about diabetes, and possible change in the ability to think aloud during the interview may have influenced the responses; participants typically compared the assessments towards the end of the interview, which was handled by a common analysis.

Transferability is limited: the findings apply mainly to populations with chronic conditions controlled by treatment and self-management and to health systems similar to Sweden, and the EQ VAS and TTO findings apply mainly to similar designs, such as the same end-point labelling and an open-ended TTO procedure; replication in other patient groups is needed.
Further research is needed to examine whether thought processes differ by severity of the currently experienced health state or by the expected progression of the disease.
