The EQ-5D-Y was adapted from an existing adult instrument rather than developed from an in-depth examination of children's and adolescents' own conceptualization of health-related quality of life, so relevant aspects may be missing.
Testing was conducted predominantly in healthy samples, which gives only limited information; population-based and clinical subgroups still need study.
The psychometric properties of the new version were not assessed in this paper and are reported elsewhere.

In Spain the two versions were given in a fixed order within one battery, so smaller differences in VAS missing values may reflect an ordering effect, and VAS scoring rules differed between countries.
Sample sizes could not be standardized between countries because resources and local situations differed.
DTA was measured after filler questionnaires and after the wheelchair TTO or EQ VAS task, but before the self-experienced-health TTO or EQ VAS task, so timing could affect the associations.
The conscious and unconscious defense measures did not show the required condition differences and were excluded from further analyses.
The study was online and had no interviewers, did not use severe hypothetical health states, and did not directly compare health states with dead.
The exploratory commercial-panel sample was not selected to represent Dutch adults and was older and differently distributed by education than the Dutch population.
The marketing bureau did not provide the number of respondents who dropped out.
Different data-collection modes across National Quality Registers could cause differences in reported HRQoL.
Comorbidities among patients and morbidities in the general population could affect comparisons, and the study did not fully address this issue.
The main analysis included only patients with complete baseline and 1-year follow-up data and excluded nonrespondents and incomplete records, which could introduce selection bias.
Fracture baseline EQ-5D-3L data were recalled after the fracture for the week before injury, so change in fracture patients is not directly comparable with change in other groups.
Nonresponder analyses found statistically significant, although small, age and sex differences between follow-up respondents and nonrespondents in many registers.
The attribution to COVID-19 depends on an observational assumption; matching controlled only observed characteristics and could not remove unmeasured differences.
The surveys differed in recruitment strategy, season of data collection, and stated purpose.
Only 2018 respondents completed ten DCE tasks before the VAS ratings, so greater familiarity or cross-task effects could explain part of the difference and the lower illogical-response rate.
Health preferences might have changed during the two-year interval for reasons independent of COVID-19.
VAS is not the method most commonly used for general-population value sets, and the results do not establish equivalent effects for TTO, standard gamble, or DCE values.
The study valued only states 11111 and 55555, and only 55555 was analyzed on the full health = 1, dead = 0 scale, so effects on common milder states are unknown.
The study could not identify which pandemic experiences caused the valuation differences, and it could not determine whether any effect was transient or permanent.
Post-operative data were limited to the 6-month time point, so longer-term quality-of-life impacts could not be determined.
The analysis did not examine utility scores by patient characteristics other than sex, such as age or disease severity.
Generalisability beyond the joint replacement population is uncertain, especially where changes in EQ-5D-5L responses concentrate in dimensions other than mobility and pain/discomfort.
Variability in reported pain and itching was relatively low, with few patients reporting severe symptoms, probably because of the long-term follow-up, which limits scrutiny of scale correspondence.

The two instruments differ in instruction: the EQ-5D-5L asks about health today and the whole person, while the POSAS asks about the past weeks and the patient's worst scar, so answers may differ for that reason.
Burn scars cause other problems measured by the POSAS, such as pliability and thickness, which might also be detected by the EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort domain but were beyond the scope of this study.
Non-response analysis showed responders were more often female and older than non-responders.
Findings may not generalise to other contexts because Ireland remains comparatively religiously homogeneous and the meaning of euthanasia varies between contexts.
The analysis is based on only 160 individuals with both TTO and attitudinal data, a relatively small sample.

Only a limited number of attitudinal variables were controlled for; factors such as experience of bereavement, caring for the dying, empathy and egotism were unobserved, and the source of the unobserved heterogeneity could not be identified.

Willingness to trade time is only the mechanism used to estimate utility, so respondents unwilling to give worse-than-dead values may still regard a state as equally undesirable; this is a limitation of the TTO method.

Data-quality exclusions could bias the sample toward younger, digitally literate participants and further limit generalizability.
The qualitative interpretive design does not provide final conclusive evidence or causal relationships. Findings show what is possible for some participants and can transfer only to similar contexts.

The cross-sectional data do not support causal inference about relationships between health conditions and pain or discomfort experiences.
Health conditions were self-reported. Participants could be unaware of diagnoses or could unintentionally misreport them.
The findings require replication before they can be generalized to different cultural and linguistic contexts.
This was a pilot study with a small sample size, so the model estimates were purely exploratory and should not be used for other purposes.
The majority of respondents were university employees who may have a higher level of cognitive functioning than the general population.
Computational burden meant not all random effects could be considered, and power was insufficient to examine interaction effects, so only main effects were modelled.
Each respondent valued two related descriptive systems in a fixed sequence. This design could bias values for the second system.
The sample consisted of young, well-educated university students. Results might not generalize to the general population.
The study tested only self-care added to EQ-4D and vision added to EQ-5D-5L. Results might not generalize to other bolt-on dimensions.
Random intercepts gave a simple treatment of respondent heterogeneity. The analysis framework could not estimate more complex random effects, such as severity-specific random slopes.

Mean age in the NHS PROMs data had to be imputed from ten-year age intervals using the corresponding intervals in the Health Survey for England.
Only 10 health states from a single block were used, which could limit generalisability of the results.
Ranking position data for the ranking without sorting arm were lost because of technical problems, so ranking-based inconsistency analysis was possible only in the ranking and sorting arm.
The study lacked a qualitative component; the authors state future studies should add one to better understand the results.
Qualitative findings must not be assumed to represent the full range of US respondent interpretations.

The study could not establish how well people with less formal education, lower literacy, or English as a second language would understand the items.
The study did not purposively sample specific patient groups, so it could not identify unique or divergent interpretations across disease states.
Most participants met more than one patient, caregiver, or social care user category, so findings specific to one respondent group could not be separated readily.
The data set had no additional established HRQoL instrument with a comparable construct, which limited comparison and generalizability.
Annual measurement intervals may have missed variation in patients' HRQoL.
The test-retest analysis used a small clinically stable subgroup and therefore requires cautious interpretation.
Combining SCA 1, 2, and 3 into one group could affect interpretation.
Use of EQ-5D-3L instead of the increasingly used EQ-5D-5L risked reduced sensitivity and restricted interpretation of the measurement properties.
Validity analyses that included all time points could have within-subject effects because participants contributed different numbers of observations.
Respondents judged hypothetical health states rather than their own actual health states.
Only 16 EQ-5D-5L health states were evaluated because of questionnaire-length and interview constraints.
No profile included level 5 on any dimension, which restricted the severity and disutility range and prevented assessment of whether concavity holds across the full range.
The survey recorded selected job characteristics rather than specific occupations; the characteristic set was arbitrary and omitted factors such as skill requirements.
Respondents were not paid, which could have reduced motivation.
Most questionnaires were embedded in a 45-minute omnibus interview, so interview length could have reduced data quality and encouraged similar answers.
COVID-19 may have changed the labor market, respondents' health perceptions, and the meanings of dimensions such as usual activities and mobility.
The Polish healthcare system, legal and economic context, and culture can limit transfer of results to other countries.
The study estimated absenteeism and presenteeism but did not resolve the disputed duration of absenteeism costs under human-capital and friction-cost approaches.
Only state 33333 was valued repeatedly under both perspectives. This design and the number of observations per state limited power to identify perspective differences for milder states.

The sample consisted of Dutch citizens and was predominantly female and highly educated, so results might not replicate in populations with other cultures or demographic distributions.

The DCE design did not include state 33333, so DCE-only models could not examine the observed gap effect.

The findings apply only to patients admitted to hospital and do not establish sex differences among people who recover without hospital admission.

Combining ethnicity into white and non-white groups did not represent the full ethnic diversity of the population.

Cardiovascular complications were not determined centrally.

The cross-sectional design could not show the course of outcomes over time or establish determinants of worse outcomes.
Selective participation or incomplete questionnaires could have underestimated or otherwise biased severity.
Age groups were uneven in size and differed in characteristics, which could have affected age comparisons.
Not all linear-regression assumptions were met for the EQ-5D index analysis, so those results require caution.

The study did not examine preference heterogeneity, including heterogeneity in power or discount rates.
Understanding of the cTTO-DCE differences was limited because the two respondent subgroups received different designs and had different interviewers.

ANA was considered in isolation and may be confounded with preference or scale heterogeneity; respondents who gave a dimension less weight could be misclassified as non-attenders, so estimated ANA may be an upper bound.
The stepwise selection of ECLC classes can affect coefficients, p-values, and standard errors and is unlikely to capture the full pattern of ANA.
The survey included no indicator that could distinguish ANA caused by preferences from ANA caused by decision heuristics.
Anchoring DCE coefficients with the published Irish value set was the only available rescaling mechanism and may have brought model-based values closer together.
Other models that accommodate preference heterogeneity and ANA simultaneously were not estimated.
Although the pooled sample was large, 80% of respondents were concentrated in only 33 health states. This concentration limited the effective sample for rare-state analyses.
Self-report error made it impossible to distinguish very rare states from physiologically impossible states with certainty.
The study reanalyzed an existing valuation data set. A prospective comparison could include and exclude states while it preserves important design features.

The exclusion criteria removed different numbers of choice tasks and observations, so the reestimations were not fully like-for-like. Controlling task or state counts would have made the comparator generation substantially more complex.
The sample mainly comprised residents who reported English as their primary language, so culturally and linguistically diverse samples require study.
All participants had enough cognitive capacity to provide informed consent; the association between cognitive status and response issues was not examined.
Only a small number of residents could state an instrument preference, and they could not explain that choice.
Randomization meant that the same residents did not assess all four measures.
The study assessed four measures selected for the Australian aged-care context and did not assess other relevant measures, such as ICECAP-O or WOOP.
The study took place in Australia, and findings may not generalize to other countries, including other English-speaking countries.
The analysis examined face validity only. It did not calculate preference-weighted utility scores or assess convergent validity, reliability, or responsiveness to change.

A convenience sample was used that was not representative of the general population: participants were younger, more often female, better educated, higher income and with fewer chronic conditions than the Canadian valuation study sample.

Participants were interviewed after completing the TTO exercise a second time within a test-retest study, which may have influenced their learning of the task and their thinking about health preferences.

Many participants found it hard to express their thought processes, particularly about valuing health states relative to dead, so respondents probably did not fully articulate their thoughts; future studies should use more detailed interviews and think-aloud methods during the valuation exercises.
Only China and Singapore had suitable updated EQ-5D value-set data, so the findings might not generalize to countries or regions with different cultural and socioeconomic contexts.
Differences in study design between early and recent valuation studies, including sampling methods, could reduce comparability.
The study cannot separate the effect of time from changes in the EQ-VT protocol, so it cannot attribute the cTTO differences only to evolving preferences.
The study does not show how the nonuniform coefficient differences would affect real-world economic evaluation results.

Only the land-based, noninstitutional population was covered; people in hospitals, old age homes, nursing homes or living on vessels were excluded, so people with more severe health problems may be underrepresented and estimates may be biased.
The sample had fewer respondents aged 45 to 54 and fewer in paid employment than the general Hong Kong population.
No previous EQ-5D-3L normative study exists in Hong Kong, so improvement in the ceiling effect from the 5-level version could not be assessed locally.
The three modifications were tested simultaneously in one test arm, so the effect of any single modification cannot be verified from these quantitative data alone.

Respondents were partly recruited by convenience sampling in a university context, so young and highly educated persons were overrepresented and the data are not representative of the German population.
Despite randomisation by the EQ-VT, the arms differed in socio-demographics and health status, which might explain some variation in values.
The lead-time TTO bounded values at -1, and no information was collected on whether respondents would have traded more than the whole lead time, so censoring cannot be excluded.
Time discounting was not accounted for, so a downward bias in cTTO values cannot be excluded.
The nonrandom quota sampling strategy could reduce generalizability, although the quotas closely matched the Saudi population by geography, age, education, employment, and gender.

Data collection had interviewer effects, task shortcutting, clustering, low proportions of negative values, overuse of the feedback module, and some inconsistencies. The pilot, training, quality-control software, meetings, and exclusions reduced these problems.
The COVID-19 pandemic caused substantial delays in data collection.
There is no clear benchmark for an acceptable mean absolute error; reported minimal important differences for EQ-5D utility range from 0.03 to 0.08.

The simulations were parameterized from the United States valuation study, and other valuation studies can have different degrees of nonlinearity and heteroscedasticity, so the size of error inflation can differ.

The study used 99 iterations per scenario. A repeat with a different seed was stable, with deviations below 2 in the second significant digit, but the iteration count was small for a simulation study.

Pre-existing hypertension may have been underrepresented among people with undiagnosed hypertension or without regular medical consultations, with possible differences between national screening and management strategies.
The registry did not contain the duration of hypertension or the quality of blood pressure control, so the study could not distinguish newly diagnosed from chronic hypertension.

Body mass index was missing for more than 30% of patients; random forest imputation had an estimated error of plus or minus 5.8 kg/m2 and may have reduced the estimated effect of obesity in fully adjusted models.

The student sample limits external validity because students are generally younger, healthier, and more highly educated than the general public; their age and likely low parental prevalence can also reduce adult-child perspective differences.
COVID-19 restrictions required online videotelephony administration without personal interviewers, which could reduce data quality relative to personal interviews.
The experiment used bisection elicitation rather than the search procedure used for EQ-5D value-set collection.
A technical error caused imbalanced health-state block assignment, with 55 respondents in block 1 and 164 in block 2.
Respondents received different incentives: some received course credits and others received money.
Conclusions about correction assume that the direct method measures time preference reliably; evidence about its test-retest reliability remains limited.
The exploratory analyses reported all tests without correction for multiple hypothesis testing.
Differences between cTTO and LT-TTO cannot uniquely identify lexicographic avoidance of death because proportional heuristics and sequence effects can also produce lower LT-TTO utilities.

Loss to follow-up could bias the responsiveness analysis, although 80% completed the 6-month follow-up and baseline characteristics did not differ significantly between completers and patients lost to follow-up.
Recruitment from endocrinology and surgical outpatient clinics at only three Hong Kong public hospitals may limit generalizability.
The small sample, especially the worsened-health subgroup, produced wide confidence intervals and makes the responsiveness results preliminary.

Preferences and scale are intrinsically confounded in discrete choice models. Choice-consistency estimates depend on preference-distribution assumptions and might not identify scale uniquely. Small nonzero preferences can also be mistaken for attribute non-attendance, or the reverse.

The base-case attribute-attendance and scale estimates depend on the included attribute-importance and level-importance parameters, although simpler and more complex sensitivity models produced nearly identical results.
The primary estimates did not adjust for possible warm-up and fatigue effects, although supplemental analyses found warm-up effects only in no-overlap arms and found no fatigue effects.
Transferability to other DCEs is uncertain. Intensity color coding needs logically ordered attribute levels and can be less useful in experiments with fewer ordered attributes.
The study tested highlighting of non-overlapped differences but did not compare it with highlighting of overlapped similarities.
The optimal amount of level overlap remains unknown because overlap reduces statistical design efficiency but improves behavioral efficiency and can permit additional choice tasks.
Few respondents reported the most severe levels of pain and discomfort, because people in very severe pain may be harder to recruit.
There is no well-established method for conducting IRT on multidimensional models, so IRT was run on separate domains after controlling for two measurement factors in the CFA.
For social care users the impact on health and wellbeing was ambiguous and there were no clear markers of sensitivity, so no known-group assessment was undertaken for this group.

Caring burden was proxied only by hours of caring, which may be a weak indicator, and the direction of the effect of caring on wellbeing is ambiguous; matching on age, gender and long-term condition may not have captured other relevant characteristics.
The six country samples did not cover the same groups, which limits between-country comparisons, and the non-UK samples had a more limited diversity of patient groups.

Online recruitment prevented full assessment of missing data because items could not be skipped, only partly mitigated by the UK paper survey; online respondents were also younger than paper respondents.
Practical constraints on distributing the paper version limited the randomization of item order, leaving a risk of order effects.

The known-group analysis was mainly a crude patient versus healthy population comparison, severity comparisons relied on EQ-5D dimension levels rather than clinical severity indicators, and no indicator assessed sensitivity to change from treatment or services.
The DIF analysis tested only statistical significance and not the magnitude of DIF, and some subgroup comparisons may have lacked power.

Merging of subdomains, particularly for China, Germany and Argentina, was data driven and could reflect co-occurrence of problems across conceptually distinct domains, so its generalizability to other patient groups is unclear.

Stakeholders had limited familiarity with health economics, QALYs, valuation tasks, and the current EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation protocol; this could have limited the depth of their responses, and their early-stage opinions could change after further education.
The investigators' framing of complex concepts and the sequence of the background presentation and discussion prompts could have introduced framing and ordering effects.
The small purposive sample of 12 stakeholders did not account for geographic or regional representation, so the findings might not generalize to broader stakeholder groups or the Pakistani public.
Only 60 of the meeting's 210 minutes were available for open discussion, which restricted interactive engagement and in-depth exploration of complex issues.
Vaccination status was self-reported and did not guarantee actual uptake.
Country-specific ethnicity categories could not be used in pooled cross-country analyses.
The convenience longitudinal subsample was not designed to be representative, so the results cannot be generalized.
Small and sometimes nonrepresentative country panel samples limited power and prevented separate country-level analyses.
Observed changes could reflect macro-level policy interventions or global sentiment that the included country terms did not fully capture.
Bonferroni correction removed statistical significance from many associations.
Feasibility was assessed only through missing responses; completion time, qualitative assessment, and participant preference were not assessed.

EQ-5D-Y asked about health today, whereas PedsQL Generic Core Scales asked about the last month; this recall-period mismatch could affect responses and reduce correlations, especially among acutely ill children.
The study could not compare responsiveness with general-population utility values because no Indonesian youth tariff was available.
The fixed presentation of EQ-5D-Y-5L first, with disease-specific modules between the two EQ-5D-Y versions, might have changed perceived health and contributed to response inconsistencies.
Stable and deteriorated follow-up groups were too small for responsiveness analysis and were excluded; responsiveness was assessed in the improved group.
The reported benefits of the extra blocks were conditional on the larger design-specific samples and were much smaller when the sample was held near 1,000.
The analysis evaluated extension of only the cTTO component of EQ-VT. The DEVINE study also increased DCE blocks, but the effect of that extension was not evaluated in this paper.
The effect of value-set model RMSE and MAE on economic-evaluation results and health technology assessment decisions remains to be evaluated.
The online adult samples were not fully representative: Chinese adults aged over 60 years were underrepresented, and higher education was overrepresented in all countries except Canada.
Education and parental status differed across countries, so adult preference comparisons across countries require caution.
The study encountered a high proportion of suspected fraudulent online responses, especially in one Australian adolescent subsample.
Country-specific ethics requirements and recruitment difficulties led to different adolescent recruitment strategies, which limit cross-country comparisons.
Computer-only completion may have reduced reach; phone completion could improve recruitment but could introduce attention and screen-presentation problems.
When adolescents were recruited through parents, the investigators could not directly confirm whether the adolescent or parent completed the survey.
Latent-scale DCE does not anchor values at 0 and 1 and gives no evidence about adult-adolescent differences in preferences for the dead state, so the results cannot directly produce QALY value sets.
Comparison of EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L results is difficult because the descriptive systems differ, the studies were about a decade apart, and the EQ-5D-3L sample was smaller and less representative.
The older EQ-5D-3L TTO protocol allowed very negative values that were arbitrarily transformed into the interval from -1 to 0; the paper did not reverse that transformation.
The respondent-specific discount parameter was estimated indirectly from TTO tasks, so the author advises caution in interpreting the discounting results.

Other model specifications, including models of respondent heterogeneity, could change the estimates; the analysis was intended to demonstrate the anchoring issue rather than select a final econometric model.

The properties and impact of the proposed method depend on the descriptive system, the severity of its pits state, respondent heterogeneity, and the population prevalence of worse-than-dead valuations.
The empirical analysis considered utilities elicited with time trade-off tasks only.
The non-probability quota sampling design may have reduced external validity and did not produce a statistically representative sample, although quotas approximated key national characteristics.
Illiterate people were excluded, so their preferences cannot be assumed to match those of the literate population.

EQ-VT was available only in English, Filipino, and Cebuano despite at least four other major languages at the sites; translation ambiguity or inaccuracy may have contributed to non-monotonic coefficients in alternative models.
The feedback module led to exclusion of 11.64% of cTTO observations, and the study could not examine whether sociodemographic characteristics influenced flagging.
The sample included adults only; future valuation work is needed for EQ-5D-Y.

The intensive daily diary repeatedly focused caregivers on today's health and may have improved recall-period adherence. Some caregivers said that diary completion affected their final EQ-5D-5L assessment, so observed nonadherence may be underestimated.
The sample of 52 dyads was too small to detect differences between fluctuation groups reliably, especially associations between fluctuation intensity and recall-period nonadherence.

The heterogeneous sample included different dementia disorders, although fluctuation patterns can differ by dementia type. This limits generalizability and prevented robust comparisons across disease types.
The EQ-5D-5L does not cover all HRQoL dimensions that fluctuated, so its measured variation may underestimate true HRQoL fluctuation.

Observed EQ-5D-5L changes cannot be attributed fully to real health fluctuations. Random measurement variation, changes in perception, or changes in patient and caregiver response behavior may also explain them, and reliability studies in people with dementia and their caregivers are lacking.
Direct generalizability is limited because income, healthcare funding, labor costs, and cost-effectiveness thresholds differ between Brazil and other countries.

The Uruguayan EQ-5D-5L value set was used because Brazil had no EQ-5D-5L value set; sociocultural, economic, and preference differences between the countries can add uncertainty to utilities, QALYs, and ICERs.
Literature health utilities used in a scenario came from an old cross-sectional study and might not represent current health states, healthcare systems, or long-term disease consequences.
Some literature inputs were combined with study data, and discrepancies between these sources could affect model outcomes.
This was a small-scale exploratory study with only 101 respondents, and variant 1 had only 18 observations because of a routing error.
The study compares whole protocols rather than valuation methods in isolation, so it cannot distinguish the effect of the valuation method itself from the effect of the surrounding study protocol.

The design cannot identify whether the difference in joint VAS results reflects the preceding valuation exercise (SG versus TTO) or the preceding instrument-specific VAS present only in the York protocol.
Respondent background characteristics differed from the original York and Sheffield samples in smoking status, housing tenure and educational qualifications.
The official 5LY was not available, so the experimental version used here is subject to further modification.
The EuroQol Group recommends the EQ-5D-Y for ages 8-15, and about 20% of the sample exceeded the upper age limit of 15.

The order of questionnaire administration was not randomised, and the mode of administration differed between baseline (face-to-face) and follow-up (telephone), which might introduce measurement bias.
No rescaled EQ-5D-Y value sets were available for reference.

Strong ceiling effects, a small sample of scoliosis patients, and lack of statistical power for clinical subgroup comparisons mean the subgroup results, especially for patients with Cobb angle above 40 degrees, must be interpreted with caution; larger studies in other paediatric patients and the general population are needed.
The analysis sample was not representative of the United Kingdom population, including in demographic composition and possibly in pandemic risk and worry attitudes.
The study used VAS, while national value sets usually use time trade-off, sometimes with discrete-choice experiments; the results might not hold with standard valuation techniques.
Only state 55555 was valued on the full health = 1 and dead = 0 scale, and this worst state is rarely experienced, so implications for common health states are unclear.
Few older people participated, although older age was an important risk factor for severe COVID-19 and could be associated with larger valuation effects.
Observed associations cannot establish causality because unmeasured traits, such as risk tolerance, could affect both pandemic experience measures and health-state valuation.
Some results were sensitive to the method used to censor or remove extremely low rescaled 55555 values.
Only about 5% reported a positive effect of COVID-19 on health; this subgroup was systematically different and had poor propensity-score balance, which weakens interpretation of its large effects.
The study was not large enough to identify the full breadth of taste and scale classes in the Peruvian general population.
Models with more than three taste classes or two scale classes were not estimated because of limited data and convergence problems.

A known criticism of the scale-adjusted latent class model is that it can fail to separate scale and taste heterogeneity; the authors tried to address this with distinct grade-of-membership covariates.
The analysis assumed discrete distributions for unobserved taste and scale heterogeneity and did not examine a hybrid approach with continuous distributions.
The online non-probability sample was subject to selection bias, was dominated by younger and highly educated respondents, and did not represent the Chinese general population.
The questionnaire collected only three age categories rather than exact age, which restricted the statistical analysis and reduced potential regression efficiency.
The cross-sectional data reflected health at one specific and potentially fluctuating time point; a longitudinal study would better support cause-and-effect relationships.
The overseas sample was too small for meaningful country-specific analyses, and the results may not generalize to Chinese people living in areas such as Africa.
Online recruitment may exclude older caregivers who do not regularly use the internet, and the adult-only sample does not represent caregivers of children.
The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions and assessment of changes in perceptions over time.
The scoring algorithm for the five-item caregiver-burden level summary score had not been validated.
CarerQoL was not developed for proxy reporting, and caregiver-completed CarerQoL had lower internal consistency than the other measures (McDonald's omega 0.65), so these results require caution.
Self-reported data can contain response bias and social desirability bias; in the online setting, the investigators could not enforce independent completion by dyad members.

Recruitment from a Qualtrics panel of self-identified caregivers can cause selection bias, can limit generalizability to all United States caregiving situations, and does not show how many dyads declined participation or why.
The review included hematological malignancies but excluded nononcological hematological conditions such as anemia and hemophilia.
The review included only adult EQ-5D versions and excluded EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L.
Eligibility required studies that explicitly assessed measurement properties, so studies with only indirect psychometric evidence were excluded.
The English-language restriction could have introduced language bias.
One reviewer extracted data and another cross-validated them instead of using independent dual extraction, which could have increased omissions or subjective bias.
The source evidence had incomplete disease coverage: no studies addressed acute lymphoblastic leukemia or chronic myeloid leukemia, and few addressed Hodgkin lymphoma or multiple myeloma.
Many studies came from China, Africa was not represented, and the concentration of countries and languages could limit transferability.
Few studies reported missing HRQoL data.
Only one source study included proxy reporting, and it analyzed patient and proxy responses together, which prevented conclusions about proxy-specific measurement properties.
The study could not make a like-for-like within-person comparison because respondents did not complete both EQ-5D versions.
The individual-level data did not show whether respondents received help. This lack of information can cause the study to underestimate feasibility problems for self-completion.
The GP Patient Survey did not include the EQ VAS, so the study could not assess its feasibility.
Respondent-level administration mode was unavailable, so the study could not control for paper, online, or telephone completion.
The decision to censor some responses at zero reflects an admittedly arbitrary judgement, and such responses may result from the interview process or from interviewer or respondent comprehension.
Exclusion criteria could have been extended to weaker inconsistencies; there are no agreed rules, and results might have differed with other exclusion judgements.

The DCE data in this design are not rich enough to detect the respondent group differences identified in the multinomial model, so DCE-only estimates rely on error distribution assumptions that are unlikely to hold for differences of opinion.
The sample underrepresented people aged 18 to 29 years, which required age-band weighting.

Constraining priors to force logically consistent level coefficients requires further justification, since unconstrained TTO estimates suggested severe was worse than extreme/unable in two dimensions, possibly due to the selection of the 86 health states.
Values came from general-population preferences. The authors note criticism of this normative approach and arguments that patient preferences can be better informed about impaired health.
Although both cTTO and DCE data were collected, the final value set uses only cTTO data, so the DCE data will not inform Mexican HTA decisions.
The authors state that TTO is subject to limitations, as are all stated-preference methods.

cTTO and DCE produced markedly different preference patterns; the analyses did not fully explain the differences, and the study did not include qualitative methods such as think-aloud interviews to investigate them.

The assumed independence of VAS and DC values is reduced by the chained task structure, since respondents rated the two states on the VAS immediately after choosing between them and consistency with the preceding choice was enforced.
For relatively similar pairs of states the chained design may have inflated differences in VAS scores, making the multi-item VAS a compound task that enforces congruence between the methods.
It is not possible to attribute observed cross-country differences to cultural, methodological, or translation causes.
In the Dutch study one block of health states (block 11) was not assessed because of a programming error.

The DC design contained only 50 pairs of health states, which may have given insufficient information and power to estimate the logistic models, leaving several coefficients non-significant or inconsistent.
The comparison of the DCdead and DCWTD models was not a direct comparison because the two analyses cover different, non-identical sets of participants.
The dead questions were administered only in the Spanish pilot, so the DCdead analysis could not be extended to the other countries of the multi-country study for comparison.
Many respondents had difficulty with the lead-time TTO exercise and some always preferred Life B, so the general impression was that many did not answer the TTO tasks appropriately.

The five-level version makes the DC task more complex, which may have led some participants to make random choices when unable to decide between states, and the results could not be directly compared with earlier three-level DC studies.

The overview is restricted to the general use of TTO for economic evaluation, where values for large sets of health states are obtained from general-population samples; TTO values elicited from individual patients for clinical decision-making are deliberately excluded because that is a different research area with different goals and premises.
The evidence is compiled narratively from recent and older research rather than by a stated systematic search, and there is no consensus in the literature on whether SG and TTO give similar values.
The authors state that it cannot be denied that the iteration steps influence the values, but the exact size of that influence can hardly be defined.

The concerns raised about the English EQ-5D-5L values may be typical of that UK valuation study, because later EQ-VT versions in other countries produced more balanced results with smaller interviewer effects.
The sample of 12 was too small to separate genuine mobility-wording preference from presentation-order effects or to select definitively between used and normally use.

Limited ethnic diversity, a gender imbalance with 75% female participants, and a high education level with 58% holding a bachelor's degree or higher may limit transferability to more diverse populations.
The qualitative evidence was insufficient to select a cognition response scale because understanding was accurate and preferences were split; quantitative measurement-property evidence is needed.
The two facilities were selected by convenience, both belonged to one interested not-for-profit provider, and applicability to private or government facilities is unclear.
Participant and facility incentives and the requirement for research consent could have altered completion rates and limited real-world feasibility.

Facility screening based on perceived capacity to consent may have excluded residents with severe cognitive impairment or complex health needs; language barriers and limited interpreter funds further reduced representativeness.
Facility staff conducted resident interviews, which could have caused social-desirability and interviewer bias toward more positive self-reports.
Inconsistent staff timing records prevented assessment of completion time.

Resource constraints, pandemic-related access restrictions, management and staff changes, and a prolonged consent process prevented repeated time-point collection, so barriers and facilitators to repeated routine collection could not be assessed.
The pilot used dedicated study collection rather than existing administrative systems, although the authors considered the procedures similar to possible routine implementation.
The valued health states cover only a small part of the full EQ-5D-5L state space, and the feasible design supports a main-effects model rather than all possible interactions.
The blended recruitment approach will not permit calculation of a response rate.
The planned sample size is not based on a formal analysis of sampling error and specification robustness; it is based on experience from prior EQ-5D-5L valuation studies.
The study is not designed to detect preference differences across participant characteristics, and nationally proportional sampling produces small samples for Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
Conference reports in Chinese and English were found but were excluded because no peer-reviewed publication records were available; only one Chinese-language paper met the inclusion criteria.
The review did not undertake a quality evaluation because methodological differences limited the validity of cross-study comparisons.
The face-to-face intervention and mobility restrictions during the pandemic could prevent correct delivery and make follow-up visits difficult.
Multiple patient risk factors for post-intensive care syndrome and chronic pain can affect outcomes, while the sample size constrains analysis of those factors.
The trial has a small sample and is conducted at one center, which limits the conclusions, including exploratory risk-factor analyses.
Patients with severe mobility limitations, especially those with more severe COVID-19, may be unable to attend visits and could cause selection bias.
The retrospective design limits the study.
The registry did not collect patient frailty, so the contribution of frailty to in-hospital mortality could not be assessed.
The registry did not collect reasons why patients were not referred to hospital or intensive care; therefore, the effect of lower referral rates among older people could not be assessed.
Only 59 of 247 possible test-retest pairs were classified as stable, so the small stable sample can restrict generalizability of the test-retest findings.
Utility-level responsiveness could not be compared because no preference-based value set was available for EQ-5D-Y-5L.
The sample did not precisely match the Irish population age profile, with fewer respondents younger than 45 years and more respondents older than 45 years.
The study was not specifically powered to detect differences related to sociodemographic variables.
Collinearity among covariates could have reduced statistical significance, including for income and insurance.
The models could have endogeneity because insurance status may relate to unobserved prior personal or family experience of the health system.
The analyses controlled for several covariates but did not control for every potential confounder.

The study used a quota (non-probabilistic) sample; younger and more highly educated individuals were slightly over-represented, although utility values did not differ significantly by educational level.

Information from the discrete choice experiment was not used, because the DC models showed inconsistencies that could not be resolved through hybrid modelling and no robust estimation method for DC data is available.
No internal or external validation of the predictions was performed, because the final sample was smaller than originally intended and splitting it would reduce statistical power.
Selection bias was possible because the sample may have included a disproportionate number of caregivers interested in health-related quality-of-life assessment and advocacy.
The study did not collect children’s intelligence quotients, although diagnoses and impairment levels were diverse.
Videoconference interviews may have produced somewhat fewer comments than in-person interviews.
The phrase health and wellbeing may have prompted participants to propose an especially broad set of additional dimensions.
Probe questions, category choices, and quotation classification were subjective, especially in the inductive analysis, and another team could have produced a different framework.

The authors did not know whether respondents completed the questionnaires themselves. Cognitive problems could have impaired completion, so some answers might have been unrecognized proxy responses that require cautious interpretation.
Recruitment through Q-fever patient and support organizations could cause selection bias, because patients with more severe or persistent complaints may be overrepresented.

Non-response could bias results in either direction: people with ongoing complaints may have been more likely to respond, while those with severe fatigue or cognitive problems may have been unable to complete the survey.
EQ VAS was used in the absence of a gold standard for HRQoL and may represent a broader health construct.

The eight-item CIS fatigue score used a past-two-weeks recall period and differed in format and concept from a single EQ-5D-style fatigue bolt-on about health today, which could affect apparent sensitivity and added value.
The study used exploratory rather than confirmatory factor analysis, so the identified structure requires confirmation.
Exploratory factor analysis is sample-dependent and data-driven, and the findings can differ in other populations or settings; interpretation is also limited to the instruments included.
The sample included only Australians aged 65 years or older who could complete an online survey, which may exclude people with severe cognitive impairment or limited digital literacy.
The analyses used no post-stratification weighting or other representativeness adjustment, so generalization to the broader older population requires caution.
The study included generic instruments but no condition-specific measures.
The cross-sectional analysis cannot assess temporal stability or responsiveness of the factor structure.
Potential selection and participation bias: fewer than 10% of invited trauma patients completed all EQ-5D surveys, so results may not fully reflect the Dutch trauma population.
The EQ-5D-3L was used instead of the more sensitive EQ-5D-5L; recall correspondence of the 5L version remains untested.
Test-retest reliability of the EQ-5D-3L has not been studied in trauma patients, so the observed correspondence could not be benchmarked against instrument accuracy in this population.
Responders were significantly younger and more often male than non-responders.
The review excluded EQ-5D-5L application studies that did not explicitly assess psychometric properties, which can omit distributional and responsiveness information.
The review excluded studies that used experimental EQ-5D-5L versions, so it did not capture early content-validity studies or investigations of bolt-on items.
Most included evidence came from Western Europe, OECD countries, and East Asia, so psychometric performance in other regions remains less established.

Heterogeneity in populations, outcomes, interventions, anchors, and subgroup definitions limited pooling and made it difficult to identify population-specific or treatment-specific responsiveness problems.
The review did not assess valuation methods or the effect of value-set choice, although both are important for EQ-5D-5L index values and responsiveness.

The calculated standard errors represent conditional parameter uncertainty only; they assume that the underlying value-set model is correctly specified and may be sensitive to alternative model specifications.
The results are standard errors of mean health-state values and do not quantify uncertainty in predicting the next observation, which can matter when value sets are used in patient-level analyses.

The publicly available MVH report contains ambiguities and inaccuracies in its exclusion description, so the 2997 records in the modeling sample cannot be identified from public information alone; the authors relied on a historical file.
The reported standard errors cover only one of the wider sources of uncertainty around HRQoL values.
EQ-5D data may have been collected differently across registers, and these collection differences may explain some observed valuation differences.
Dead was not anchored, which limits immediate use of the EQ VAS valuations in economic evaluation.
VAS and EQ VAS provide no explicit choice or trade-off and can be affected by end-aversion bias.
Although EQ VAS and EQ-5D-3L correlations were moderate to high, discrepancy remained between the two measures.
Few participants reported level 3 self-care or mobility problems, which may have contributed to inconsistent severity decrements.
The pooled cross-sectional samples were not a panel, so patient fixed- or random-effects methods could not control for unobserved persistent patient characteristics correlated with health.
Observational cross-sectional data cannot test causal relationships.
Deprivation was measured for small residential areas rather than individuals, which creates measurement error and may bias estimated deprivation associations toward zero.
The GPPS stopped including EQ-5D-5L after 2016/2017, so the study could not include more recent data.
Recruitment through an online panel may not represent all United States caregiving situations, especially people without regular internet access.
The sample included only adult caregiver-care recipient dyads and excluded caregivers of children.
Social desirability bias could have affected responses despite instructions not to discuss responses.
Shared method variance or random measurement error could have affected convergent-validity results.
The initial simple-sum CARE-2B scoring method requires further validation and comparison with factor or weighted scores.
The cross-sectional design does not support causal or directional conclusions.
The multivariate factor analysis was exploratory and requires confirmatory factor analysis in future studies.
Performance in specific caregiver-care recipient relationships and caregiving contexts remains to be established.
Assessment of acceptability was incomplete: administration time and patient views about the instrument were not collected.
No EQ-5D-Y value set was available, so an unweighted summary score was used, which does not allow cost-utility analysis.
The EQ-5D-Y does not cover the social dimension, a key aspect of children's HRQoL.

This is a secondary analysis of a trial designed for another purpose; the 9-month interval between test and retest is too long for reproducibility, little change was expected from the intervention, and the small stable subsample (n=18) means stability results must be interpreted with caution.
External validity is limited: results should not be generalised to other chronic conditions.

The authors stated that generalizability was limited by the qualitative nature of the study. They said that the resulting hypotheses need verification and that similar studies in other Asian and Western countries would permit comparison.

Although quota-sampled, participants were more often female, more educated, and higher income than the Australian adult population, which can limit generalizability and contributed to many highest responses.
Participant characteristics and medical conditions were self-reported, so reporting bias was likely.
EQ-5D-5L was always completed before EQ-HWB; the nonrandom order can cause conceptual error, random error, or repetition bias.
The instruments used different recall periods: current health for EQ-5D-5L and the last seven days for EQ-HWB.
The survey did not include established subjective well-being measures or experimental EQ-5D-5L well-being bolt-ons, so comparisons were limited to EQ-5D-5L and EQ-HWB.
The utility models did not assess other quality-of-life factors such as geographic remoteness, loneliness, or health behaviors.
The EQ-HWB-S analysis used a United Kingdom value set because no Australian value set was available, which can limit comparability with Australian EQ-5D-5L utilities.
EQ-HWB-S remains experimental, and its ability to detect changes in broader quality-of-life dimensions unique to the measure remains uncertain.
Participants agreed to allocation to either mode, so they may not represent people willing to use only one mode or the wider UK population.
The study occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic, when reluctance to attend in-person interviews and health preferences may have differed from other periods.
The lowest socioeconomic groups and people with less education were underrepresented, possibly because interest required video capability, internet access, and a computer or tablet.
Sample sizes were imbalanced between modes because video acceptance was higher and in-person collection stopped when COVID-19 transmission increased.
The study was conducted only in England and only in Sheffield and Oxford, which limits transferability to other settings.
Pandemic distancing required separate screens in the in-person interviews rather than the standard single-device EQ-VT setup; its effect on understanding, engagement, or interaction is unknown.
The study evaluated TTO but not discrete choice experiments because it was designed to inform a UK EQ-5D-5L valuation that would use only TTO.

The original survey sample was not representative of the Alberta population. Weighting improved comparability, but respondents with large weights could overrepresent problems if their HRQL did not represent their demographic group.
The pandemic survey recorded self-reported gender identity, while the pre-pandemic norms reported HRQL by sex, which made the subgroup measures non-equivalent.

Urban or rural dwelling was collected only in survey 2 and was used as a proxy for health zones. This reduced the available observations, and rural health zones also contain cities, so dwelling did not represent health zone well.
Actual LMWH dose was unavailable for the full cohort, so the authors could not verify protocol compliance outside two academic hospitals; protocol deviations could weaken the instrumental exposure.

Clinical characteristics at HDU or ICU admission were unavailable, so balance at that time could not be checked. Dose tertiles and a continuous log-transformed dose were also less clinically relevant than dose-intensity categories.
The analysis assumed that hospitals did not differ in other treatment policies that affected the outcomes. This assumption was checked only for hydroxychloroquine and not for all treatments.
Pulmonary embolism could have been misclassified because there was no central adjudication and hospitals could differ in testing practices; time-related awareness could also affect diagnosis.

Generalizability is uncertain because the sample was limited to Dutch HDU or ICU patients during the first pandemic wave, later variants and treatments differ, and only six patients had a protocolised therapeutic LMWH dose.

Some event dates were missing and imputed, 12 patients had missing outcome information and were treated as discharged alive, missing weight affected dose assignment and model inclusion, and transferred patients could include unidentified duplicates.

The comparison with the Chinese EQ-5D-5L study may be affected by different quality-control procedures: the youth study used a minimum cTTO task-time indicator, whereas the adult comparator did not use the same quality-control process.
The sample was slightly over-represented by females and participants with higher education compared with the general population of China.
The sample covered Peninsular Malaysia only, so the results may not generalize to Sabah and Sarawak in East Malaysia.
Minor demographic imbalances required census weighting, although the reported design effect was small.
The cross-sectional design does not support causal inference.
Data were collected in 2016 and represent a pre-pandemic baseline.
The fixed order of EQ-5D-5L, EQ VAS, and EQ-5D-3L administration may have caused sequence effects.
The norms came from the same sample as the Malaysian EQ-5D-5L valuation study rather than an independent population survey, although health data were collected before valuation tasks.
Some demographic strata were small, including the Other ethnicity group with 10 participants.
The EQ-5D-3L index used a VAS-based value set, which limits direct international and between-version comparisons.
Small Global Rating of Change subgroups limited exploration of different thresholds for health improvement and worsening.
Recall bias in retrospective measures and response shift in prospective measures over the 12-month interval could affect interpretation of perceived change in dimension and symptom-severity scores.
Preferences were collected during the COVID-19 outbreak, and the effect of the pandemic on EQ-5D-5L preferences was unknown.
The study did not use a controlled comparison with face-to-face interviews, so videoconferencing mode-of-administration effects could not be ruled out.

Internet-access and computer-literacy requirements could have caused selection bias, especially among older, less educated, diseased, or less technically skilled people; feasibility in middle- and low-income contexts remains uncertain.
The study did not explore model specifications beyond the standard main-effects specifications for which the EQ-VT protocol was optimized.
The sample was younger than the Italian general population, and perfect age representativeness was not achieved despite recruitment through local recruiters.
The study did not collect feasibility evidence from interviewees and therefore did not cover their experience of videoconferencing administration.
The interviewer evaluation form could have been affected by acquiescence bias because the best response category was shown on the left.
Two investigators were members of the EQ-VT support team; their experience and frequent feedback might have improved interviewer performance beyond what less experienced study teams could achieve.
The study setup combined recruitment by a market-research company, online scheduling, reminders, and support, so the contribution of each component to feasibility could not be isolated.
Experience scaling summarizes HRQoL but not life expectancy; the authors recommend reporting life-expectancy gains separately.
Perspective-specific values may not be comparable across conditions, such as values from people with diabetes versus values from people with cancer, which limits use across all interventions.
The approach does not establish which stakeholder perspective has deliberative authority and can permit analysts to select the perspective that favors an intervention.

Adults can value child HRQoL differently depending on whether they use their own or the child's perspective, and mothers and fathers do not necessarily represent the societal perspective that usually governs child resource-allocation decisions.

The method is innovative and specialized, needs development across child ages, problem durations, countries, and marginalized groups, and lacks open-source kaizen-task software that would support wider access.
The existing electronic medical record did not permit direct patient entry, so the workflow required paper completion and clinician entry after review.
The Enterprise Business Intelligence environment limited how PROM data could be reported and displayed.
Only a small staff sample was surveyed, and the authors called for a more robust staff evaluation in the new electronic medical record.
Limited clinician preparation time prevented some staff from routinely using the PROMs Clinic List.

Online surveys that use a marketing panel can have data-quality problems and might not generalise to the Australian general population, especially people with less education and people who do not take part in online surveys or panels.
The paper supplies the survey instrument, experimental design, and analysis plan only for wave 1 because wave-2 materials will be adapted after wave-1 evidence is available.
Paired comparisons require respondents to choose between profiles of health problems and can be more burdensome than choosing improvements, especially when the profiles concern a 1-year-old child.
Whether adolescents can reliably report their parents' occupational status is uncertain, which may limit the socio-economic status proxy.
A large share of respondents (23.1%) had missing or ambiguous answers on parents' occupational status and were excluded from that comparison.
The survey was administered during school hours, so adolescents with severe health problems who cannot attend school may be underrepresented.

HRQoL was assessed 1 month after injury, by which time many patients with mild TBI, the majority of the TBI group, may already have recovered cognitively; the earlier 1-week measurement had too few respondents.
Non-TBI patients had significantly higher Injury Severity Scores than TBI patients, so the TBI group showed a larger ceiling effect.
The three-level EQ-5D suffers from ceiling effects, and the 5L version might have reduced them.
Only 27.6% of invited patients returned complete EQ-5D + C and EQ-VAS data.
All patient participants were from Shandong Province. This geographic concentration can limit generalizability to people with COPD across China.
Considerable conceptual overlap between some bolt-ons and the original EQ-5D-5L dimensions remains unresolved.

Some terms were interpreted specifically in the COPD context despite EQ-5D-5L being generic. In particular, Limitations in physical activities due to shortness of breath can overlap substantially with Usual activities.
The review included only studies published in English.
The search may have missed studies of broader well-being measures and early theoretical or conceptual work that preceded preference-based-measure terminology.
Because the included evidence covered diverse study types, the authors did not evaluate the quality and strength of all included studies.
Published reports may not have provided enough methodological detail to determine the extent of engagement with Indigenous communities.
The survey did not permit missing CHU9D responses. This could force an arbitrary answer and prevented assessment of content validity through missing-response patterns.
The study could not determine how the guidance notes affected respondents' cognitive processing.
The short-interval test-retest sample included only 53 general-population respondents; limited response variation and ceiling effects could reduce the reliability estimates.
Responsiveness subgroups were small, especially groups with worsened health, which limited hypothesis testing and required cautious interpretation of effect sizes.
CHU9D utilities used scoring algorithms developed from preferences of older populations because no value set exists for the proxy version in children aged 2–4 years.
Proxy-reported health-related quality of life can disagree with child self-report, especially for subjective dimensions such as worry, sadness, and pain.
The study did not evaluate whether the CHU9D dimensions fully and appropriately represent health-related quality of life in children aged 2–4 years.
The guidance notes had not first undergone qualitative content-validity testing for this age group.

The sample predominantly included less-educated Indonesians with lower economic status, and response heterogeneity or cultural reluctance to report health problems may have produced more favorable self-reported health.
The Australian FACT-8D value set and pilot United Kingdom EQ-HWB-S and United Kingdom SWEMWBS value sets might not represent Indonesian preferences precisely.
The measures were administered in a fixed order, which could have introduced order bias.
Global Rating of Change might not capture the full range of changes measured by EQ-HWB because EQ-HWB extends beyond health constructs.
Different recall periods across instruments might have affected the results.
The relatively long test-retest interval and heterogeneous treatment reactions might have affected item-level test-retest reliability, although unchanged health was self-reported.

The inconsistency metric potentially overestimates the effect of the feedback module, because removing any cTTO response lowers the number of possible inconsistencies, so random removal would also improve apparent consistency.

Implementation of the feedback module was not straightforward: it displayed complex information to possibly fatigued respondents, and interviewers struggled to guide respondents without implying that a response was wrong, so better interviewer guidance might have increased its effect.

Compared with the general population, males were underrepresented and older individuals overrepresented in both jurisdictions, and the Dutch sample was a convenience sample from one day hospital valuing a single block of health states.
Feedback module results for 31 Dutch respondents were lost because of a software bug.
Respondents were not individually randomized to the standard or split version, because interviewers switching between protocols simultaneously could cause spillover effects.
Exclusion of people who were not continuously insured and people who died during the five-year period limits generalisability to those populations.
The costing approach omitted drugs supplied during hospital stays and some specialty drugs for oncology, transplantation, and renal care.

Administrative data did not provide comprehensive race or ethnicity, housing insecurity, self-reported health, smoking, physical activity, or other social and behavioural factors; neighbourhood income was only a proxy for socioeconomic status.
The data did not contain detailed information about prevalent long-term conditions or comorbidities.
Participants in the cognitively demanding source valuation study may have been cognitively and physically healthier than older people who did not participate.
The source sample represented the German general population rather than the elderly population specifically, and people living in institutions may have been underrepresented.
These selection mechanisms may have caused the study to overestimate health in the German elderly population.
The sample was small for a reference-value study, which reduced precision and caused overlap between confidence intervals for adjacent age groups.
The oldest age group had only 38 respondents, which limited the robustness and generalizability of its reference values.
Important bolt-on papers could have been missed because the main review included only peer-reviewed published work and might not have retrieved unpublished working papers.

Studies that found no added value for a bolt-on might be less likely to be published, which can cause publication bias; the authors tried to reduce this risk by also reporting conference presentations found in the search.
The analysis used data from only one valuation study; the findings from the sensitivity-imposed simulations may differ in other data sets.
The severity association for negative utilities was demonstrated with simulated data rather than with an actual modified cTTO procedure.
The comparison of original and reshuffled RDS results used no formal similarity measure; the reported similarity was judged from figures and parameter tables.

Level sum score is a crude severity measure that weights all dimensions and adjacent level changes equally, and using it to assess utilities that were developed to improve on such crude scores has a potentially circular aspect.
Subsetting on the sign of utility creates selection bias, and the smaller negative sample, spikes, and censoring can also make the negative slope and R2 smaller.

Slow recruitment required a change from the Statistics Denmark sample to recruitment through a Danish market-research company for the final sample. The authors noted possible differences between the two respondent sources.
The final sample slightly under-represented people aged 18 to 24 years and people with the lowest educational level.
The interviewers were concentrated in and near the North Denmark Region, which limited available interview days in other regions and may have hindered recruitment.

DCE values are not anchored on the 0-to-1 QALY scale, and the hybrid model used a multiplicative constant as a statistical solution. The authors stated that the utility-theory basis of hybrid modelling requires more research.
Eye-tracking data alone cannot conclusively determine the feasibility of self-reported HRQoL or produce definitive guidance on self-report versus proxy assessment.
The MMSE cognition thresholds were NICE classifications, but no universally accepted MMSE thresholds define cognition subgroups.
Participants knew that their eyes were tracked, which could have changed normal fixation patterns, although the non-wearable device may reduce this bias.

The sample was small because of time and resource constraints, including the COVID-19 pandemic; no sample-size calculation was done because the study was exploratory, and a larger sample could characterize subgroup differences more precisely.

Data were collected in familiar residential facilities rather than controlled laboratories; differences in lighting, furniture, sound, movement, and other environmental factors could affect gaze-data quality in ways the analysis could not account for.

Four older adults did not provide usable data because calibration failed or gaze data were poor; thick or multifocal lenses and eyelid dysfunction can also make eye tracking impossible for some older people.
Multi-stratification produced small cell sizes and reduced power; COVID-19 status could not be added as another stratifier.
The multivariate regression did not account for within-person heterogeneity and may have introduced bias.
Only 41% of T1 respondents completed T2, creating possible attrition and nonresponse bias; the follow-up sample was older and highly educated, which limits generalizability.
The forced-choice questionnaire could have contributed to nonresponse, social-desirability, and response-set bias.
Healthcare access information was limited and did not include aspects such as access to medication; country differences in pandemic measures could have distorted the early-pandemic access measure.
Socioeconomic status used only educational attainment because income data were missing, and marital status was not measured, causing loss of information.

Residual confounding prevented mediation analysis; oversampling in New York State and New York City and dichotomizing chronic disease status may also have biased or reduced the information in results.

Merging two cohorts restricted the analysis to shared clinical measures and a limited set of sociodemographic factors; BMI was available only at baseline, which could overestimate the obesity association.
Differences in the diagnosis and measurement of restless legs syndrome across cohorts led the authors to exclude it from the main analysis.
Eight patients at a premanifest stage were retained because of prior recruitment, although sensitivity checks suggested that they did not affect the results.
SCA6 differed from SCA1-SCA3 in progression, so pooling the disorders could overestimate or underestimate other factor effects.
The source cohorts were collected in different periods over more than 15 years; changes in symptomatic treatment and health services could limit generalizability.
The analysis could not assess disease duration or cognitive impairment because the cohorts had limited compatible measures, which could bias estimated factor effects.
The analysis did not use population weights, so age-related HRQoL decline could be overestimated.
EQ-5D-3L can overestimate health problems relative to EQ-5D-5L, and newer or disease-specific measures might better capture HRQoL in SCA.
Both cohorts were conducted primarily in European countries, which limits generalizability to regions with substantial SCA populations, such as South America.
Respondent behaviour during the choice tasks could not be observed, so the use of heuristics and response strategies is unknown.
Only one set of states was generated for each Type I design; a range of designs could have been developed and matched on the number of pairs with differing durations.
The extent to which the non-zero prior values represented the preferences of the tested population is unknown, limiting inferences about the use of prior values in DCE with duration generally.

Differences with the earlier PRET-AS study include the design algorithm, sample size, internet panel and number of choice sets per respondent, so the duration attribute is not the only difference across studies.

The study did not estimate a cTTO-mixed-logit hybrid model because of methodological complexity; standard econometric software such as Stata cannot estimate this model without a tailored implementation.
The study was not sufficiently powered to formally compare language-specific value sets, and English and Hausa samples differed in several sociodemographic characteristics.
Only English and Hausa EQ-PVT versions were used, which may have excluded some local-language groups.
The language analysis tested 20 parameters, but a Bonferroni correction could not be applied; significant language differences therefore require cautious interpretation.
Data were collected during escalating tension over the planned government relocation of riverbank residents, and the effect of this uncertainty on subjective wellbeing could not be judged.
Recruitment through a local non-governmental organization and door-to-door invitation may have biased sample representativeness, and non-responders could not be counted.
The study compared level sum scores rather than utility scores because no preference-based value set was available for the EQ-5D-5L versions containing the bolt-ons.
Other chronic diseases in the cohort might have increased the sensitivity of standard EQ-5D-5L and therefore underestimated differences between it and the bolt-on versions.
Some referred patients might have been asymptomatic or unaware of their sleep problem, which could have reduced observed effect sizes.
The four bolt-ons were tested in a specialist setting among Asian patients, so results might not generalize to other bolt-ons, populations, or settings.
The authors state that replication with larger samples, other target populations and contexts, and longer recall periods is needed.
The cross-sectional design cannot establish causal relationships or control unobserved heterogeneity; longitudinal data would be needed.
Further research is needed to assess how the use of population norms for disease-absent health states changes Indian economic-evaluation results.
Anxiety or depression was assessed with the single EQ-5D question, which cannot replace clinical history and examination or a clinical diagnosis.
Additional determinants of Indian HRQoL were not examined; caste was one example that requires study in larger samples.
Social desirability bias remained possible despite instructions that dyad members not discuss answers before survey completion.
Shared method variance or random measurement error may have influenced convergent-validity results.
Cross-sectional data show differences at one time point and cannot assess responsiveness or change over time.
Some people, especially parents, can take up to 2 years to identify themselves as informal caregivers, which may affect recruitment and the study scope.
Older caregivers who were less familiar with the internet may have been excluded, and the adult-dyad focus omitted caregivers of children.
The English-only survey may have excluded caregivers who do not speak English.
Online-panel recruitment may not represent all United States care recipient-caregiver situations, and the number and reasons for dyads that declined participation were unknown.
Convenience recruitment through a webpage linked to an online dementia course may have selected people with a personal interest in dementia or higher digital literacy.
The sample was limited to English-speaking people in Australia, so findings may not generalize to other populations or patient groups that need proxy reporting.
Think-aloud and probing captured only the cognitive processes that participants verbalized, and the amount verbalized varied by participant.
Emotional factors in reporting for a person with dementia may have caused participants to omit sensitive topics.
The study did not assess how well carers could remember the care recipient's ability to self-report, although this can affect the choice of proxy perspective.
The study did not examine proxy-patient subgroups in depth, including relationship, carer role, cultural background, and prior proxy-reporting experience.
Nearly all participating carers were women, although the authors stated that it was unclear whether this was a limitation.
The study did not establish that the matched EQ-5D-5L and PROMIS-29+2 states were equivalent; raw-score and T-score matching cannot locate EQ-5D-5L on the PROMIS construct with certainty.
The main PROPr analysis used PROMIS-29+2, so some characteristics might differ with other PROMIS instruments, T-score methods, or score intervals, which limits generalizability.
