The study did not test the value sets with patient-reported or longitudinal data and therefore did not directly compare QALY estimates in clinical contexts.

The sample represented the Dutch general population rather than health or social-care service users. Its relatively good health could have reduced response variability and affected the dimensions identified.

Factor-analytic results depend on the selected item pool. PHDT, CAP-AWB, and HR-SWB are less commonly used than EQ-5D-5L, ICECAP-A, and BRS and have less evidence about validity and psychometric performance across contexts and populations.
The analyses did not account for each instrument’s conceptual model or theoretical framework. This could have limited identification of relevant QoL domains and subdomains.
EQ-5D-5L was the only HRQoL measure. This may explain why physical-health factors such as vision, hearing, and speech were not identified.

The long questionnaire could have caused participant fatigue. In addition, some factors contained items from one instrument only, and the fixed instrument order and similar wording or proximity could have influenced factor identification.

The development and testing samples were separate random draws of 80% from the same 1002 participants. They therefore reused some participants instead of providing two nonoverlapping validation samples.

The correlation analysis was exploratory. It did not model complex factor relations or causal assumptions; VAS-Happiness was a limited, strongly welfarist proxy for wellbeing; and its anchors differed conceptually from the best or worst imaginable health anchors of VAS-Health.
A greater number of small areas would have given a wider geographic spread of data.
Younger males were slightly under-represented and the sample did not match population characteristics on all parameters.
Survey effort was not evenly distributed across interviewers.

Data on medications affecting mood and on sensitive life experiences were not collected, limiting interpretation of the valuations, because survey length and respondent fatigue constrained data collection.
Recruitment from tertiary hospitals limits generalizability to pediatric eczema patients treated in primary care.
EQ-5D-Y-5L was analyzed with a level sum score because no value set was available, so the results might not reflect the measurement properties of an EQ-5D-Y-5L utility score.
Chinese value sets were used for EQ-5D-Y-3L and CHU9D because local Singapore value sets were unavailable.
CDLQI had not been validated in Singapore, although it was used to assess convergent validity.
The sample was too small to assess responsiveness to worsened health; only three patients reported worsening.
The findings apply to children and adolescents aged 8 years or older and might not generalize to younger children who typically use proxy-reported instruments.
Test-retest reliability was not assessed because follow-up intervals varied substantially and the instruments use a recall period of today, so stable health could not be assumed.
A patient-group value set still averages potentially heterogeneous patient preferences and can remain mismatched with an individual patient's preferences.

The relation between EQ VAS ratings and EQ-5D-3L profiles can change from before to after surgery; the reason is unclear, and the study selected preoperative valuations because they reflect preferences at the decision time.
No TTO valuations from hip-replacement patients were available, so the effect of valuation source could be assessed only indirectly and the VAS result cannot be generalized to TTO.
Generalizability is limited to total hip replacement and the hospital-choice decision examined.
Limited provider variation in intake health and health gain after total hip replacement can reduce the effect of value-set choice on hospital performance estimates.
The smaller general-population current-health sample had sparse observations for severe dimension levels, which produced large standard errors for some GP-VAS-OWN coefficients.
The participant sex distribution differed from that of Ghana, with more men in the sample.
Differences by interview language could not be examined because only 3% of interviews were in Twi and 97% were in English.

The sample was smaller than in other valuation studies, and each respondent completed more tasks; this could have caused interviewer and respondent fatigue and affected responses, although strict quality control was used to reduce the effect.
The study could not completely distinguish general-public participants from carers, and carers differed in responsibilities and burden that could affect their priorities.
The sample was not fully balanced by sex, education, or place of residence; most participants came from Chongqing and Guizhou, which limits transferability to other parts of China.
The study was limited to China, and cultural values can affect preferences; broader cultural and geographical study is needed.
Some participants had difficulty understanding or interpreting specific Q-sample statements, especially emotional items that used phrases such as “free of feeling.”

Because Q methodology is subjective and exploratory, the factors are interpretive rather than statistically representative or predictive of participant categories; each factor also contained people from different backgrounds.

Sampling covered only clusters in Peninsular Malaysia because of resource constraints, so residents of East Malaysia (Borneo, 20.4% of the population) were not sampled and possible preference differences were not assessed.
The convenience, quota-based recruitment strategy means no response rate can be reported.

People employed full time or self-employed were slightly under-represented and those outside the labour force over-represented, although the difference in mean observed C-TTO values between these groups was not statistically significant.
A slight interviewer learning effect was observed, since most excluded respondents came from the first cluster.

Model fit to individual observations was not used as a performance criterion, and cross-validation was performed only over C-TTO blocks, so hybrid models lacked apparent counterfactual observed values and different criteria could favour different models.
The main limitation is the age of the data: collection took place in 2005-2006 and publication was substantially delayed because earlier modelling produced non-monotonic values.

The sample of 225 respondents is small; the EuroQol Group Association now recommends about 1,000 respondents for a valuation study with sufficient statistical power, but such recommendations did not exist in 2005 and the study was financially and time constrained.

Only 23 health states were directly valued, which together with the sample size made it difficult to obtain a monotonic value set and raised concern that regression results were susceptible to random error.
Attempts to remove non-monotonicity by applying exclusion criteria failed, indicating that the inconsistencies were not caused by a small subgroup of respondents with conflicting preferences.
Whether the observed diminishing sensitivity to increasing health problems is unique to this study population is unknown and warrants further investigation.
Combining TTO and DCE data in a hybrid model was an arbitrary decision taken because no consensus exists on which elicitation method is better, and it necessarily worsens the model fit.
The religiosity scaling is described by the authors as probably the most controversial assumption in their model.

The simple specification with only main effects, no constant and no interaction terms was chosen for practical usability, and a more complex model would probably be needed for better predictive validity of respondents' answers.

Some comparative statistics (for example the percentage of states with negative utility, and the unimodal versus bimodal value distribution) are driven mainly by the descriptive system rather than by the value set itself.
The methods and results of the planned experimental substudy (experimental TTO blocks, excluded here) are reported elsewhere, so they are not available in this paper.
Face-to-face interviewing may have caused respondents to report better health because an interviewer was present.
Ethnic group, marital status, and having children could not be analyzed because these characteristics had little variation.
Although the regression models adjusted for several possible confounders, unmeasured differences between groups may have influenced the results.
Ward routines and visits by relatives interrupted some interviews, and questions about diseases before the TTO task may have influenced willingness to trade life-years.
The 37 respondents described as answering the modified open-ended task were not randomly selected.
The modified task changed both wording and visual presentation, so the study could not identify which change had the larger effect.
Cultural attitudes toward death and reporting poor health may limit generalization from Chinese respondents to other cultures.
The findings from face-to-face interviews may not generalize to other administration modes.
The findings from patients with type 2 diabetes may not generalize to other patient groups.
TTO data show clustering at certain values and selective scale use, possibly linked to task difficulty, the composite TTO structure and the automated administration process.
Interviewer effects on TTO responses may be important given differences in interviewer ability and engagement.
The choice of model and of exclusion and censoring rules necessarily reflects researcher judgements, and alternative specifications could have produced different value sets.
The value set applies to England only; whether UK-wide preferences match is unresolved and will be reported separately.
The greater descriptive sensitivity of the EQ-5D-5L may be counteracted by the compressed nature of this value set.
Some EuroQol-recommended bolt-on criteria, such as translatability and negative wording aligned with core EQ-5D-5L dimensions, are not fully applicable to cultural bolt-ons and require adaptation.
The patient and general-population samples may not represent the whole Chinese population, especially people in remote areas and ethnic minority populations.
Patient data will cover only diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease, so performance in other conditions with specific symptoms will remain unclear.
The study design will not assess responsiveness of the candidate bolt-on items.
The study will not assess how the developed bolt-on items affect health-state valuation; the authors plan this for a follow-up project.
Adolescents valued health states from their own perspective, while adults used the perspective of a 10-year-old child; the analysis cannot separate the effects of age group and framing perspective.
Class membership was probabilistic, and the chosen probability threshold of at least 0.5 could change class assignments compared with other thresholds.
Separate modeling of scale and taste classes or use of different model-fit criteria could select a different number of latent classes.
The equal-sample adjustment assumes that doubling the adolescent sample would preserve the observed class distribution and scale contribution.
Quota sampling was not strictly enforced because of recruitment feasibility, which underrepresented some groups, especially among adolescents.

The quality-control rules and self-reported feedback are imperfect indicators of respondent behavior, and social-desirability bias could help explain differences between observed violations and reported understanding.
Reliability and responsiveness could not be assessed because the protocol was not repeated in the same sample.
Known-groups construct validity was not assessed in relation to multimorbidity.
Diabetes diagnoses were self-reported and were not based on clinical assessment.
The fixed questionnaire order could have introduced an order effect, although placing SF-12 between EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-3L may have reduced response-memory effects.
The international protocol did not require records of how many people were approached or refused, so the sampling flow was incomplete.
Online disease status and respondent identity could not be verified; responses could have come from caregivers rather than patients.
Face-to-face responses could have social desirability bias because interviewers were present.
The models included a limited set of control variables and omitted possible socioeconomic, lifestyle, and treatment factors.
The cross-sectional design cannot establish the causal direction between positive mental well-being and EQ-5D-5L outcomes.
The single-country dataset and use of only EQ-5D-5L and SWEMWBS limit generalizability to other cultures, contexts, and PROMs.
Only nine paired comparisons were available for the statistical heuristic models, and the DCE design was not efficient or tailored for estimating the ten-parameter model.
All DCE tasks followed cTTO tasks, so fatigue could have increased heuristic responding in both perspective groups and masked differences.
Stated preference data could not show whether respondents actually used heuristics or whether their preferences only coincided with heuristic predictions.
The analyses pooled countries and EQ-5D-3L with EQ-5D-Y-3L and did not model respondent characteristics, although these effects could be larger than the effect of heuristic processes.
Each analysis represented one heuristic at a time, although people can use multiple heuristics interchangeably or simultaneously.
No quality-assessment tool was available for MID studies, so all study types were included regardless of methodological quality; this may have affected the quality of the pooled estimates.
The authors state that exclusion of non-English studies may have introduced language bias.
The DCE sample was representative for gender, age group, education, and region, but it was not necessarily representative for other variables.
Online DCE administration can produce low engagement or random responses. The quality rules reduced this risk but could not ensure that every included respondent was fully engaged.
The cTTO sample was a convenience sample rather than a national probability sample, and highly educated respondents were overrepresented.
The COVID-19 pandemic may have changed preferences among the 32 later respondents, and their online video interview mode may also have affected values.
Parents and non-parents differed in demographic characteristics, so the study could not separate parental-status effects from demographic effects.
The parental-status subgroup analysis was not planned in the experimental design and was not part of the EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation protocol.
Comparisons with other national EQ-5D-Y-3L value sets were limited by different anchoring, modelling, and cTTO design choices.
The sample under-represented some minority groups, especially Black pregnant people, which can limit generalizability through selection bias.
The observational study relied on self-reported information and can be affected by reporting and recall bias.
Cross-sectional data without longitudinal follow-up prevented retest analysis, conclusions about test-retest reliability, within-person HRQoL trajectories, and responsiveness assessment.
Pregnancy or postpartum month was linked with calendar time, so the influence of the COVID-19 pandemic was difficult to separate from gestational-stage effects.
Marital status was not available even though it is known to affect health status.
The Trinidad and Tobago value set may not exactly represent health-state preferences in Barbados or Jamaica.
The EQ-5D-5L index values were based on a crosswalk from the Trinidad and Tobago EQ-5D-3L value set rather than a directly elicited EQ-5D-5L value set.
Exclusion of observations judged inconsistent meant that the final samples were no longer strictly representative, although the authors considered the number of exclusions small.
The age limit of 64 years in the Barbados and Jamaica surveys prevented collection of data from older age groups.
The study assessed EQ-5D-3L, not EQ-5D-5L. The results therefore do not capture possible sensitivity gains from the five-level version.

The pre-existing UK MS Register data were not designed for this research question. Suitable events with known timing and a detectable expected HRQoL effect were difficult to identify, which limited the responsiveness analyses.

Event timing relied on participant self-report and could contain measurement error or temporal misclassification. Fixed three- or six-month collection intervals also prevented analysis of shorter-term effects.

PROM participation declines with time since diagnosis, and the extract required at least five EQ-5D-3L time points including a complete Spring 2023 response. This may under-represent people with advanced multiple sclerosis and introduce selection and survivorship bias.
Relapse and symptom onset were assessed in isolation, without control for other events during the same period that could affect HRQoL.
The UK MS Register portal does not allow partial instrument responses, so acceptability could not be examined at the individual-dimension level.
The authors could not retrieve five potentially relevant full-text records and did not make further access attempts after library support.

Both authors did not extract every full text because of the volume of records; this can reduce the reliability of inclusion decisions and extracted data despite periodic coordination and final checks.
The judgment that a method was unique was partly subjective, and debatable decisions excluded some adaptations and large-scale applications of existing methods.

The scope excluded animal research, theoretical work without empirical discount-rate estimates, reused data, revealed preferences, and market-behavior estimates, so it omits relevant methodological contributions.
No quality or risk-of-bias assessment was performed.
The synthesis treated each method as one observation regardless of influence, and citation counts could not show why a method was cited or whether it remained in use.
Study duration and task-count data were often not reported or varied by implementation, which limited operational comparisons.
The sample was restricted to the online MTurk platform, which has mixed external validity depending on context.

MTurk workers were more likely to have flexible or remote-compatible work and reported less job loss than national figures, so the survey likely underrepresented people with substantial employment or income loss and may have overestimated HRQoL.
The pre-pandemic comparison sample was small (n=40), and most age-specific pre-pandemic groups had fewer than five respondents, which limited meaningful age-group inference.

The open online, non-probability survey introduced self-selection and underrepresentation of socioeconomically disadvantaged people, people with limited internet access, and people less willing to complete questionnaires. Inverse probability weighting addressed observed sampling imbalance but could not correct latent selection processes.
Both instruments were self-reported and could have differential item functioning across demographic groups. The study did not investigate whether construct patterns differed by subgroup.

The Tufts CEA Registry is restricted to English-language CUAs indexed in MEDLINE, so non-English CUAs and work outside peer-reviewed journals, such as health technology assessment submissions, were not included.
The data ended in 2021 because of the registry update process, so the study could not assess whether the 2019 ISPOR good-practice report improved later utility identification, selection, and use.
The validity of the England 5L value set cannot yet be judged because the independent external validation is still ongoing.
Allowing both value sets in parallel risks inconsistency between future decisions, since evidence will continue to be submitted using both the 3L and the 5L for years to come.

The general population sample contained relatively few respondents with impaired health, so reference dependency estimates rest mainly on mild health states and could not test whether the effect differs by EQ-5D dimension or is nonlinear across severity levels.
Reference dependency was based only on respondents' current health status, ignoring past illness experience and the health experience of people close to them.
The sample over-represents older people and females despite a purposive top-up of 102 respondents, although weighted analyses found no material differences in results.
EQ-5D-3L data, health care use and doctor-diagnosed conditions were not collected, to limit respondent fatigue and protect the quality of the preference and health status data.
Only one father participated, despite men forming 37% of the survey sampling frame.
The length of the 25-item instrument limited the depth of probing, so the researchers could not obtain detailed relevance and comprehension information from every participant for every item.
The interviewer presented the CarerQoL items as possibly missing content, so support for these domains was weaker evidence than an unprompted report of missing content.
Researcher error caused omission of the CarerQoL questions from the first seven interviews.
Respondents valued health states for a 10-year-old child, but the value set is intended for ages 8-15 years; preferences or dimension interpretation may differ for adolescents.

COVID-19 could have changed respondents' health and preferences and forced cTTO interviews to switch from face-to-face to video conference; this mode also selected a younger and more female sample and could exclude older people or people without Internet access.

The ten-state cTTO protocol could not model diminishing marginal utility or estimate a full hybrid or ten-parameter additive model, and anchoring to state 33333 meant that not all collected cTTO data contributed to the final value set.

The cTTO sample had fewer people older than 70 years and a somewhat higher female proportion than the Belgian population, and both samples were more highly educated; the samples were not stratified by characteristics such as having children or education.
The sample was older, more literate, more highly educated, and more urban than the Pakistani general population; rural and illiterate respondents were difficult to recruit.
The EQ-PVT could not randomize the cTTO and DCE blocks, so each interviewer received a specified sequence to balance block administration.
OPUF value sets may systematically differ from value sets made with other valuation methods, and the personal utility functions predicted hard and moderate DCE hold-out choices poorly.
The OPUF method assumes an additive preference model, which might not represent non-additive preferences or interactions.
The web interface and task instructions remain under development; some participants reported navigation, slider, or instruction difficulties.
Evenly spaced level ratings and relatively homogeneous dimension weights might indicate inattention, incomplete understanding, or simple response heuristics.
Online recruitment through a patient organization made the sample unlikely to represent all patients with rheumatic diseases in Germany.
The random DCE hold-out state generator did not ensure that health states were plausible or realistic.

Quota sampling was used for time and cost reasons; random sampling could have given a more representative sample, as seen in the education attainment and general health of respondents aged 65 and older.

The sample sizes were small relative to the US population, with each face-to-face respondent representing about 290,000 inhabitants; these valuation data were nonetheless the best available because the EQ-5D-5L is not in any large-scale US general population survey.

Mean index and EQ VAS values by self-reported diagnosis should be used only as general guidance for disease burden because these subgroups are heterogeneous in disease stage, acuity and patient experience.
Norms could not be generated for the five respondents who identified as non-binary because of the limited sample size.
The lengthy household-level and individual-level survey relies on self-reported data and can have measurement error from self-reporting bias.
Attrition in later waves is expected and can affect the analysis and results.
The first-wave recall of pre-COVID-19 HRQoL and socioeconomic circumstances from approximately 3–4 years earlier can have recall bias.
Only articles published in English were included, so psychometric studies published in Spanish or German were excluded.
Studies reporting only feasibility or distributional properties were not included; an eligible study had to report at least one endpoint on reliability, validity or responsiveness.

The included studies scored poorly on the sample size calculation domain, with only about one-fifth presenting such estimations, although most had large or medium sample sizes and only 30% were based on fewer than 100 children.

Substantial statistical heterogeneity (I2 at or above 80%) was present in most meta-analyses because the included studies differed in population age, country, clinical area, disease stage and the comparator quality-of-life instrument.
Almost all participants with high economic status lived in Java and urban areas (97.8%), which limits generalization of the economic-status finding.
The analysis did not include other possible HRQoL covariates, such as physical activity and parental status.
The authors described the sample size as relatively modest, although they considered it sufficient for national estimates by sex, age, and residence.
Economic status and participating school were not included in the quota design and were not representative of the general population, which could cause selection bias.
The experimental EQ-5D-Y-5L had no available value set, so the authors could not perform the same range of analyses as for EQ-5D-Y-3L.
The study examined EQ-5D-5L preferences in Trinidad and Tobago, so generalizability to other countries, cultures, and instruments requires care.

The DCE-with-duration data did not have the established quality-control procedure used for the cTTO data; there was no interview debrief, so respondent understanding and engagement could not be assessed beyond speed exclusions and face validity.
The study could assess population-level but not individual-level agreement because different respondents completed the DCE-with-duration and cTTO tasks.
The sample included only US caregivers recruited online, which may cause selection bias and limit generalizability.
The study included caregivers of adults, so the results may not apply to pediatric caregiving contexts.
The exploratory factor structure requires replication with confirmatory methods.
The cross-sectional design prevented assessment of test-retest reliability and responsiveness over time.

The high occurrence of self-reported anxiety and depression may have strengthened emotional-item correlations; samples with lower psychological morbidity may have restricted variability and weaker associations.
The factor analysis combined items with three- to five-level response scales; differences in scale granularity may have affected factor loadings.
The review included only quantitative results, but many source articles used mixed methods and did not clearly separate qualitative from quantitative findings, which complicated extraction.
Source studies varied in their definitions and measures of preference and comprehension, which limited comparison across studies and validation of new designs.
There is no standardized toolkit for measuring PROM visualization preferences and comprehension.
The ASReview stopping rule could leave relevant records unseen; one record marked relevant by one reviewer was not seen by the other reviewer's algorithm and required consensus handling.
Evidence for group-level visualization was limited, and only one included study addressed predicted PROM presentation; none tested comprehension of predicted PROMs.
A full UAE value set could not be modelled because of the limited sample size, restricted geographic coverage and small number of health states in the design.
Older and less-educated individuals were underrepresented, limiting generalizability; such respondents might have found the computer-based tasks even more difficult.
Large amounts of data were excluded because of interviewer protocol non-compliance, and excluded respondents may hold systematically different preferences.
Semantic issues in translation, such as the absence of an exact Arabic equivalent for 'full health', risk the TTO being interpreted differently than in other countries.
The study did not include a full validation exercise to establish whether the dimensions and level descriptors are relevant and culturally appropriate for the Emirati population.

Self-reported influence of religious beliefs may be driven by social desirability bias, and no empirical data support the conjecture that Islamic teachings explain the low rate of worse-than-dead valuations.
Data on marital status, employment status and education were missing for 34 respondents because of a recording error.
Comparisons with other country studies are difficult because of considerable differences in sample composition, particularly age.
Any adaptation of the standardized valuation methods would limit the comparability of results across countries.
The authors did not conduct a quality assessment of the included articles because they wanted to maximize inclusion, so evidence quality was not used to qualify the synthesis.

The review included only the general population and generic questionnaires; disease-specific patient-reported outcome instruments were excluded because variation among patient groups could affect HRQoL definitions.
Classification of concepts, domains, and facets was inherently subjective, despite independent grouping by two reviewers and resolution through team discussion.

The findings say little about preference heterogeneity; a function that fits aggregate data may not predict an individual's utility, and demonstrating the power function as an individual utility function would require respondent-specific adaptive elicitation.
Selection bias in online surveys is a concern; low socioeconomic status was associated with dropping out and nontrading behaviour, which may reflect preferences, inattention, or cognitive difficulty.
Respondents were university students rather than a general population sample, and their limited experience of ill health may raise the reporting of implausible states.
Each respondent valued about 200 health states with EQ-VAS, far more than in standard TTO valuation, and without software or interviewer support that helps respondents imagine states.
Interviews took place several weeks after the valuation and rating tasks, so recall bias may have occurred and interviewees may have mixed thoughts from the two tasks.
Recruitment from people willing to take part in qualitative research may have introduced selection bias and may limit generalizability.

The numbers of adolescents, non-parents, parents of healthy children, and parents of children with health conditions were unequal, which may have limited the diversity of perspectives captured within each category.

The Australian setting may not transfer to countries with different social norms and values, including collectivist settings where adult children have important financial and caregiving roles for older adults.
All interviewers were female, and interviewer gender may have affected participant responses about the sensitive topic of prioritizing children and adults.

The study did not use formal researcher reflexivity such as a reflexive journal. The interviewers' health-economics backgrounds may have influenced their focus on rational trade-offs and data interpretation.

Discussion that scrutinized or challenged participants' views remained light because the topic was sensitive, especially for parents of children with health conditions. The prompts did not generate enough discussion about whether PTO questions captured the intended relative weights.
Broad child-versus-adult categories in attitudinal questions hindered direct comparison with PTO responses based on specific ages.
Interviewer-led completion may have biased responses, although neutral prompts, an introduction video, and presentation of alternative viewpoints were used to reduce this risk.
Roma ethnicity was self-identified, and self-identification and observer identification do not generally overlap; self-identification is also more common in compact communities with higher poverty.

Most Roma respondents were recruited by snowball sampling, which could select people with similar traits and living conditions and overestimate differences by emphasizing more disadvantaged communities.
The 2011 census guided settlement selection, but stigma can cause underreporting of Roma identity and Romania has no agreed sampling frame for Roma populations.
Administration mode differed: the Roma survey used pen and paper, while the general-population survey was computer assisted; this difference could affect HRQoL and sociodemographic responses.
Women were overrepresented because fewer men were available, especially in rural areas, which could reduce representativeness.
The matching procedure reduced the sample to 70% of its original size, and the authors noted that matching-related sample loss can increase bias and imprecision.
The Singapore sample included only people older than 40 years, so the findings might not capture views of younger Singaporeans.

Two Singaporean researchers analyzed the Japanese data, so nuances might have been lost in translation. The authors judged this unlikely because a Japanese investigator oversaw translation and coding quality.
Costs were simulated so that between-group cost differences were not statistically significant.
Only the Netherlands, the United States, and Japan were investigated, although EQ-5D value sets exist for many countries.
Small but statistically significant differences remained between the sample and national statistics for some age, education and ethnicity groups, and no weighting was applied.
Recruitment through personal networks of interviewers and respondents may raise questions about the objectivity and representativeness of the sample.
92.9% of respondents lived on Java Island, so it is unknown whether values would differ for people interviewed on other islands of the archipelago.
Most survey data will be collected online without an interviewer, so the design assumes that respondents will concentrate and engage with cognitively demanding questions.
Quota sampling can improve representation on observed characteristics, but a commercial panel and voluntary participation may not capture all social groups.
The study collects English-language data only in Australia, so findings may not generalize to other countries or cultural settings.
PTO matching questions can focus attention on patient age and assume that gains to different people can be aggregated; these features may influence the elicited social weights.

A limited iterative search can leave uncertainty between an unwillingness to trade and a very strong preference; the analysis therefore infers midpoint equivalence values and separately reports extreme preferences.
The study tests selected, simplified life-extension and temporary quality-of-life gains and does not cover the full range of real health-care trade-offs.

The test-retest sample lost 16 of 101 participants because follow-up calls were unanswered, and the 4-year-old retest subgroup contained only 18 respondents; the authors recommend larger retest samples.

No EQ-5D-Y value set suitable for QALY estimation was available. The latent DCE scoring system was not on a QALY scale, and the adult UK EQ-5D-3L Dolan tariff used different questions and adult time-trade-off values that did not account for children.
The acute- and chronic-illness samples were heterogeneous, so the investigators could not specify expected differences between those two clinical groups.

The general-population group came from the hospital's local geographic catchment. Race, home language, and socioeconomic status were not collected, so results could not be generalized to the wider Western Cape population.
Participants who had been admitted to a ward or intensive care unit were overrepresented, which could have increased the observed prevalence of post-COVID-19 condition.
The outcome used post-COVID-related symptoms that are not specific to post-COVID-19 condition, so symptoms caused by unrelated conditions could have been classified as the outcome.
Restricting the analysis to participants who completed the questionnaire could have introduced self-selection bias and reduced generalizability.
The feasibility sample was small (n = 24) and was not designed to support inference about preference weights.
Interviewer presence in the supportive sessions could have influenced participant responses.
Participants were in relatively good health, no participant reported a disability, and the sample may not represent adolescents with poorer health.
The study did not compare the measurement properties of EQ-5D-Y-5L and EQ-5D-5L.
DCE tasks used only levels 1, 3, and 5; levels 2 and 4 were interpolated and might differ from weights obtained in a full DCE.
Other valuation methods can produce different results.

The Canadian EQ-5D-5L valuation study was one of the first conducted, and later studies used stronger data quality control, so some respondents may not have understood the TTO task; replication in more recent valuation studies is needed to establish generalisability.

TTO and DCE tasks were assigned to individuals in blocks, potentially creating a block-by-latent-class association; no relationship was found in the univariate latent class models, but statistical power for this check was low.
Latent class membership was less certain for the DCE data (mean membership probabilities 60% to 80%) than for the TTO data (over 80%), which could have contributed to the finding of poor agreement.
The study cannot determine whether the two tasks measure the same quantity (health utility); a qualitative study would give better insight.
PHQ-9 and GAD-7 overlap conceptually with the EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression dimension, which could contribute to the observed correlations.
The findings apply primarily to tertiary-care outpatients because the study did not include primary- or secondary-care users or inpatients.
Convenience sampling at one hospital can cause selection bias and limits generalizability, although the site is Ethiopia's only specialized psychiatric hospital.
The sample had a higher literacy level than the Ethiopian adult population, which limits national extrapolation.
Interviewer administration could cause positive-response bias and limits application of the results to self-completion settings.

Combining data from seven cohorts is challenging because cohorts do not collect the same clinical information; only a minimal set of background variables, comorbidities and confounders could be harmonised post hoc.

Former COVID-19 patients admitted to hospital ward or ICU are over-represented compared with patients who had COVID-19 at home, which may over-represent severe long COVID and affect prevalence estimates; post hoc stratification with community-based cases is planned.

Especially in the first pandemic wave, non-hospitalised cases were often not tested because of test-material and capacity constraints, so COVID-19 status in the community-based POPCOrn cohort partly relies on self-report and controls may include unrecognised cases, giving possible misclassification; sensitivity analyses restricted to confirmed infections are planned.
The final number of CORFU participants is uncertain because it depends on survival, response rates and overlap of participants between cohorts.
The CLiK response rate was about 23% and the sample came from one UK borough, limiting generalizability and leaving it unclear whether the segment distribution reflects the underlying population.
Chronic conditions and health behaviors were self-reported and could not be externally verified.
The cross-sectional data prevent causal inference between health and lifestyle-related attitudes, and the attitude segment is treated as static.
Excluded respondents with missing data were older and in poorer health than the analytic sample.
COVID-19 and related protective measures created difficult and changing conditions for recruitment and home assessments.
Caregivers could miss diary entries or fail to report fluctuations on unsupervised days despite checks on days 7 and 14, which could underestimate the influence of fluctuations.
Patient and caregiver perceptions of health can differ, so caregiver reports can emphasize the caregiver perspective.
The study is limited to Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, although the authors cite prior dementia-care studies in support of wider national generalizability.
Recruitment during the Covid-19 pandemic relied on packs sent home, so non-response bias is possible and reasons for refusal were not collected.
Although participants were instructed to complete the measures without help, there was no way to ensure unassisted self-completion.
The relatively small sample of children with cerebral palsy limited more extensive analysis; larger samples with better spread across GMFCS levels are recommended.
The level sum score is a crude summary of dimension responses with known limitations, used because no utility value set exists for the EQ-5D-Y-5L.
The selected population of adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis undergoing brace treatment does not represent all patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis or other adolescent populations.
The second survey did not ask whether health had changed, so participants with change could not be excluded from test-retest analysis; the authors judged substantial change unlikely.
The sample of 107 participants was small, although it met COSMIN criteria and was homogeneous.
The relatively healthy study population produced skewed data, which reduced kappa values relative to the observed absolute agreement.
No pre-study baseline data were available on the number of patients consulting a neurosurgeon after discharge, so the improvement in follow-up consultation is only anecdotal.
Follow-up extended only to 3 months post-discharge, although problems for patients and families are documented to continue beyond this period.
Reported low levels of trouble accessing care must be interpreted within a local culture that accepts delays and long waiting times.
EQ-TIPS-3L used a today recall period and severity response scale, whereas PedsQL used a past-month recall period and frequency response scale, which limits direct comparison.
The health conditions were heterogeneous, which made severity comparison difficult; the study therefore used an EQ VAS threshold rather than condition-specific, clinically defined severity criteria.
Limiting inclusion to caregivers and children able to complete English surveys limits generalizability within South Africa.

Several PedsQL items were not well matched to developmental stage: school items had much missing data among 2-to-4-year-olds, and walking or running items could reflect normal development in younger children rather than impaired HRQoL.
Both anchoring approaches used the matched-pair format, although this is not the conventional format for the immediate-death approach.
Efficient-design arms used approximately twice as many choice sets as generator-developed arms because the efficient designs used two data-collection rounds.
Each arm had only about 220 to 250 respondents, which may have contributed to variable discount-rate estimates.
The analysis tested only exponential discounting and did not compare other discount functions that might fit better.
Potential bias and data-quality problems in the Peruvian dataset may have affected parameter and discount-rate estimates.
The study examined only EQ-5D-5L, so its findings do not establish whether nonlinear modeling is suitable for other instruments or younger populations.
Convenience sampling in only 3 western countries may limit generalizability of the findings to other continents and cultures.

The sample was balanced on age, sex and having children, but other factors such as socioeconomic background or living with a child with impaired health were not accounted for, and respondents' views may differ from those of the general public.
Some respondents may have had personal experience of impaired health, which might have affected their valuations.
Not all thoughts may have been verbalized in the think-aloud technique, and opinions may change or crystallize while respondents verbalize them.
The study focused strongly on adults as parents in the Circle of Life; the role of adults without parenting experience needs further investigation.
Only adults valued the health states, so the preferences of children and adolescents themselves were not studied.
No priors for the interaction terms were available when constructing the experimental design, so interaction priors were set to zero and no pilot study was run.
Health states were assessed by a general population sample; experience-based methods using patients might reveal larger interaction effects.
There was no theoretical hypothesis for testing specific interactions; the study tested all second-order interactions jointly rather than particular terms such as N3.
Patients completed either the 3L or the 5L version, so no head-to-head within-patient comparison was possible.

The 5L sample consistently had lower baseline WOMAC scores than the 3L sample; although mean differences were small (1.4 to 3.9 on a 0-100 scale), baseline heterogeneity in quality of life may bias the results.
Because of the shift from 3L to 5L over time, the interval between baseline and surgery was longer for 5L patients, reflecting lengthening Alberta wait times, which may cause bias.

Only about one third of patients with complete baseline records also completed the WOMAC and the same EQ-5D version at 3 months; no imputation or comparison of completers and non-completers was done, and the direction and magnitude of the resulting bias could not be estimated.

Only the WOMAC was used as anchor, and the 20/50/70% change criteria applied to the WOMAC overall score are stricter than the WOMAC user guide criteria, so responsiveness of the EQ-5D may be overestimated relative to usual WOMAC interpretation.

Cohen's criteria used to interpret the standardized response mean may over- or underestimate change, and effect-size estimates for deterioration groups were less robust because very few patients deteriorated.

No minimally important difference could be estimated because more than 90% of patients were classified as having at least a small but important improvement, and the unbalanced sample appeared to bias the anchor-based receiver operating characteristic approach.

Changes in the local study team and interviewer team could have affected training, feedback, interviewer motivation, and consistency of interview delivery despite standardized training and regular quality control.
The sample differed from the Romanian population in age, sex, and residence; men were underrepresented, particularly in rural areas.
Survey weighting intended to address sample differences caused the final model to lose logical consistency for the slight and moderate self-care parameters.
The authors noted that there is no agreement on the best value-set modeling strategy and that a robust theoretical basis for combining cTTO and DCE data remains disputed.
The study converted available EQ-5D-3L value sets to EQ-5D-5L values with a mapping equation created for the United Kingdom, which could add preference-related uncertainty.

The study could not rule out that observed country differences resulted from methodological differences between the source valuation studies rather than true differences in population health preferences.
The Polish migrant sample and matched Irish sample were relatively small.
The sample may not represent the Polish community living in Ireland.
The dataset lacked potentially important variables, including individual time preference and health status before migration.
The analysis did not control for respondents' proficiency in English.
Unobserved factors could affect cTTO valuations because propensity-score matching balanced only observed covariates.
The sample was clustered within six regions and showed a small middle-class bias, although it was otherwise representative for age, sex, education and employment status.
Prediction accuracy could not be assessed as mean absolute error because there is no counterfactual for hybrid model predictions.
Neither elicitation technique captures values perfectly: cTTO may be affected by scale compatibility and loss aversion, and DCE by lexicographic preferences and attribute non-attendance.
Further research is required to examine the practically relevant evaluation space and the discriminative properties of the German EQ-5D-5L in patient populations.
In the feedback module respondents could only flag health states for reconsideration but could not re-value them.

Respondents completed tasks themselves after a prerecorded video instead of taking part in one-to-one interviewer-led valuation; COVID-19 restrictions prevented personal or digital interviewer-assisted interviews.

The student sample was not representative of the general adult population and differed in age and education; participants were still transitioning to adulthood and likely did not have children, and Dutch valuation characteristics can also limit generalizability.
The bisection TTO elicitation procedure differed from procedures used or recommended in other studies, and elicitation procedure can affect TTO results.
The final assignment to the two health-state blocks was imbalanced, which suggests that a randomization error could have occurred.
The within-person design can be sensitive to order effects and anchoring; respondents could have anchored on the first perspective and adjusted later responses too little.
The exploratory analyses were reported without correction for multiple hypothesis testing.
No EQ-5D-Y value set existed, so utility scores were derived from adult Chinese EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L value sets, and wording and perspective of value sets affect EQ-5D-Y health-state values.
Findings based on Chinese value sets may not generalise to respondents in other regions and countries.
Simultaneous administration of two similar questionnaires may have introduced bias.
Generalisability to other populations or ethnicities is unknown, and cultural differences could produce different ceiling effects.
A 3-month follow-up may be too short to detect clinically significant HRQoL change, especially for postoperative patients who need 1 to 2 months for stiffness and soreness to resolve.
The cohort came from a single centre.
The small numbers of patients with improved or worsened health over 3 months may not give robust responsiveness estimates; a larger multicentre sample is needed.
Correction introduces additional measurement error, because time preference and loss aversion are measured with chained methods whose two extra parameters may increase variability in utilities.

After correction cTTO utilities are no longer bounded at -1, so utilities for states worse than dead became much lower, which may be problematic in practice and may also explain why confirmed utilities (elicited on a scale bounded at -1) were higher than corrected utilities.
The model applies loss aversion to life duration only and not to quality of life, which has counterintuitive consequences for life years spent in states worse than dead.
The corrective approach may overcorrect, since the difference between confirmed and corrected utilities exceeded the difference between elicited and confirmed utilities for several states.
Respondents left most utilities unchanged in the validation task, which may mean they saw no need to adjust or that they were confused by the task.
Non-random quota-guided recruitment means the sample was not designed to give representative cTTO utilities, and the mode of data collection had to change mid-study because of the COVID-19 lockdown.
The corrective approach cannot capture lexicographic non-trading, only reluctance to trade life years to the degree captured by loss aversion.
The online survey may have selection bias because people without access or confidence to complete an online survey, or people who were unwell, may have been less likely to participate.
Self-reported variables such as income and education may be subject to response bias, although anonymity was intended to reduce this risk.
People with higher education and higher income were overrepresented; because utility and EQ VAS scores can increase with education, this imbalance could influence the norms.
The cross-sectional data provide one population snapshot and restrict causal inference about associations between health-related quality of life and sociodemographic characteristics.
The study was not informed by a formal power calculation and the sample size was small, although comparable to similar studies.
No hospital-based survey could be conducted in the South region because of limited resources, so that region is under-represented and results may not generalise to the whole country.
The sample was dominated by respondents who lived in urban areas, were more educated, and had higher household monthly income, mostly coming from the online survey.
Respondents to the online survey may differ from respondents to the hospital-based survey in education, rurality, and age, which could affect the reported HRQoL.
Differences in HRQoL across stages of treatment were not statistically significant because of the small subgroup sample sizes.

Aggregation into nine region-divisions could mask state-level and individual variation; it also prevented detailed study of urban-rural, cultural, and political differences, so state-level or individual-level extrapolation is tenuous.
Raking improved representativeness, but unobserved differences could remain between online Amazon Mechanical Turk participants and the US adult population.
Generalizability outside the US general-population context and to other countries is limited.

Online administration required internet access and may have selected people seeking income or with low opportunity cost of time; unsupervised administration also limited clarification and follow-up and can reduce data quality.
The descriptive analysis did not identify the specific causes of regional HRQoL differences and did not assess socioeconomic disparities within and between regions.

The adolescent sample included a larger proportion of 16- to 17-year-olds than the population, and it excluded 11-year-olds, which limits representativeness and generalizability to younger adolescents.
Adolescent responses were unevenly distributed across the 10 DCE blocks, which could cause measurement error and reduce model quality.
Differences in health profiles, collection periods, and administration formats could explain some group differences. Adolescents used paper questionnaires, whereas adults used an electronic survey.
The study did not collect composite time trade-off data or anchor latent DCE values to the QALY scale, so it did not estimate utility values with 0 for death and 1 for full health.
A relatively large proportion of adolescent respondents failed the dominant task, which suggests incomplete understanding or engagement; these respondents were excluded from modeling.
Data came from one academic hospital in Shanghai, and participants had relatively high socioeconomic status and parental education; this limits generalizability.
The study slightly modified EQ-TIPS and EQ-5D-Y-3L instructions to emphasize the pandemic's impact, which could affect responses relative to standard instructions.
The study group was small and came from one center.
The study used only one questionnaire, the EQ-5D-5L.
Respondent burden was almost tripled compared with the standard EQ-VT protocol because each respondent valued 30 health states plus 6 exercise states.

Respondents were university students with fewer socioeconomic differences and more homogeneous health preferences than a general population sample, so general-public studies might need larger samples to reach the same prediction accuracy.

Comparisons were made for only the 136 valued states rather than all 3125 EQ-5D-5L states, and the EQ-VT design accounted for 63% of those states, which advantaged it in the overall prediction result.
Judging what change in RMSE is acceptable rests on an arbitrary evaluation.
The number of observations per health state was fixed at 100 with a small subset of states; the alternative of sampling more states with fewer observations per state was not tested.
The reason for the considerable coefficient differences between the three designs could not be determined and requires further study.
Because data were collected during the COVID-19 pandemic, the authors did not know whether or how the pandemic affected preferences and results.
Virtual participation required computer access; excluding people without computers could have changed the sample composition.
Respondents with a bachelor degree or higher were overrepresented, possibly because computer ownership and the cognitive demands of valuation studies favor more highly educated participants.
Married respondents were slightly overrepresented and single respondents were underrepresented, which could reflect differences in willingness to participate.
Only three of the 120 possible EQ-5D-5L dimension orders could be tested because of design constraints.
Only a small number of health states were valued, limiting interpretation of the TTO and DCE coefficients; DCE standard errors were large and the models unstable.
No formal experimental design was used; larger samples, more states and a formal design are needed in further research.
The modelled coefficients for mobility differ from the other dimensions and are of particular concern.
The analyzed preliminary items differed slightly from the final EQ-HWB-S wording, including combined items, examples, and use of the term depression, so response patterns can change.

The US online-panel sample can differ systematically from samples recruited through other modes, can underrepresent racial and ethnic minorities, and used general-population quotas only for age and sex.
Self-administered online responses can differ from telephone or face-to-face interviewer-administered responses, which limits generalizability across administration modes.
The cross-sectional design did not permit evaluation of sensitivity to change over time.
No EQ-HWB-S value set was available, so the study compared descriptive classifications rather than index scores and could not determine effects on estimated intervention gains.
Logistical difficulties with ethical and governance approval across the included countries made iterative decision making challenging.

General population, patient, carer, and social care perspectives were not all obtained in every country; social care users were recruited in only 3 of the 6 countries (Argentina, England, and Germany).
No new qualitative study was undertaken to generate items, contrary to COSMIN advice; items were drawn from existing published qualitative reviews and established measures instead.
Audio recordings of the PPIE and stakeholder discussions and the face validation interviews were not transcribed verbatim as COSMIN recommends; data were extracted from recordings and notes instead.
Interviews were conducted by trained study nurses rather than researchers, which may have reduced the depth of questioning.
The interviews were embedded in a larger mixed-methods study, so the study framing may have shaped caregivers' preferences for the recall period they had been assigned.
Only the proxy-proxy perspective was examined; results may differ under a proxy-person perspective.
The retrospective interview design may have introduced recall bias, and adherence to the recall period was self-reported and could not be verified.
Dementia type was not assessed and the influence of cognitive impairment or disease severity on caregiver perceptions was not explored.
Most interviews were coded by a single researcher, with double coding only for a subset.

Preference patterns were identified from point estimates of relative weights; 95% confidence intervals overlapped for some dimensions, so differences between dimensions may not be statistically significant.

A minimal important difference criterion (relative importance difference over 0.03 assuming a scale length of 1.5 and an MID of 0.05) was not applied because the actual latent scale length of each study is unknown.

Although a standardized protocol was used, the demographic questions were customized by each local study team, so the authors could not test how sampling and demographic variations affected the preference differences.

Participants recruited in the existing literature may not be representative of the general population or of specific disease groups; respondents in one US general-population study were more likely to be older and white.
Seven of the nine included studies were from the United States, so the results may not be generalisable to other settings where PROMIS-29 has been translated and used.

Evidence on the performance of models predicting EQ-5D utilities from PROMIS-29 is mixed, the regression-based Revicki model suffers regression to the mean, and the recent European EQ-5D-5L prediction model has no external validation.

The scale transformation from PROMIS-29 utilities to EQ-5D-3L utilities has not been validated by any external study, and methodological considerations about the choice of value sets have not been fully addressed.
Studies available only as conference abstracts, and two studies that calculated PROPr from 14 questions rather than PROMIS-29, were excluded from the review.

The design could not separate the effect of interviewer presence or administration mode from the effect of respondent source because online-panel recruitment and online administration occurred together.
The unequal arm sizes could affect some performance comparisons, and greater random error in online responses could require a larger online sample.

Adjusted analyses could not account for all preference-related respondent characteristics because some were unmeasured, such as personality, or could be affected by social-desirability bias, such as health and illness experience.
The generalizability of the specific online TTO implementation was unclear.
The findings cannot be generalized to the Western Cape or South Africa because the study did not collect ethnicity, language, or socioeconomic data for comparison with the general population.

The TANDI level sum score was a crude substitute in the absence of utility values: different profiles can have the same score, and it assumes equal differences between levels and equal weights for dimensions.
The clinician severity rating was subjective, and moderate and severe groups were not distinguished by the TANDI scores.
The preschool comparison group came from the same referral region as the hospital group but was not matched to it.

A technical error meant only one of the two DCE with death blocks was implemented, limiting the analysis to 19 health states, allowing comparison with composite time trade-off for only nine states, and preventing estimation of DCE with death models.
Differences across countries from unobservable characteristics and different recruitment strategies may affect pooled results, and power was insufficient for country-specific analysis.
In the adult perspective respondents valued their own health while in the child perspective they valued another person's health, which could have influenced the results.
The choice of adults as taxpayers to value child health is a normative decision rather than an empirically settled scientific decision.
Framing the target as a hypothetical 10-year-old child was somewhat arbitrary, and preferences may differ for children or adolescents of other ages.
The Netherlands DCE with duration results may not generalize to other jurisdictions because Dutch attitudes to quality-length trade-offs may reflect the national euthanasia context.
The protocol is subject to future improvement, especially for respondent perspective and age framing.
The ten-state cTTO design is insufficient for TTO-only modelling, and a TTO-only value set is not recommended because adult time preferences can affect valuations of child health states.
Only six health states were valued in this exploratory study, which prevented assessment across a broad health-state spectrum or estimation of a value set.
Almost all interviews (94.78%) used Zoom videoconferencing, which might have affected participant engagement with the TTO tasks.

Treating spikes and clustering as data-quality indicators is based on earlier EQ-5D quality-control practice and psychological theories of satisficing rather than preference theory; its validity is debatable, especially in small samples.
COVID-19 interrupted data collection before the planned 1000 final interviews were completed.
Available software could not adjust DCE values for attribute non-attendance and combine those adjusted values with hybrid modelling on the QALY scale.
Rural residents, illiterate adults, and older adults were underrepresented; marital status and health-insurance coverage also differed from population distributions.
The visual aids used to support illiterate participants were not fully validated, and the intended quota for illiterate participants was not met.

The sample was relatively small, and findings may not generalize to all older aged care residents, older people in other care settings, or other generic or dementia-specific quality-of-life instruments.
Cognition subgroup representation differed between the randomized cohorts; the think-aloud cohort included a greater proportion of participants classified as having no cognitive impairment.
Think-aloud and interviewer-reported grades relied on subjective assessments.
Tiredness, fatigue, sensory impairment, communication difficulty, or limited communication with the interviewer could cause an amber or other grade for reasons independent of cognitive capacity.
Eye-tracking measurements can be imprecise when participants look away from the screen or when key text uses small font, which can reduce data quality and sensitivity and cause interpretation errors.
No pre-injury measure of personal wellbeing was available; only a single pre-injury life satisfaction question could be used as a proxy.
Collapsing EQ-5D 'some' and 'extreme' problems into 'any problems' loses detail, although too few participants reported extreme problems for precise separate estimates.
Retrospectively recalled pre-injury health status may be biased by over-rating, although earlier analysis of this cohort suggested such bias was minimal.
Most participants were in paid employment at the time of injury, so findings cannot be generalised to retired people or those not in paid work.
Participants reporting consistently maximum scores across all PWI domains may reflect response sets, but were retained in the analysis.
The online panel sample can differ substantially from a representative general-population sample, and online samples can produce more worse-than-dead valuations.

Each respondent valued more states and a larger share of severe states than in standard EQ-VT studies. A general-population EQ-VT sample could produce fewer worse-than-dead observations and require more respondents to assess the severity association.
No feedback module was used, so respondents could not retrospectively flag utility values as elicited incorrectly; such exclusion can affect logical inconsistency results.
Level sum score is only a rough severity measure because it gives dimensions equal importance and treats differences between adjacent levels as equal.
The number of respondents per arm was insufficient to estimate full dimension-level coefficients or produce a complete value set, and arm C needed a larger sample for precise estimates.
Data came from older adults in two Fuzhou communities, which limits generalizability to other populations, climates, and socioeconomic settings.
Snowball sampling produced a high proportion of women and may have selected healthier or more socially active participants, which limits representativeness and may overestimate HRQoL.
City-level outdoor monitoring did not capture indoor conditions, local microenvironments, or personal activity patterns, which can cause exposure misclassification.
HRQoL is subjective and can have reporting bias; the study did not measure participant awareness or use of weather forecasts.

The observational analyses could not fully separate the independent and cumulative effects of temperature and humidity despite adjustment for multiple sociodemographic, behavioral, and health variables.
COVID-19 restrictions affected school recruitment and may have caused nonresponse bias.
The researchers could not ensure that school participants in the chronic-condition and general-population groups completed the measures without influence from others.
The instrument order was not randomized: Y-5L was always completed before Y-3L, which created a possible ordering effect.
The standard pretest included only outpatients with type 1 diabetes or rheumatic disorders. More severe, acute, neurologic, or oncologic conditions can show different cognitive impairment.
The review of pediatric HRQoL instruments used existing reviews and a manual search, so other instruments and cognitive content can have been missed.
Home completion might not have occurred on day 5 despite a reminder call, and health status could have changed between administrations.
The study occurred only in Germany, so the results are not generalizable to other countries.
The study did not assess test-retest reliability or responsiveness of the EQ-5D-Y plus bolt-on.
Strong correlations between bolt-on items can have caused multicollinearity and reversed signs in the linear regression coefficients.
The factor analysis did not give one unambiguous structure; one-factor and two-factor solutions were both reasonable depending on rotation.

Respondent age group was confounded with valuation perspective: adults valued a hypothetical child, while adolescents valued for themselves, so the study could not determine whether observed differences came from perspective or from the respondents’ preferences.
Adults imagined an unspecified 10-year-old child, the cognitive representation could differ between respondents, and no 10-year-olds were included in the adolescent samples.
Preferences may differ when respondents imagine children of other ages within the EQ-5D-Y-3L age range, so results for a 10-year-old target might not extend to other child ages.
The online survey could exclude people with limited internet access or technical skills, including some older or remote populations.
Without face-to-face contact, researchers could not directly assess participant understanding, engagement, or interest; time and dominant-pair quality checks only reduced this concern.

Information often came from only one or two registry representatives, could depend on the contact person, and could reflect different interpretations of the questions; some information may have been missed and aggregate results require caution.

Registry representatives may not know how data are used in clinical practice or by other stakeholders, especially for local quality improvement; detailed investigation would have required many care-giver interviews and was outside the study scope.
The template included examples of feedback channels and data uses, which may have influenced responses.
The study contacted only registries currently licensed to use EQ-5D and therefore could not assess why other registries did not use EQ-5D or had stopped using it.
The study considered only EQ-5D use, although the registries also collected other health outcome measures.
The sample was small.
Improved anxiety and depression could have been partly due to improved physical symptoms, especially among patients who received topical ozone therapy only.
The nonrandomized design could not rule out placebo effects or effects of closer follow-up during treatment.
The sample was clinically heterogeneous in diagnoses and in cancer-related and noncancer-related symptoms.
Not all patients had anxiety, depression, or treatment for these conditions, which could have influenced the results.
The sample was collected in five urban areas only and is not representative of the whole Chinese population, including rural residents.

Recruitment in public locations may have excluded people unable to go outside, biasing the sample towards healthier respondents and underreporting mobility and usual-activity problems; no correction was made.
The cross-sectional design cannot establish causal relationships or control unobserved heterogeneity; longitudinal data are needed.
Observed QALE inequalities might partly reflect different reporting styles across socioeconomic groups; the HSE had no validated anchoring vignettes to test this.
Available data included only quintiles of the composite Index of Multiple Deprivation, so the study could not examine inequalities across its seven component dimensions.
QALE calculations assumed that HRQoL below age 16 equaled HRQoL in the youngest observed age group, which could underestimate QALE if younger children have higher HRQoL.
Approximately 11% of otherwise eligible HSE participants had incomplete EQ-5D-5L responses and were excluded; missingness was higher among males and residents of the most deprived neighbourhoods.
Dimension contributions depend on the coverage of the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system and on the general-population value set; socioeconomic groups might value dimensions differently.
Because HSE adopted EQ-5D-5L only from 2017, these estimates are not directly comparable with earlier HSE estimates based on EQ-5D-3L and cannot provide a consistent long-term policy trend.

The weights for levels 2 and 4 of each dimension were not elicited but interpolated with Bézier interpolation, because only levels 1, 3 and 5 were included in the DCE to restrict the number of questions; the authors call this a potentially important limitation and an area for future research.

About half of the participants (2644 of 5112) were excluded, which could be considered a high rate of data wastage, and excluding participants who met the time threshold but failed the repeated-question consistency check could be regarded as too stringent since decision-makers are not always perfectly consistent.
The reasons for inconsistent answers (disengagement, misunderstanding, genuinely changed preferences or simple mistakes) could not be distinguished.
Almost half of the high-quality sub-sample found the DCE questions difficult to answer, and 13% said the dimension ranking produced by the DCE was not as they expected.
The comparison with other countries' value sets was cursory and further analysis would be worthwhile.
Validity of the partial-profile PAPRIKA questions depends on the assumption of joint factor independence, which was assessed only informally.

All respondents completed the bolt-on version; the authors considered a split design in which half completed the bolt-on and half completed the standard EQ-5D-5L more optimal because responses to one dimension can depend on responses to other dimensions.
Some clinical parameters came from earlier assessments than the 2017 EQ-5D-5L plus respiratory bolt-on questionnaire, although most parameters were stable during the three-year period.
English patients completed the descriptive system, but utilities were calculated with a Dutch tariff because no English EQ-5D-5L plus respiratory bolt-on tariff was available.
The EQ-5D-5L plus respiratory bolt-on was measured once, so responsiveness to clinical change could not be assessed.
The study could not assess responsiveness because too few adolescents reported improved or worsened health between baseline and follow-up.
Online data collection made it impossible to determine whether adolescents completed the HRQoL instruments with caregiver assistance.

The analysis covered self-reported descriptive-system data only. No EQ-5D-Y-5L value set was available, so the study could not assess comparability after preference weighting or the full implications for QALYs.
The post-hoc retrospective design makes residual confounding unavoidable.
Baseline (pre-PCI) quality of life was not available, so change in quality of life could not be assessed.

Adjustment for pre- and post-procedure characteristics does not sufficiently control confounding by indication, although the authors judge that this bias would favour worse 30-day quality of life in the prior CABG group.
Post-PCI ejection fraction was not recorded, preventing further analysis of the ejection-fraction subgroup findings.
A large number of patients (25,236) did not complete all five EQ-5D items and were excluded; non-completion was related to clinical characteristics and was addressed only by raking weights.
The purposive, non-probability sample was restricted to Buenos Aires residents, and the qualitative study did not aim to provide national generalizability.
The response-option ordering exercise had a small sample and exploratory analyses, which prevents firm quantitative conclusions about label ordering.
Loss to follow-up differed by sex and social participation, so selective attrition mechanisms cannot be ruled out and the direction of any bias is uncertain.
Whether symptoms predated the infection relied on recall two years after infection, so recall bias is possible.
Other potential influences such as unrelated health conditions, life events or reinfection were not assessed.
Men were overrepresented because of the sampling of the contributing cohorts, and some subgroups were underrepresented in the stratified analyses, so secondary patterns are exploratory.
The trend of decline in high baseline health and improvement in low baseline health may reflect moderate measurement reliability of the EQ measures or regression to the mean.
The EQ-5D-5L index is an aggregate score that does not separate physical and mental domains, limiting comparison with domain-specific studies.
Interval definitions for paths with fewer than three steps were assumptions that could have affected the modelling results.
A consistent heteroscedastic model could not be estimated, so the P values of the coefficients must be interpreted cautiously despite the use of cluster-robust standard errors.
The external validation data came only from one Spanish region (Canary Islands) and were not representative of the Spanish population.
Narrow intervals were more informative than wide ones, so the interval analysis emphasised respondents who understood the C-TTO task, which may affect generalizability.
