The EQ-VT protocol has since been updated to version 2 with quality control and a feedback module, so the robustness of this value set should be assessed with data from the newer protocol.
The single three-month follow-up interval limited conclusions about how recall bias and response shift depend on elapsed time; recall bias could be larger over longer intervals.

At T2, respondents completed current EQ-5D-3L and EQ VAS measures plus similarly worded recall and then tests. This difficult paper task could reduce complete responses and response quality, and the researchers could not verify understanding of the distinction between recall and then tests.
Use of EQ-5D-3L rather than the more sensitive and precise EQ-5D-5L may have reduced observed contrasts.
The low response rate and differences between completers and non-completers created possible participation bias, including possible underrepresentation of older patients with memory problems.

Even the expanded 23-state cTTO design was too small: few cTTO values were collected where the value curve bends most, and the design could not support model specifications other than main effects, so the decision between mapping functions rested largely on two outlying observations.

DCE and cTTO participants were sampled differently; cTTO data came from one island (Java) with quotas only on age and sex, so the cTTO values were less representative of the Indonesian adult population than the DCE values.
The number of observations per cTTO state was halved to about 100 to allow more states, which lowers the reliability of each individual data point.
Disability estimates relied on proxy reporting by household informants, which often under-identifies subjective problems such as mental and emotional difficulties.
Depression and other mental disorders are likely under-reported because they are not covered by the Washington Group Short Set.
Children younger than 5 years were excluded because the Washington Group Short Set is not validated for that age range, giving a skewed view of disability and of services required.
The number of refusals in Nyanga could have added to the disability prevalence and needs investigation.
The sample size was estimated using 2001 census data, because the proposal preceded release of the 2011 census.

The convenience sample came from a community-dwelling population and included recruitment at community hospitals. Selection bias and the high proportions of older and rural participants can limit generalization, especially to patient groups.
The study took place only in China, so the results might not apply to other countries or cultures.
Mild cognitive impairment was identified only with education-specific MMSE cut-offs. The study did not use a clinician opinion or diagnostic tests for validation.
The compound cognition items were hypothetical. Their scores assumed the worse level counts rule, so the study did not test how respondents would understand or answer the compound wording.
Recruitment from a volunteer pool in a patient organization's internal network may have favored patients in better health and caused selection bias.
All questionnaires were self-reported and could be affected by recall bias.
The web-based format could not fully guarantee data quality, and poor physical or mental health could reduce engagement with the long survey and affect reliability.
Clinical information, including comorbidities, was not collected from medical records because data collection was conducted with a patient association, which could affect validity.
The retrospective observational design without a counterfactual does not provide a rigorous assessment of rehabilitation effectiveness.

Selection bias and non-response bias were possible; patients with cognitive impairment were not invited, and differential loss to follow-up could occur among patients who completed only intake measurement.
EQ-5D-5L was not implemented at all Alberta community rehabilitation sites, so the sample was not fully representative.
Observed change could reflect regression to the mean, natural disease progression, aging, or comorbidity complications rather than rehabilitation.
The generic EQ-5D-5L may not detect all condition-specific or program-specific effects of rehabilitation.
Patients who reported problems at intake had more room to improve, which could overestimate associations in the bivariate analyses.
The EQ-5D-5L data could not be linked to other patient data, which limited analysis and interpretation and prevented assessment alongside other patient parameters.
Only intake and end-of-care snapshots were available, so the study could not establish how health would have changed without rehabilitation.
The study was conducted only in Indonesia; cultural and contextual differences can affect interpretation in other settings.
Online administration likely selected more urban and higher-income participants.
Participants with tertiary education were overrepresented, which may have affected dimension prioritization, including the prominence of cognition.
Health states used only levels 2 and 4; inclusion of level 5 might have produced different results.
Bolt-on order was fixed within each arm, so the first encountered bolt-on may have received more weight.
Forward and backward groups had different prior exposure to bolt-on health states, so outcomes such as EQ-5D-5L valuations are not comparable across the groups.
The effect of measurement reasoning on valuation outcomes remains uncertain; some coded instances may instead reflect expectations of conceptual coherence.
The data lacked detailed clinical information, such as severity, stage, symptoms, and functional limitations, which limited adjustment for underlying true health.
The general-population sample had limited variation in health. This required collapsed EQ-5D-5L response levels and exclusion of self-care from domain-specific models.
Online administration excluded people without internet access or enough computer literacy. The prior DCE quality-control exclusions could also select respondents with higher cognitive ability.

The original ZTPI has criticized construct validity and dimensionality. The 17-item version performed well in prior Hungarian psychometric tests, but some items might measure beliefs, values, preferences, or other constructs instead of time perspective.
The sample did not include inpatients, who are likely in worse functional status, so the patient-population difference may be under-estimated.
Only cardiovascular disease and cancer were studied, so specific findings may not generalise to other patient populations.
The general population sample was recruited in shopping malls, and the pleasant leisure setting could have affected valuation and representativeness.
The study was powered only for overall comparison of mean utility across all health states, not for separate mild, moderate and severe comparisons, so findings are exploratory.
The limited number of health states and sample size prevented evaluation of the impact of individual EQ-5D-5L dimensions on preference differences.
Findings are limited to valuation of hypothetical health states and may not generalise to valuation of experienced health states.
The analysis relied on level sum scores because Australian value sets were not available for either EQ-5D-Y-3L or EQ-5D-Y-5L.
The two-day test-retest sample was relatively small compared with the samples used for the other analyses.
The study did not include child–caregiver dyads, so self-report and proxy-report psychometric characteristics could not be compared directly.

The T3 response was low, and younger people, people with low or high education, and people with chronic disease were less likely to complete all three surveys; this selective attrition could affect estimated frequencies of consumption change.
Self-reported alcohol consumption is vulnerable to social-desirability bias and under-reporting.
Recruitment from voluntary internet panels could introduce selection bias and under-sample people with extreme or problematic alcohol intake.
Retrospective reporting of pre-pandemic alcohol consumption could introduce recall bias and threaten internal validity.
The design could not identify country-level contributors, such as government restriction stringency or alcohol-control policies, to observed country differences.

The later cognitive-interview rounds included healthy children only, so the overall sample contained many more healthy than sick children; future validation should include more children with health conditions.
One first respondent was excluded because of task confusion that could have resulted from unclear interviewer instructions, the child’s difficulty with the task, or both.
Only two of three sick questionnaire completers showed apparent disagreement between the descriptive profile and EQ VAS, so the authors cautioned against overinterpreting that pattern.
Itching had relatively low variability and few participants reported severe itching, possibly because assessment occurred at long-term follow-up.
Mapping the 10-level POSAS itching scale to five levels was arbitrary and may have caused autocorrelation and measurement bias.
The POSAS and EQ-5D-5L instructions used different timeframes, and POSAS assessed itching in the scar rather than over the whole body.
The cross-sectional design did not permit evaluation of within-person change or responsiveness of EQ-5D-5L + Itching.
The sample was much smaller than the number of possible profiles, which limited a fair estimate of Shannon Evenness.
The extent to which results are specific to the matched pairwise choice format, the fixed full-health alternative and the 10-year duration was not explored.
Efficient designs were not compared with other design generation approaches that do not need strategies to enhance the spread of the data.
No health state selection effect was found for DCE-death, but it is unknown whether this holds for other descriptive systems, such as disease-specific ones.
Assuming an unbounded normal distribution for the parameters may be inappropriate for monotonic attribute-level effects and may violate monotonicity.
Durations were presented in both months and years and converted to years, but respondents may not treat months and equivalent years in the same way.

Life tables and health-related quality-of-life data reflect current populations, so the estimates are period quality-adjusted life expectancies and medical and societal progress will change life expectancy and quality of life for future cohorts.

About 10% of Health Survey for England participants did not report their EQ-5D-5L health profile and were excluded, which may have introduced selection bias, although earlier work suggests imputation changes QALE by less than 0.01 QALYs.
Utilities were obtained by crosswalking EQ-5D-5L data to the EQ-5D-3L value set rather than by direct EQ-5D-5L valuation, with associated loss of information.

The Health Survey for England covers only the noninstitutionalized population and excludes people in care homes or hospitals, prisoners and asylum seekers, so health-related quality of life is likely overestimated.
The survey provides only a cross-sectional snapshot, so future health trajectories may differ from those observed.

EQ-5D-5L data were available only by grouped age band, so health-related quality of life was assumed constant within each band, and children aged 0 to 15 years were assumed to have the same health-related quality of life as those aged 16 to 17 years.
Life expectancy calculations assumed an average survival of 6 months in the year of death and closed the life table at age 100 years.
Differential loss to follow-up could have occurred among patients who completed only the baseline survey.
Missing data, the absence of a control arm, and the limited repeated-measure sample created methodological challenges.
The researchers could not link EQ-5D-5L records to other patient data, which limited the analysis.
The findings are not generalizable to other populations, although the authors considered them potentially transferable to similar primary care populations and programs.
The study did not confirm whether each proxy was the child's main caregiver.
The findings might not generalize to other pediatric conditions because diseases can affect child and proxy perspectives differently.
Responsiveness used proxy-reported EQ VAS improvement because no follow-up clinical data were collected; this subjective anchor was not optimal.
Relative Y-3L and Y-5L performance must be interpreted cautiously because analyses used a value-set index for Y-3L but a level sum score for Y-5L.
The study excluded children unable to self-report, which limits generalizability to more severely affected children who require proxy assessment.
Known-groups and responsiveness samples were small, and responsiveness was evaluated only for improvement.
The survey used only online video-conference interviews. There was no in-person explanation, and respondent comprehension, engagement, and interest were difficult to assess.
Each DCE perspective group had 500 respondents, which was smaller than the 1000 respondents suggested by the valuation protocol.
cTTO data were collected only from the child perspective, which prevented a comprehensive cTTO comparison between perspectives.
The sample had more respondents with postsecondary or degree education than the Hong Kong general population, which can limit generalizability.
The high proportion of older adults in Hong Kong and their limited access to technology reduced representativeness for that age group.
The main analyses considered only age and sex; ethnicity could also affect obsolescence, although a United States sensitivity analysis found no effect from changing ethnic composition.

Historical demographic shifts could be smaller than future changes, although the included countries had large shifts and the author judged them as large as or larger than projected changes over the next 20 to 25 years.
The analysis assumed that the original preference structure observed in each TTO dataset remained constant over time; the study could not directly test temporal change in health-state preferences.
Online panellists may not represent the United Kingdom and German general populations, and the diabetes and rheumatic-disease samples differed demographically from their patient populations.
The study did not collect data that identified when or why respondents in the German samples discontinued, which limits explanation of their low completion rates.
Respondents with suspicious or potentially implausible responses were not excluded beyond the stated anchor and German logical-rating rules because further exclusions would reduce sample sizes.
OPUF assumes an additive preference model and cannot practically account for interactions between EQ-HWB-S dimensions.
This was a first exploratory feasibility study, parts of the analysis were ongoing, and the results and value sets were preliminary.
OPUF is still a relatively new method and needs further refinement, validation, practical demonstration, and wider accessibility.

As exploratory work, no anchoring to the latent scale (for example a duration attribute) was included, so the estimates are not on the full health to dead utility scale and cannot yet be used to estimate QALYs.

As with all online studies, respondent engagement with the DCE task is difficult to assess, and no detailed qualitative information was collected on whether the imposed level overlap and shading supported completion.
Interactions between EQ-5D-5L and ASCOT dimension levels could not be assessed because this was beyond the scope of the exploratory design.
The wording and severity descriptors differ between the instruments, which may influence valuations and mask the importance of some domains.
Full randomisation of dimension order was not imposed, and an order effect was found, so the pooled estimates aggregate over the presentation orders.
The sample was more highly educated and more likely to be born in Australia than the general Australian population.
ASCOT utility scores for the sample had to be calculated with the UK value set because no Australian ASCOT value set is available.
A Hawthorne effect cannot be excluded: care quality could improve because health professionals know that they are being assessed, although the authors expect this effect to decline during follow-up.
Patients are likely to fail to report some use of private facilities.

The groups can have unbalanced reporting bias because multiple observers record integrated-care assessments, whereas one home-care team records all functional-care assessments; investigator training is intended to improve consistency.
Relatively few participants took part in the survey and all were members of the EuroQol Group; the authors plan to involve researchers outside the group in future.
Categorical responses and an arbitrarily chosen majority rule were used instead of the more common ranking and mean scores, although the authors argue the result would be unchanged.
CREATE reflects current theory and methodology in health preference measurement, so future methodological advances may require updating the checklist.

The combined impact of the interaction effects is not restricted to be smaller than the main effect of each domain, so illogical preference reversals are not precluded unless such a constraint is imposed when value sets are computed.

Positioning intermediate levels on a single optimal scale assumes that intermediate levels have a proportional impact on both main and interaction effects; this can be relaxed with separate scales only if the sample size permits.

Including interaction effects requires an experimental design that identifies main effects and interactions and a larger sample size, so the model is not estimable for many existing valuation studies optimised for main effects only, including EQ-5D-5L valuation studies that use only 86 of 3125 health states.

The most important limitation of the Australian cTTO application was the relatively small sample of 400 respondents, which precluded random parameters and left half of the interaction parameters with 90% or 95% credible intervals containing 0.

All combinations of mobility level 3 with level 1 usual activities and self-care (19% of possible health states) were blocked from the Australian design, which could explain the unexpected negative and significant self-care by usual activities interaction.

The DCE with duration design was not optimised for identifying 2-way interactions, did not comprise a QALY-balanced selection of health states, and was not optimised for measuring nonlinear duration preferences.
The sample was small, so the exploratory quantitative results can only suggest associations and patterns that need confirmation in larger studies.
Most participants were from Hamburg, Germany, and people with lower education were underrepresented, which limits population and geographic generalizability.
Selection bias is probable because participation required willingness to complete an ambulatory assessment.
The study did not establish full psychometric validity or reliability; larger studies must compare these properties with the standard EQ-5D-5L and confirm feasibility.

Repeated-assessment missing data were common and complicated score calculation; the study also could not calculate complete EQ-5D index scores at each alert because not all five items were administered each time.
The retrospective coverage approach can be affected by recall bias and still requires averaging within each short recall interval.
The CVP design had no multi-level improvements, which prevented direct estimation of conditional-logit main effects.
The fixed CSOR attribute order confounded positional behavior with attribute importance.
The inference that hold-outs reduce positional behavior came from a comparison of different surveys and designs rather than a randomized within-survey comparison.
The smaller-sample precision result was based on bootstrap simulation and requires confirmation in a subsequent valuation wave.
Available evidence did not support use of kaizen tasks with nominal attributes or attribute interactions.
The online mode of administration of the TTO is still experimental and yielded low task engagement, with most respondents using few iterations.
Values could not be compared with a non-experimental EQ-5D-5L tariff because the EQ-5D-5L valuation protocol was still under development, so mapped estimates had to serve as the comparator.
The different minimum attainable values across TTO specifications distort comparisons of mean values and of variances, so only tasks with comparable value ranges could be compared directly.
Larger standard deviations may reflect genuine preference heterogeneity rather than poorer task engagement.
The online panel was not fully representative: respondents were slightly older than the Dutch average and included more women.
The single-centre design limits generalizability; feasibility must be confirmed at the provincial level before province-wide implementation.
Patients reported that the EQ-5D-3L questions and three response levels could fail to capture the full range of quality-of-life experiences during cancer treatment.
In-person collection imposed a high coordinator burden and made recruitment and follow-up appointment identification cumbersome.
Measurement during chemotherapy can provide a suboptimal snapshot because treatment and moment-to-moment changes can influence responses.
Limited English fluency created a barrier for some otherwise eligible patients.

Significant interviewer effects may have biased the final estimation model; interviewers varied in mean moves per TTO task, time on task and use of negative valuation despite training, a pilot and quality control meetings.
The model was not validated because the sample size was insufficient, so all available data were used in estimation.
Respondents with the lowest educational level were under-represented relative to the general population, though education was not a significant modeling variable.
The study population comprised general public respondents only and might have missed forms of discomfort relevant only to patients with specific health conditions.
The survey was conducted in Hungarian, which may restrict generalisability of the interpretations of discomfort to other languages and populations.

Positioning the individual subdomains after the composites might have enhanced under-reporting in the composites, as repeated exposure to the same item may lead respondents to reconsider their previous response.
Questions about pain and discomfort preceded the EQ-5D and individual subdomains for worst recalled health, which might have caused overstating of pain and discomfort for worst recalled health.
Associations between respondent characteristics and discomfort interpretation were tested only with univariate analyses, so the independence of these associations could not be assessed.
All coding was performed by one researcher and may therefore be prone to errors.
Recruitment challenges in routine care limited the sample to 140 participants rather than the originally planned 280.
The trial did not compare the individualized PROMs-based decision aid with a standard, nonindividualized patient decision aid.
The decision aid had individualized PROM data for surgical patients but not for nonsurgical patients, so evidence from other studies informed the nonsurgical sections.
The sample size was not powered to detect significant differences in the secondary outcomes reported at approximately 1 year.
Surgical expectations were measured with one broad question only at approximately 1 year; participants could have forgotten their specific presurgical expectations.

Deciding the robust number of clusters involved analyst judgement rather than exact criteria, and cluster analysis gives extremely weak evidence about whether value sets generate clusters; the methods suit specifying known clusters better than detecting unknown ones.

Generalisability is limited because the data come from three specific patient samples that differ from the populations previously analysed for the EQ-5D-3L, and evidence on the 5L value distribution is at an early stage.
Respondents lived mainly on Java island, so representativeness for the whole archipelago is uncertain; interviews in Sumatera, Kalimantan and Papua would be needed to test for differences.
The retest interval overlapped the WHOQOL-BREF four-week reference period, which might bias the test-retest results.
The COVID-19 pandemic prevented an in-person presentation, which could have reduced the interaction between participants.
The small number of experts in patient preferences and outcome research limited the discussion of the more complex issues.

The authors note that the prioritisation proposal remains a live document, that it is difficult to summarise quality and confidence criteria for utility data in a single table, and that only trained experts can judge complex examples.
The study was uncontrolled, so placebo effects and natural symptom evolution could not be excluded.
The small sample limited detailed subgroup analysis and may have reduced power in the radiotherapy subgroup.
The sample was heterogeneous in treated symptoms and tumor types, especially in the radiation-induced subgroup.
It is not known whether findings from the Taiwan population generalize to other populations with similar health preferences.
The added willingness-to-accept question increased task complexity, and participant comprehension and deliberation could not be assured.
The analysis assumed proportional cTTO trade-offs regardless of respondents remaining life expectancy, which may not hold.
Some extreme responses may represent aversion rather than valuation; interval regression cannot resolve this distinction, and the embedded design could not vary lead-time and disease-time ratios.
The study did not address discounting introduced by longer alternative lead-times.
Normative problems in applying utility to QALYs were outside scope, including implausible gains above one QALY without life extension.

The raw sample overrepresented women and urban residents. Survey weights corrected those imbalances, but differences from the Romanian population can remain because official control data did not fully account for emigration.
The five interview blocks had a fixed, nonrandom order. EQ-5D-3L and the second EQ VAS were completed after EQ-5D-5L and the valuation tasks, which could have influenced responses.
The long interview could have caused fatigue and satisficing near the end and reduced the quality of EQ-5D-3L responses.
The informal comparison with other Central and Eastern European surveys used studies from different years and administration modes; health and EQ-5D values could have changed over time.
The predominantly female sample (94.2%) limits generalizability to male caregivers and mixed-gender populations.
The pre-post design had no control group, which limits causal inference and permits regression to the mean and time-varying confounding.
A single nonblinded interviewer and self-reported outcomes could introduce interviewer and social desirability bias.
The Perceived Change Scale was collected only at six months, so baseline comparison was not possible.
Income reporting could be biased because participants relied on social benefits and might underreport earnings.
Six months was too short to determine whether improvements were sustained.
The specific setting of vulnerable Brazilian families with chronically ill children limits generalizability to other populations, cultures, and social-intervention models.
Subjective VAS ratings can be affected by perception, emotional state, and response bias, which can reduce sensitivity in small or heterogeneous samples.
Covid-19 restrictions on school recruitment may have introduced non-response bias.
Home completion in the chronic and general population samples could not be verified as unassisted despite explicit instructions to parents.
A relatively high ceiling effect, most notably in the general population sample, may have influenced the correlations between measures.
The non-randomised fixed order of the questionnaires may have produced an order effect.
Only English questionnaires were used, so people who speak or write one of the other ten official South African languages may be under-represented.
No ethnicity or socio-economic detail was collected, limiting judgement of the generalisability of the sample.
Reasons for refusal of consent or assent and reasons for missing data were not recorded.
The distribution of responses across the EQ-5D-Y and PedsQL descriptive systems cannot be directly compared because of different severity versus frequency reporting and recall periods.
Although EQ-TIPS was designed for ages 1–36 months, the available P-MIC subset included only children aged 2–3 years; validity in infants aged 1–24 months remains to be studied.
Health conditions were reported by parents rather than confirmed from hospital records or clinician assessments; condition-specific samples were small and few children had severe conditions.
In the absence of preference weights, EQ-TIPS was summarized with a crude level sum score that gives equal weight to dimensions and can assign the same score to different health profiles.
The responsiveness sample was small, worsening health could not be examined, and responsiveness was not tested during an intervention or treatment with clinical measures.

No South African value set exists, so utility scores had to be derived with the Slovenian value set, with the Japanese value set as a check; no consideration could be given to factors such as literacy level or social structure of the source countries.
No data on race, home language or socioeconomic status were collected, so the general population results cannot be generalised to the greater Western Cape region.
There was a high proportion of non-responders among 8-10-year-olds (n = 260, 55%) and the reasons for non-response or refusal of consent or assent were not collected.
A high number of children with orthopaedic problems (n = 21, 20%) withdrew during interviews.

Responses may be affected by social desirability bias in interviewer administration, acquiescence bias, and observation bias strengthened by the interviewer also being the physiotherapist who rated the WeeFIM.
This is the first study to use the MFQ as a comparator for the Worried, Sad or Unhappy dimension, so comparison with other studies was not possible.
The program had not determined whether access to PRM information changes clinician behavior.

The authors noted instrument-specific limits: EQ-5D-5L had a high ceiling effect and low effect-size variability, NDDI-E responsiveness to change was unclear, and TSQM had not been validated in people with epilepsy.

The centre had conducted no implementation study to test how to improve patient uptake or optimize clinical use, and the perceived increase in completion after electronic implementation was not formally evaluated.
The high volume of search results led to many exclusions at title screening, which could have excluded relevant articles.
Psychometric appraisal was restricted to original work by instrument developers, so later psychometric evaluations were not included.
The review included only peer-reviewed and English-language material, so relevant gray literature and local-language studies could have been missed.
The CASP case-control checklist was used to appraise cross-sectional studies because a specific appraisal tool for cross-sectional designs was unavailable.
The internet-recruited convenience sample can differ from people who do not respond to internet survey requests.
The sample differed from national birth statistics in race, age, and educational attainment. Post-stratification weighting could not fully remove response bias or limits to generalizability.
The cross-sectional design does not permit causal conclusions.
The Health Belief Model constructs were proxy measures rather than direct questions about children's perceived risk and disease severity, so direct measures could produce different results.
The evidence and solutions are not intended to be definitive because each obsolescence case can require a response tailored to local conditions.
The authors did not reach consensus on who should monitor and declare obsolescence; responsibility can lie with instrument developers, end users, or both and can differ by jurisdiction.
The framework does not specify how large a value difference must be to justify new valuation work; the authors state that this may require case-by-case judgment and can be unanswerable.
The validity definition is tentative because there is rarely an external gold standard for HRQoL values and no agreed definition of validity in this context.
The sample came from one country and one geographical location, which can limit transferability.
The focus groups occurred in two periods 16 months apart because of a funding break, and views could have changed during that interval.
Themes identified in early groups could have influenced and restricted later discussions, although the researchers explored less-developed ideas and reported saturation.
The authors state that dignity was not included because no data were available, although this statement conflicts with the procedure, which lists dignity among the five included consequences.
The way the comparison information was presented, including omitted information, could have influenced participants despite efforts to present both sides.
The sample is small and not representative, being a convenience sample of ten respondents from Groningen.

The eye tracker could not capture eye movements precisely for respondents wearing glasses because of lens reflection, so three respondents were excluded even though many members of the general public need glasses to read the tasks.
The device precision of 0.5-1 degrees was critical when designating small areas of interest for individual attribute statements, so more sophisticated equipment would be needed.

The analysis assumes that information that is seen is also cognitively processed, but eye movements do not necessarily reflect cognitive processing and peripheral viewing may allow attention outside the fixated area.
Only fixation number and length were used; pupil dilation and eye blinks, which index cognitive load and processing shifts, were not investigated.
COVID-19 restrictions limited data collection to one wave, so test-retest reliability and responsiveness could not be evaluated.

No EQ-5D-Y-5L preference-based value set was available, and the analysis used adult United States EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L values for childhood health states; this limits the empirical-validity assessment.
Cut points used to dichotomize self-rated general health and PedsQL scores were necessarily arbitrary and could change the conclusions.
Only 12 children aged 8-12 years were healthy, which may have distorted the child known-group comparison.

The study used a convenience sample in one urban Malawian setting, and the authors state that limited use of pediatric preference-based HRQoL measures in sub-Saharan Africa restricts wider African generalization.

The protocol relies on online surveys through a marketing panel and may not generalize to the United States general population, especially people with less education and people who do not participate in online surveys or panels.
The article provides only the wave 1 survey instrument, experimental design, and analysis plan because the authors will adapt the wave 2 materials after they review wave 1 evidence.
The online survey may underrepresent people with limited internet access or low digital literacy and may reduce generalizability.
Quota sampling used broad age bands, while analysis used narrower age groups; differential response rates can bias the age-specific findings.
The study did not analyze utility values, so it does not show how component- and composite-level responses affect utility measurement or health technology assessment.
The general population sample may not generalize to clinical populations, including groups with a higher prevalence of self-care problems.
Composites preceded component items and component order was fixed, so the study cannot separate true first-component effects from presentation-order bias.

The simple DCE used one full-factorial design with three alternatives, 200 respondents, 25 choice sets, a constant, and one variable for each alternative; results may differ for larger studies with more complex designs and models.
The data-generation process used only lognormal random parameters; symmetric or discrete distributions may give different results.
The specifications represented interpersonal heterogeneity only and did not include intrapersonal variability in a person's parameters across tasks.

Children as young as 8 years might have insufficient experience with poor health to judge comprehensiveness and relevance, although indirect experience was elicited and children with chronic conditions were recruited.
The study did not examine the relative importance of elicited health dimensions, including dimensions in the EQ-5D-Y descriptive system.
Content validity was assessed only for the EQ-5D-Y descriptive system and not for EQ VAS, so the findings cannot be applied to EQ VAS instructions, labels, or response format.
The cTTO data came from respondents in four countries whereas the DCE data came from one country, so alignment between the two datasets may be worse than when both come from the same country.
The selection of health states used in the cTTO task differs from that of other EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation studies, limiting comparability.
A conditional logit model was used although alternative models have been shown to fit the DCE data better, because consistency with the hybrid model approach was required.
Only linear mapping without a constant was examined, although other specifications such as a constant, non-linear terms, or modelled cTTO predictions for all 243 states could be tested.
Further research is needed on the hybrid model experimental design, sample size requirements, and the impact of the relative proportions of DCE and cTTO data on the resulting value sets.

The EuroQol database counts used for international comparison are only approximate, because records identified for each country can differ from the number of studies meeting the review inclusion criteria.

The distribution of clinical areas in CEE cannot be compared with other countries or regions because no equivalent classified data, such as ICD groups or diagnoses, exist for globally registered EQ-5D studies.
Multicountry randomised controlled trials that did not report individual CEE country results were excluded, which may partly explain the low observed share of randomised trials.
Completion of both similar EQ-5D versions could have caused respondent fatigue or box-picking, although the version presented first was randomized.
The RPQ was developed for post-concussion symptoms and not specifically to assess fatigue in the general population.
Recall periods differed: EQ-5D asked about health today, whereas the RPQ fatigue item referred to the past 24 hours.
The web-based survey had no predefined sampling frame, so selective non-response and possible overrepresentation could not be assessed.

The Integrated Values Survey and World Bank databases contained many missing values, reducing the dataset from about 500,000 to 157,583 (and 100,590) respondents, mainly due to missing macroeconomic data and unasked survey questions.
Survey waves were collapsed into a single wave, assuming that the association between cultural values and self-reported health does not change over time.
Cultural subgroups within countries may show different associations than the country-level aggregate, and this could not be controlled for.
Differences in response styles between countries may affect self-reported health, but the World Values Survey holds no information on response styles.
Linear regression was used although self-reported health is categorical; a conditional probit model would have been more appropriate but less easy to interpret across levels.

The study used an other-adult perspective for adult valuations and an other-child perspective for child valuations. This design differs from studies that used self-perspectives and limits direct comparison with them.
The fixed-choice bisection procedure differed from the EQ-5D titration procedure used in earlier work and could produce different valuations or strategic responses.
The sample contained only Dutch respondents, which limits external validity and leaves possible country-specific effects untested.
The 10-year TTO duration and lead time mean that part of the valuation period concerns adult years when respondents take the perspective of a 10-year-old child.
The study considered only a 10-year-old child, whose health priorities might not represent the full EQ-5D-Y-3L age range.
The relatively small sample and small number of tasks could contribute to differences in equity weights between treatment contexts.
Data were collected by video interview, and equivalence with in-person interviews was not established.
VAS values were not anchored at dead = 0, which hampered comparison with TTO and led the authors to place the VAS analysis in the supplement.
The model assumed that full health had the same utility for adults and children; the authors noted that unequal full-health values could also affect PTO preferences.
The free text comments were coded by one researcher with no formal secondary coding.
The content analysis counted comments and therefore assumes each comment carries the same strength.
The reliability of the online DCE with duration used as the baseline is itself uncertain and was beyond the scope of the study.
Non-iterative tasks yield no cardinal value per respondent, and non-iterative TTO without lead time must extrapolate values below zero from ordinal preferences observed in the positive range.
Many included studies used different classifications of complications and co-morbidities, which made pooling of results difficult and restricted pooled means to six subgroups.

Variability in reported scores may be caused by differing study populations, inclusion criteria, small sample sizes and the value set used, for example the unexplained low general-population value of 0.61 in one Swedish study and small samples in the Greek and Spanish studies.

Pooled means for micro- and macrovascular complications were higher than the pooled general population mean, indicating heterogeneity in the general population group with Type 2 diabetes; the retinopathy subgroup is wholly contained within the microvascular subgroup, explaining its wider confidence interval.
Articles published in languages other than English or Spanish were excluded.

The guidance represents the consensus view of a purposively sampled group of subject-matter experts, and acceptance of invitations may have produced a group sharing the view that inclusion of spillovers is important.
No members from Latin America participated, so practices and implications of spillover incorporation in that and other regions remain poorly understood.

The scope was restricted to spillovers on family member and caregiver health-related quality of life from a healthcare system or health payer perspective, so impacts on others, wider welfare effects and interactions with broadly incurred costs were not fully examined.
The task force did not differentiate first-order from second-order spillovers, and gave limited consideration to cascade effects from shared genetic information.
Consultation with patients and caregivers was restricted to the later stages of the process, which may have limited the potential for their input to shape discussions.

The 2019 interviews were face to face, whereas the 2024 EQ-VT interviews used videoconference; this mode difference could introduce sampling bias because people who agree to online interviews can differ from those who agree to face-to-face interviews.
The online DCE survey was at risk of responses from bots; reCAPTCHA v3 and manual review of an open-ended answer reduced but could not eliminate this concern.
The 2024 study was a small-scale replication rather than a complete valuation study because collecting cTTO data is expensive and logistically difficult.
The 2024 online DCE used an expanded 19-task design, whereas the 2019 study used only the standard seven-task design; estimates and consistency therefore also depended on design.
The study was not powered to detect specific differences among particular study groups.

The design of the qualitative and quantitative stages cannot guarantee that the results are widely valid for the Argentine population; the psychometric sample was significantly younger than the face validity sample.
Online data collection restricted participation to people able to self-complete rather than being interview-administered, which may have affected the results.
Known-group analysis compared healthy people with people with some health condition and did not assess discriminant ability within specific disease groups.
The cross-sectional design meant that change over time could not be assessed.
Argentina was the only Spanish-speaking country and culture in the collaboration, so cultural and linguistic adaptation to other Spanish-speaking contexts remains for future studies.

cTTO data were collected through videoconferencing interviews rather than the recommended face-to-face interviews because of COVID-19 lockdown measures; sample selection due to recruitment strategy may affect the collected values.
Soft quota sampling for the cTTO led to over-sampling of highly educated respondents.
The DCE survey under-sampled respondents with the lowest attained education and over-sampled lower-middle and upper-middle educated respondents.

The performance of the cTTO health state design used here cannot be compared directly with the design recommended by Ramos-Goni et al., because the recommended design is not a subset of the design used.
Sampling problems may be partly related to using panel companies for recruitment of both samples.
Respondents within households are selected by the birthday rule, which is only a quasi-probability selection procedure, although it is the easiest and least time-consuming to train and administer.

Survey weights must be based on 2011 census data that have not been updated for the large and growing number of Romanian emigrants, so the weights may not correct the representativeness of the two samples accurately.
The samples include only people residing in Romania at the time of data collection, while about 17% of the population (3.3 million of 19.6 million), many of them of Roma ethnicity, work abroad.
The troubled political context in Romania may lower the propensity to participate, especially in urban areas, causing lower than predicted response rates and non-response bias.

The Roma survey uses self-identification, which does not overlap with hetero-identification; self-identified Roma tend to be more impoverished and more residentially segregated, so the comparison may overestimate differences between the two groups.

People living in nursing homes and other institutions were poorly represented in SHARE wave 4 (0.75%), so no in-depth analysis of institutionalized older people was possible, and nursing home residents were excluded for Denmark, Poland and Slovenia.
The data were collected in 2011 and 2012, and population health in some countries may have changed since then because of migration, healthcare system change or economic factors.
As in all household health surveys, selection bias may be present, leading to underrepresentation of institutionalized and vulnerable populations.
Using the European VAS value set to derive index values, while needed for cross-country comparison, hampered comparison with other studies that used country-specific value sets.
The EQ-5D-3L was used although the EQ-5D-5L is a more refined version with robustly better measurement properties.
Comparisons with other norm studies were complicated by differently defined age groups, different value sets and aggregation of levels 2 and 3.
Educational years had many missing values (n valid = 28 527 of 50 013), so the education data did not allow a conclusive picture of the sample.
Interpretation of cross-national results is complex and would benefit from longitudinal data and an explicit theoretical framework, which this study did not use.

Recruitment through an online panel can cause sampling bias, participant self-selection, inattention, and inability to verify that reported child self-completion occurred, although P-MIC used quality checks and minimum quality criteria.
Several subgroup analyses, especially reliability analyses, had inadequate sample sizes and could not be reported dependably.
Autism was defined by caregiver report of a diagnosis by a health professional and was not confirmed with a multidisciplinary assessment.
Responsiveness could not be evaluated because too few children reported a health-state change between the initial and follow-up surveys.
The representativeness of the Dynata panels could not be directly evaluated, which can limit generalizability.
Weighting cannot fully remove residual bias related to unobserved characteristics such as health literacy, digital access, socioeconomic vulnerability, or propensity to participate.
Dynata is a nonprobability convenience panel and can introduce selection bias.

The sample over-represented respondents with higher education and under-represented those with primary education, partly because primary-educated people are mostly older and rural and appeared to find the valuation tasks difficult.

Severity descriptors were highlighted in red to help respondents distinguish similar traditional Chinese characters, a deviation from other countries' studies whose effect on giving up all life years is unknown.
Interviewer effects were observed, possibly related to protocol violations, data quality and EQ-VT data collection, and their impact on modelling results was not established.

Only practice-level data were available, not individual patient data; therefore, the study could not relate condition-specific clinical quality measures to the health of patients with those conditions.

The study used retrospective observational data and could have confounding, although the authors used extensive practice and patient-population covariates and practice fixed effects to reduce this risk.

The tTTO tasks were piggybacked onto the valuation study, so the EQ-VT cTTO tasks had to be presented first; it is unclear whether experience with the EQ-VT affected tTTO responses, and future studies should randomize the order.
Only 18 of the 86 health states were valued with tTTO and only two severe states per participant, and selection of the 18 severe states was made arbitrarily by the authors.
Negative tTTO values required arbitrary transformation (division by 19) to be bounded at -1.
The mode of administration was not randomised and the study was designed as two national valuation studies rather than as an experiment comparing modes.

Potential sources of variability were not controlled at the design stage, namely interviewer learning effects, respondent demographics and possible changes in health preferences caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, which limits generalisation.
Splitting the face-to-face interviews into the first 20 and subsequent interviews reduced statistical power and may have hidden real differences between modes of administration.

In Spain, interviewers were inactive for five months and one was retrained before the videoconference interviews, so learning effects may also have occurred during the videoconference phase; the small sample size prevented testing them.

Recruitment quotas targeted national representativeness rather than balance between the comparison subgroups, so age, sex, location and education cells were unevenly filled and further subgroup analysis was not possible.
Sample homogeneity may also have been affected by respondents information technology skills, because recruitment for videoconference interviews depended on their feasibility.
Values were elicited from the perspective of a 10-year-old child rather than the respondent own perspective, which future controlled comparisons should use.
A learning effect is possible in the 2017 study because respondents completed the EQ-5D-3L after valuation tasks for the EQ-5D-5L.
Limited shared covariates between the two data sources leave the possibility of unmeasured confounding, for example socioeconomic status affecting how health issues are viewed.
Fitting EQ-5D-3L responses to the VAS may be endogenous, because it is unclear whether rating health problems influences the VAS or the global health evaluation influences reporting of problems.
Generalizability to the US general population extends only to people similar in age, ethnicity, race and health to the two samples.
The study gives limited insight into specific population subgroups and into the complexity of factors that shape health perceptions.
The two source studies differed in sampling strategy and in mode of administration and VAS presentation (pen and paper in 2002 versus computer in 2017).
The sample of 1182 was smaller than samples in some other population-norm studies.
The sample was about four years younger than the Italian adult population and underrepresented people older than 65 years, so mean index and EQ VAS values were likely overestimated.
Videoconference participation required basic computer skills and may have contributed to the age imbalance.
Interviewer administration may have caused social desirability bias, especially for sensitive EQ-5D dimensions such as anxiety/depression.
The analysis used a simple linear model for EQ-5D data although generalized linear models were an alternative.
Data were collected during the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, so exceptional events and government restrictions may have affected self-reported health.
Effect sizes cannot be compared between the two datasets because VAS wording and the number of education categories differed.
Generalizability is limited because all data came from high-income settings.
The ten selected EQ-5D-5L profiles mainly represented relatively healthy respondents, and larger samples are needed to test more severe health states.
Educational attainment was the only socioeconomic-position proxy; other indicators such as income could give different information, although income has reporting and reverse-causality concerns.
The analysis tested possible underestimation against only one subjective outcome, EQ VAS, whose psychometric properties vary; other health outcome measures are needed.
The investigators administered the 25-item EQ-HWB and derived EQ-HWB-S results from its nine items; they did not administer EQ-HWB-S as a separate instrument.
The sample was too small for subgroup analysis by caregiver gender.
The study did not collect longitudinal outcome data that could test responsiveness to change, which is important for QALY use.
The analysis used the only available pilot United Kingdom EQ-HWB-S value set, and Australian-specific preference weights were not available.

The baseline response rate was 21%, and differential nonresponse and the long original P-MIC survey could limit generalizability; the investigators also could not track invitees to compare this sample directly with P-MIC.
Probable reversed responses to the first three EQ-HWB items at baseline may have affected results, although the investigators retained these responses and observed no similar anomaly at follow-up.
No statistical measure exists to compare hybrid econometric models with cTTO-only or DCE-only models, since AIC, BIC, mean square error and mean absolute error cannot be applied to a hybrid model.
Known biases of the cTTO task, namely scale compatibility and loss aversion, and lexicographic responses in DCE, are neither compensated nor removed by combining the two techniques.
Face-to-face computer-assisted personal interviewing is expensive and can be a significant limitation for studies with a limited budget.
Excluded respondents may not be mistaken but instead reveal personal characteristics or family and social context effects, and there is no golden rule for exclusion criteria in valuation studies.

Alternative preference elicitation methods still need exploration because of methodological challenges in measuring preferences in particular groups such as children, the elderly, and specific diseases.
The quality control process was outside the scope of this paper, so its results are not described.
Anchors were elicited for a child aged 10 years and may not apply to younger or older children; respondents often said that child age would affect their answers.
DCE-with-duration results depended on design and model specification, and child-perspective models produced logically inconsistent utility orderings because duration dominated some choices.
Most respondents did not classify 33333 consistently across VAS, TTO, and LOD methods, and the study did not explain why methods produced different answers within persons.
LOD rescaling combined current responses with latent utilities from a separate sample and therefore assumed strong agreement between the two samples' preferences.
The LOD method inferred utility functions from limited information and had no agreed way to locate dead when a respondent considered dead worse than 33333 and outside the descriptive system.
The adult task used the respondent's own health, whereas the child task used another person's health, so differences can reflect self-versus-other perspective as well as age.
The complex four-method, two-perspective design restricted the number of tasks per method; more VAS and TTO states could have tested whether the pattern for 33333 held across the health-state range.

The lag-time TTO scenario for a 10-year-old extends into young adulthood, so traded time can include adult and child years; its minimum value and severe-state distribution also depend on the ratio and amount of lag time.
Participant burden limited the study to five instruments, so important comparator measures could have been excluded.
No adults with genetic intellectual disability were interviewed because the think-aloud method was not sufficiently inclusive; only three carers of such adults participated.
The qualitative approach provided detailed insights but cannot confirm formal instrument validity, generalisability, or responsiveness without additional quantitative analyses.
The sample was predominantly female and highly educated, which can limit generalisability.
Results are based on complete case analysis representing 67% to 81% of the original cohort, and those lost to follow-up had poorer baseline health, so a missing-at-random assumption is unlikely.
The MID estimate treated as a threshold of meaningful change cannot indicate how difficult it is to achieve a change at least as large as the MID.
Estimates require further testing and validation with other methods and in other clinical contexts, including approaches that seek patient input directly.

All samples were general population children and adolescents, so no evidence is available on EQ-5D-Y performance in clinical or specific populations, and school-based recruitment excluded severely ill children.
Ethical constraints prevented collection of objective clinical data, so known-groups validity relied on self-report screeners and associations may reflect same-source-of-information bias.
Sensitivity to change (responsiveness) and content validity of the EQ-5D-Y were beyond the scope of the paper.
Large ceiling effects limited computation and interpretation of kappa coefficients and correlations, and national samples were not designed to be representative.
Respondents completed the EQ-5D-5L before the paired comparisons, so showing the items and labels in advance biases the estimated prevalence of preference inversions downward.
The U.S. and Brazilian samples differ demographically, particularly in age, which may affect the health preference evidence.
Only labels in the existing English and Brazilian Portuguese versions were tested; alternative labels or translations were not explored.
The Version Management Team replaced the Brazilian mobility Level 5 wording with the European Portuguese wording, complicating interpretation of the results.
Recruitment used two clinical convenience samples (a cancer center infusion clinic and a cardiology institute) rather than general population samples, although the clinical focus is also a strength.
The general-population sample contained few respondents at the two most severe levels of each bolt-on item.
A block of other health questions between EQ-5D-5L and the bolt-ons could have affected responses, and the fixed order of the nine bolt-ons could have caused order effects.
Explanatory-power analyses could be affected by heterogeneous interpretation and scoring of EQ VAS and by the content of PROMIS Global Health and SWLS.
Using level sum scores alone for known-group validity can equate response combinations with different overall severity and can therefore introduce bias.
Known-group tests did not evaluate clinical severity and were restricted to health condition, age, general health, and well-being groups.

The CFA had too few items for cognition and no condition-specific comparison items for vision, hearing, breathing, or skin irritation; this likely caused four distinct constructs to load on one other-physical-symptoms factor.
Analyses that used external measures depended on the validity of those measures.

The web-based survey excluded people without computer or internet access and people who could not read or understand the survey; this may have caused participation bias and underrepresentation of people with low health literacy or low socioeconomic status.
The recruitment system did not permit a detailed analysis of nonresponders.
Educational level was used as a proxy for socioeconomic status instead of an indicator that also included income or financial security.

The study used level sum scores rather than country-specific utility scores because no Italian EQ-5D-5L value set was available; use of the Dutch or UK value set for Italy would have been arbitrary and would mix profile differences with differences in health-state preferences.
EQ-5D may not include all health aspects important to Māori, such as spirit, environment, the Māori world, and family.
Selection bias is possible because completion of an online survey can depend on computer and internet access, available time, and confidence.
Males, people aged 18-24 years, and people with income of $20,000 or less were under-represented; people with post-secondary education and people with long-term disability were over-represented.
Because higher income and education are associated with higher utility, mean EQ VAS and utility values may be higher than values from a more representative sample.
TTO tasks were self-administered without close interviewer supervision, so respondents may have made mistakes or indicated indifference randomly.
Time preference was not assessed or adjusted for in the analysis, although it may be important in lead-time TTO.
Study participants were Asian, so culture-specific valuation behaviour may limit generalisability to Western populations.

No restriction was placed on the methods of patient selection, so the included samples came from a variety of injury settings and their conclusions may not apply to injury patients from other settings.
The review covered a broad range of injury types and severity levels, which may complicate comparability of results between studies.

More than half of the included studies had recruitment and follow-up difficulties, with patients who could not be contacted, had died, refused, or could not complete questionnaires, limiting the generalisability of their results.
In some included studies pre-injury HRQL was assessed months to years after the injury, which may have inflated recalled pre-injury EQ-5D scores.

Not all included studies reported HRQL scores in text or tables, so in three publications the scores had to be read manually from graphs, which may cause small differences in the reported pre- and post-injury levels.
Many bolt-ons were developed ad hoc, have limited validation, may not align with EuroQol standards, and can interact with core dimensions in ways that complicate valuation.
Valuing child and very-young-child health states raises methodological and normative challenges that are greater than those for adult health states.
Further work is needed to ensure that instruments are relevant and comparable across disparate health, socioeconomic, cultural, and Indigenous groups and in the oldest age groups.
EQ-TIPS, EQ-HWB, and bolt-ons are experimental and are not yet widely available because validation, translatability, and minimum language-version evidence are incomplete.
New valuation methods can produce value sets with characteristics that differ from older sets, and no settled rule identifies when an old value set becomes obsolete.
Differences between age-specific descriptive systems and value sets can cause discontinuities in measurement and valuation at transitions across the lifespan.
The wording of the EQ-HWB candidate items differed slightly from the experimental version, although the authors considered the differences unlikely to affect the results.
Recruitment through an online panel company depended on its selection system and can cause selection bias, which limits assessment of sample representativeness.
Health conditions were self-reported, so the study could not confirm whether they had been clinically diagnosed.
The sample was young and highly educated, which limits representativeness and limits use of the score distributions as normative data.
EQ-5D-5L is not designed to measure well-being, so the comparison cannot support conclusive claims about the well-being component of EQ-HWB.
Caregiver status was self-reported, care type was not specified, and caregiving burden was not measured directly.
Alternative model specifications were explored only to a limited extent because the EQ-VT experimental design was optimized for a main-effects model.

Generalizability to the US general population may be limited because data collection took place in metropolitan areas and during the summer, and a seasonal effect has been detected in self-reported health, although it is unclear whether stated preferences for hypothetical states are affected by season.
Quota sampling was based on the US Census, which does not ask about citizenship status, so the sampling approach pertains to US residents rather than citizens.

Children with surgical conditions are relatively few in number, so data collection may be challenging, in particular for identifying parents and healthcare professionals; this will be mitigated by a thorough recruitment strategy.

No prior studies exist to supply prior values, so accurate power calculations are not possible and the sample size relies on typical sample sizes in the health literature and simple minimum sample size rules, with a pilot of about 80 respondents used to assess power.
Existing paediatric quality of life instruments have not been validated in children with a surgical condition, so quality of life is represented in the descriptive system only as good, fair or poor.
The external validity of the summary metric algorithm will not be assessed in this study but in a separate study.

Differences in study designs, language versions, and survey methods limited generalizability and could confound psychometric test outcomes; the broad moderator groupings did not permit the more granular analysis that the authors preferred.
The review included only English-language reports, which excluded evidence from non-English-speaking populations and further limited generalizability.
Cognitive debriefing involved only 10 caregivers, which could have failed to identify difficulty with the translated concept of health or the EQ VAS.

Age and health-care group were associated: most inpatients were aged 0-12 months, most outpatients were aged 12-24 months, and most crèche children were aged 24-36 months. This made age-related instrument performance difficult to separate from health-group effects.
The inpatient and outpatient samples had heterogeneous diagnoses, and many caregivers did not know the child's health concern.

Independent completion may have been difficult for crèche caregivers; seven crèche baseline packs were excluded for high missingness, and a researcher was available for clarification in the hospital but not reported for the crèche group.

The investigators did not record reasons for changes in dimension responses, and the retest sample consisted of generally healthy crèche children with little variation in reported problems rather than children with stable health conditions.
The study could not determine the causal direction between care setting and health or quality of life, so care-setting results were descriptive.
The study could not control for respondent cognitive status, and mental conditions may have been underrepresented despite concerns about EQ-5D use in dementia.
The convenience sample was unlikely to be representative, so results cannot be generalized to the full population of older aged care recipients.

The two-stage recruitment process may have caused positive selection because people with poor self-perceived health or low interest often refused, and severely ill or highly dependent nursing-home residents may be underrepresented.
Quota sampling from an online panel does not address unobservable factors and typically underrepresents people with low income and low educational attainment.

Non-white respondents other than Hispanic and black or African American were underrepresented compared with the 2010 US Census, possibly because of missing quotas for other racial categories and no 'two or more races' option.

The study did not use the interview-based TTO approach or the constant proportionality assumption used in the six other country-specific EQ-5D-5L valuation studies, which complicates comparison between value sets.
Differences in EQ-5D translation into non-English languages may explain further differences between country value sets.

The sample did not reach the targeted 1000 respondents, because of the COVID-19 pandemic and general difficulty recruiting from a short list of randomly selected, geographically dispersed candidates; the authors argue the smaller sample still gives sufficient power for the more parsimonious selected model.

More interviewers worked in the field than foreseen in the protocol because of replacements and drop-outs, and part of the variability in the data, particularly in states valued worse than dead, appears attributable to differences between interviewers.

Severity level 2 of the mobility dimension was incorrectly labelled in the Dutch version of the EQ-VT software ("lopen" instead of "rondwandelen"); the impact was expected to be limited because interviewers used a correctly labelled printed overview and no unexpected pattern appeared in mobility valuations.
In deviation from the EQ-VT protocol and recent valuation studies, health states flagged in the cTTO feedback module were not excluded by default, in order to avoid further reducing the sample size.
Representativeness on demographic and health characteristics does not necessarily imply representativeness in terms of health preferences.

The authors note that EQ-5D appears not to perform well for some health problems, such as hearing and vision difficulties, and that adding bolt-on dimensions raises non-trivial problems for health state valuation of the expanded instruments.
Both authors are members of the EuroQol Group, one having chaired it from 2010 to 2014, and the article was funded by the EuroQol Research Foundation.
A nonprobability quota sampling method was used because of limited resources, and the sample covered only urban residents of five metropolitan areas.
Some participants gave logically inconsistent values, and logical inconsistency was associated with certain interviewers and decreased toward the end of the survey, suggesting interviewer effects.

No observations or participants were excluded for logical inconsistency or idiosyncratic behaviour; excluding a small number of participants who valued all states as worse than dead, as full health, or identically improved model fit but would have impaired sample representativeness.

Nonlinear regression models are less accessible in practice, as standard software such as STATA provides no nonlinear mixed-effects function, and their coefficient standard errors cannot be used directly to compute standard errors for predicted values.
Convenience sampling and lack of information about general-population nonparticipants limited generalizability.
The heterogeneous acute- and chronic-illness groups limited the generalizability of known-groups validity.
Only 23 general-population children completed the retest, producing little response variance and limiting test-retest analysis.
No cognitive debriefing followed completion of the final TANDI, although it could have assessed comprehensibility and acceptability.

Results were limited to English-speaking caregivers and the sampled South African acute-illness, chronic-illness, and general-population groups, so they cannot be generalized to other languages and cultural groups.

Respondent engagement could not be fully assessed beyond self-reported feedback and completion time; methods such as eye tracking would be needed but sample size requirements would preclude model estimation.
Each respondent saw only two of the four approaches, so feedback across all approaches could not be obtained.

An opt-in incentivised online panel was used, which may not be representative in unmeasured characteristics, and respondent health literacy was unknown despite its known influence on valuation consistency.

Validity of each approach is difficult to judge without a gold standard value set, and it remains unclear which approach best reflects respondent preferences or what an appropriately 'easy' DCE task is.
The sample contained a higher proportion of younger female respondents than the Australian general population because a quota group was left open by the panel provider.
The sampling strategy could cause selection bias because patients with more severe illness may have declined, and the number of refusals was not recorded.
All patients came from surgery departments and were mainly people with acute conditions or postoperative patients, so effects of chronic conditions on well-being require further study.
Demographic characteristics differed across the patient, carer, and general-public groups and could confound the comparisons.
Disease information was not collected for carers or the general public; unobserved health conditions could affect known-group validity results.
EQ-HWB-S responses were derived from the EQ-HWB responses, so results can differ when EQ-HWB-S is administered independently.
The frequency and content of interviewer explanations were not documented, so acceptability under fully self-administered conditions remains uncertain.
The exploratory factor results require careful interpretation because some concepts may have too few items, and the study did not perform confirmatory factor analysis.
Chronic conditions were self-reported, with no information on their severity or duration.

Other potentially relevant variables were not explored, including parenting (having children) and adherence to religious practices, although most respondents stated that the valuation tasks did not conflict with their religious beliefs.

Small numbers required respondents whose gender was reported as Other to be combined arbitrarily with females, and the study had no follow-up question to test possible gender differences in interpretation of EQ-5D mobility and usual-activities items.
The cross-sectional observational design supports associations, not causal effects of individual or national factors on HRQoL change.
Restriction to people with internet access can create unobserved differences from national populations despite quota sampling and post-stratification weighting.
Population QALY loss assumed that age- and country-specific HRQoL changes remained stable for one year and used common published lower and upper QALY-loss estimates per death across countries.
The prepandemic EQ-5D-5L assessment was retrospective and is subject to recall bias; respondents can remember baseline HRQoL as better than it was, which can overestimate deterioration.

India and Uganda were sampled mainly from urban populations and were not nationally representative; their samples were more educated and self-selected than their national populations, so results are not generalizable to the whole country.
The survey occurred during a new global wave of cases and deaths, so current-health responses may have been lower than at other pandemic times.
Chronic condition data were self-reported without severity or duration, so results may not generalise to more severely ill individuals.
Data were lacking on other potential determinants such as family status, religious beliefs and belief in afterlife.
The health literacy measure captured only functional health literacy, and reading ability was required for participation, which may explain the low observed prevalence of inadequate health literacy.
Most participants were highly educated, urban and health-literate, limiting generalisability to all Canadians, especially ethnic minorities.
Interviewer effect could not be fully assessed because two sites had only one interviewer each, although it was insignificant at the two sites where it could be tested.
The study did not collect break-off or partial-response data because clinic staff were limited. It therefore could not formally assess respondent burden or fatigue, which could affect data quality.
Only 12 experimental items were administered. Therefore, the study could not compare the experimental and modified instruments at the scale level.
The low follow-up rate and high stability prevented responsiveness testing. The study also did not collect detailed medication or intervention changes during the retest interval.
The fixed instrument order could cause order or fatigue effects. The modified EQ-HWB always preceded the 12 experimental items, so prior exposure could bias the version comparison.
Validity comparisons involved instruments with different recall periods and contextual framing, so these results require caution.
The sample was younger and more educated than the wider population, which could limit coverage of cultural and socioeconomic variation in mental-health reporting in China.
The stable-patient definition used unchanged global health status and could miss changes in the broader wellbeing content of EQ-HWB.

The tWTA question used a simple, noniterative design without visual aids because of the standardized EQ-VT tool, budget limits, and concern about respondent fatigue; this may have made the task difficult.
The categorical tWTA response scale did not permit precise estimation of values below -1.
