Assigning -6.5 to the response that rejected living in the severe state was arbitrary and converted a theoretically negative-infinite response into another censored value, although sensitivity analyses used -7.0 and -11.0.
Extended lead time may increase the effect of time preference on utility values.
The study did not investigate respondents' perceptions of worse-than-dead states or the tWTA question, so it could not explain their thought processes or unwillingness to accept very poor states.

The synthesis did not cover comparisons in which adults used a child perspective and adolescents used their own perspective because perspective and respondent age changed together and their effects could not be disentangled.
The available evidence did not establish which alternative to child-perspective valuation is most promising in practical, ethical, or stakeholder-alignment terms.
Evidence on direct preference elicitation from children was limited, and the paper identified no pediatric application of group-based deliberative valuation for generic HRQoL instruments.
The online-panel sample was not representative of the Chinese general population, especially for educational level, and was younger and more highly educated than samples in earlier EQ-HWB studies.
The study did not use parallel or crossover testing of the original and modified EQ-HWB, so it could not directly attribute performance differences to the modifications.
The fixed questionnaire order could have produced order effects.
The cross-sectional design did not permit evaluation of responsiveness or test-retest reliability.
Age was categorical and the highest group was 65 years or older; the authors state that future studies should divide older ages into more groups.
The ordered-logit explanatory variables were dichotomized to retain comparability with the 2012 analysis, which reduced category detail.
Although the study tried to prevent repeat participation by panel members, survey 1 did not use the panel, so some duplication may have occurred.
The norms combine three surveys with online and face-to-face computer-assisted modes; two surveys used a survey-company panel and participants received incentives.
The inequality measures were limited to the health dimensions in EQ-5D-5L.
The online, unsupervised experiment could have produced noisier data than a laboratory or interviewer-led study.
The sample was not representative and overrepresented women, which limits external validity and may help explain differences from the England EQ-5D-5L value set.

Mouselab measures information search through mouse clicks. Mouse-based and eye-tracking methods can differ in search time, systematicity, revisits, and variance; requiring clicks may have increased these differences.

Respondents saw detailed health-state vignettes at the start and later saw short labels, so they may have forgotten relevant state information; keeping full multi-attribute descriptions visible could change attention allocation.

The analysis could not determine whether age and chronic-condition differences arose from those factors or from an unmeasured cohort effect; it did not adjust for possible influences such as income or GDP per capita.
The analysis used only the EQ-5D-5L Anxiety/Depression dimension rather than the complete instrument, although other EQ-5D dimensions can also capture anxiety or depression symptoms.
The comparison was structurally imperfect because EQ-5D-5L Anxiety/Depression refers to problems today, whereas GAD-7 and PHQ-9 refer to symptom frequency over the last two weeks.
GAD-7 and PHQ-9 were treated as gold standards, but they are self-rated screening tools rather than diagnoses established by a diagnostic interview; PHQ-9 specificity can also differ by age.

No completely new design was created; the TTO states and DCE pairs were subsets of the EQ-VT design complemented with the respiratory dimension, which maximised comparability but other designs could have been more efficient for model identification and estimation.

TTO values were collected for only 20 health states, which ruled out a main-effects TTO model with parameters for all levels of the six dimensions and limited the modelling options to the hybrid model.

The comparison with the Dutch EQ-5D-5L valuation study is a between-study comparison, and the current data were collected with the later EQ-VT protocol version 2.0 including practice states, a feedback module and quality control, which may have affected the comparison of TTO values.
Adding a disease-specific bolt-on dimension reduces the comparability of EQ-5D outcomes across diseases, which is currently regarded as a strength of the EQ-5D.
A discrepancy was observed between the qualitative and quantitative development data on the relative importance of the two bolt-on candidates.
Cultural influences on how respondents perceived and reported the bolt-ons may limit transferability and require cross-cultural validation.
Several known-groups classifications relied on reference values because validated cutoff scores were unavailable for PSSD, SSS-24, and SHAME and because several POEM bandings exist.
The cross-sectional design and the lack of a control group constrain interpretation.
The fixed questionnaire order may have caused order effects and more missing data for the EQ-5D-5L and bolt-ons placed at the end.
Different recall periods across instruments may have reduced comparability.
The mixed clinic and online recruitment approach produced geographic concentration, with approximately 57% of participants from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Online recruitment may have caused self-selection of younger, more digitally literate people with milder symptoms and may limit generalizability.
The sample size was relatively small.

The study used DCE-TTO, which is not the valuation method in the recommended EQ-5D-5L valuation protocol; it is an ordinal method that relies heavily on econometric modelling and assumptions, so the validity of the anchored values may be questioned, and DCE-TTO may be particularly vulnerable to manipulations such as splitting composite dimensions.
Data were collected by an online survey of a commercial internet panel, which excludes certain populations and may involve limited respondent engagement, unlike face-to-face interviews.
The study was conducted in the United Kingdom with the English version of the EQ-5D-5L, so the results may not hold in other language versions or populations.
Only 4 of the 240 possible attribute orderings were examined, and the effect of position may have interacted with the dimension itself.

The sample was relatively small compared with similar studies, because access to children with cancer is difficult (low prevalence, adverse treatment effects, parental protection), so the findings should be taken with caution.
Feasibility was limited to missing responses; other indicators such as completion time, comprehensibility of questions and participant preferences were not assessed.
Not all measurement properties were assessed: validity, responsiveness and reliability were not evaluated.
Chronic conditions were self-reported and could not be verified.
Limited access to mass testing prevented certain distinction between respondents with and without COVID-19; respondents with possible infection were therefore excluded from regression analyses.
Use of one main national survey language per country could exclude people who spoke another language or were not literate and could reduce representativeness.
Younger males and people with lower educational attainment were under-represented, which could cause underestimation of mental-well-being and educational differences.
Use of the United States EQ-5D-5L value set for every country supported comparison, but a different value set could produce different findings.
All participants came from an existing online panel. This raises data-quality concerns, and the quality controls cannot fully remove low-quality respondents or bots.
The models treated duration as continuous. This can miss discrete time preferences and related preference heterogeneity.
The pooled order-effect regression combined both designs and could contain scale heterogeneity, although its main purpose was to identify interaction terms.
EQ-HWB item wording and domain representation changed after this study. These changes can affect the exact preference weights, although the authors expect the feasibility findings to remain robust.
Only English and Mandarin EQ-VT versions were used, which may exclude speakers of other languages and reduce representation of Singapore's multi-ethnic population.
Non-probability quota sampling, despite alignment with census distributions, may cause selection bias.
Virtual EQ-VT administration during the COVID-19 period may have influenced responses, although prior evidence suggests small mode differences.
Self-reported responses may be affected by social desirability or inaccurate reporting, despite quality control and interviewer feedback.

The qualitative questions asked about general influences on health-state valuations rather than probing WTD preferences specifically; the authors used sensitivity analyses to justify pooled qualitative results.

Results may not generalize to other color coding schemes, such as traffic light coding, and the benefit of intensity color coding is likely smaller when only a subset of attributes has an ordinal level structure.

The size of the dropout effect may not transfer to other panels: a comparable EQ-5D DCE in the scientific LISS panel had a dropout rate of only 1%, so panel type and financial compensation likely moderate the effect.
Preferences and scale are inherently confounded in discrete choice models, so the measurement of relative choice consistency relied on randomization of respondents across study arms.

The main model assumed an identical underlying preference structure in all study arms; sensitivity analyses show that overlap and color coding did affect the estimated preference structure, although relaxing the assumption did not change the conclusions.
The cross-sectional design permits only associations, and reverse causation cannot be excluded, so no causal inference is possible.
Participants may not fully represent the general Canadian population, with overrepresentation of females, married individuals, high school educated and employed people, limiting generalizability.
Neighbourhood, behavioural and psychological factors that may mediate the association between individual deprivation and HRQL were not included.
This was a pilot study with a small sample size, so model estimates and the relative impact of dimensions might differ in a full-scale study.
The printed booklet used to show health states to illiterate respondents made interviews longer and made it challenging to navigate between the computer screen and the booklet.
Although quota sampling was used, participants came from only 3 large urban centres and their surrounding rural areas, so they may not truly represent the Pakistani population.

Literacy, cultural and religious factors vary greatly among Pakistani provinces, which might affect TTO and DCE choices, and the number of nontraders might differ with a larger sample and stricter quota stratification.
Some quota groups showed inconsistencies with the intended population distribution because only the highest demographic groups were ensured in this pilot.
The feasibility study used a relatively small sample and did not reach its target of 600 participants.
Online recruitment was difficult, and online participants may not represent the wider population; the sample was highly educated and may have been more able to engage with the tasks.
Interviewers completed different numbers of interviews at different speeds, and possible interviewer effects may have influenced the results.
The nine-dimension mixed cTTO states may have been more difficult than the five-dimension EQ-5D states for which EQ-VT was developed.
Reducing the number of valued states per participant lowered burden but also reduced the number of valuations for each state.
The cTTO and DCE designs covered only a small fraction of possible EQ-HWB-S states, and cTTO coverage across level-sum scores was low.

Predicted VAS values are based only on adolescents aged 13-18 years, so no information is available for younger children, and some differences from the study of children aged 10-11 years were observed.

There was no direct observation of the value for dead, so the predicted value for the worst descriptive-system state 33333 was used as the anchor, although the value for 33333 might not equal the value for dead in this group.
Further research on ways to anchor VAS values on the 0 to 1 scale is needed before the VAS is used for QALY calculation in economic evaluation.
Comparison with other value sets must be cautious because valuation method, perspective, modelling and the age of the valuing person can all influence results.
Questionnaires were completed in small student groups, which could cause response or social-desirability bias.

All participants came from the healthy general population and had no reported health conditions; the concentration in full health caused high ceiling effects and limits conclusions about clinical populations.
The study did not determine whether EQ-5D-Y-5L detects health variation or responsiveness to change in heterogeneous or clinical subgroups.
The different scoring ranges of EQ-5D-Y, KIDSCREEN, and the Cantril ladder could complicate the convergent-validity comparison.
The authors advised caution because use of Shannon indices in HRQoL research was relatively new and comparable youth studies were lacking.
Non-random missing data could have under-represented patients with severely impaired HRQoL because these patients were less likely to return complete questionnaires.
The generic EQ-5D-5L may not detect fine HRQoL differences that are important in advanced or metastatic colorectal cancer.
Some patient characteristics, including comorbidities, were recorded only at the start of palliative treatment; later changes were unavailable, so misclassification bias could not be excluded.
Residual confounding from unmeasured variables could not be ruled out; examples not collected included depression, urinary disorder, social network, income, socioeconomic status, and stoma status.

The predefined thresholds for acceptable increases in predictive error were somewhat arbitrary, being based on the standard deviation of mean absolute errors from published three-level EQ-5D valuation studies.
Only main effects were considered when deriving latent utilities, and model specification remains debatable.
All responses were included without excluding logically inconsistent TTO valuations, as there is no consensus on handling inconsistencies.

Generalizability of the global or western regional function is strictly limited to the contributing countries, and the findings apply to EQ-5D-5L valuation studies rather than other utility instruments or valuation types.
DCE is easy to understand but may not be easy to complete for multi-attribute health states, since choosing between two EQ-5D-5L states requires trade-offs across five dimensions.
The cross-sectional design did not show how quality of life changed over time.
The pragmatic use of three different data sources prevented a stratified design that would yield a representative French IBD sample.
The set of covariates was limited; for example, the study did not collect associated comorbidities.
Few participants were aged 75 years or older, which produced wide confidence intervals for quality-of-life and disease-activity indicators in that group.
Patients younger than 18 years were excluded, so further studies are needed to estimate utilities in that age group.
Comparison with prior studies was difficult because most samples were small and studies differed in value sets, sites, methods, and patient characteristics.
The sample differed from the Egyptian general population in several background characteristics because pilot interviews used a convenience sample of educated participants in urban Cairo.
The pictorial representation and EQ-5D-5L colour-coding tools were not fully validated.

The study used a nonstandard non-stopping TTO elicitation and a nonstandard DCE-TTO derived from it, and theoretically irrelevant changes to elicitation can influence respondents, which may reduce generalizability.
The choice pairs came from the TTO iteration sequence rather than from an efficient experimental design, so the design is inefficient and unrealistic for a typical DCE study.

Health states were never compared with each other but only with varying durations of perfect health, so respondents probably attended more to duration than in a standard DCE-TTO where all attributes vary.
Repeating many choices for the same health state may have produced answers with less error than in standard DCE tasks.

The worse-than-death choice sequence was imputed for respondents who did not invoke the worse-than-death task, which may have imposed strict preferences where respondents would have expressed an indifference range spanning zero and negative values, shifting both TTO and DCE values downward; the authors call this a clear limitation.

Only 10 health states were included, so more complicated models could not be explored, and the analysis relied on models assuming independent, identically distributed error terms and no dependence on attributes outside the two state descriptions.
The experimental design had no repeated tasks or dominated health-state pairs, which limited stronger tests of reliability and internal validity.
Mode of administration and respondent source were linked, so the study could not estimate their separate effects.
Personality was not measured in either comparator.
The online practice task and warning for responses completed in 7 seconds or less could have affected the comparison.
The primary multinomial logit model did not account for preference or scale heterogeneity, while seven tasks per respondent limited the stability of exploratory mixed logit models.
Level sum score gives equal weight to all dimensions and levels and cannot distinguish health states with the same sum, so it is only a general guide to severity.

The cTTO sample included relatively few respondents younger than 30 years and few people with lower education, although subgroup comparisons found no statistically significant differences in mean cTTO values.

DCE data were collected in December 2021 to January 2022, but cTTO data were collected in February to May 2023 after COVID-19-related delays and a switch to online administration; the pandemic might have affected cTTO results.
The DCE design and analysis did not consider non-linear time preference because the international valuation protocol did not address it.
The expanded cTTO design included only one very severe state, 33333; a broader range of poor states might reduce the linear mapping approach's overprediction of the worst states.
The garbage-class approach does not perfectly identify low-quality responses in difficult online choice tasks.
The exhaustive and lengthy interview can cause respondent fatigue and can adversely affect valuation of health states in the later part of the interview.
The original five EQ-5D-5L dimensions were developed in a European context and can miss aspects of health that are important in Indian culture.
The study appears underpowered to detect differences in performance between the competing models, so no strong conclusions can be drawn about the additional dimensions.
The data are relatively old (patients treated 1996-1998) and treatment advances such as immunotherapy in NSCLC may change the role of primary diagnosis as a predictor.
External validation in a separate, larger and more contemporaneous dataset is still required.
The sample is limited to patients with known painful bone metastases rather than a broader advanced incurable cancer population.
Performance status was assessed by specialists, so the comparison with non-specialist assessed performance status could not be made.
EQ-5D performance may differ in routine clinical practice, especially if patients know the responses inform clinical decision-making, and questionnaire non-completion increases near death.
Test-retest reliability of the EQ-5D dimensions has been reported as only moderate to excellent, and the acceptability of this approach to patients and clinicians was not assessed.
Convenience sampling on a first come, first served basis may have influenced results and produced few male participants (n = 4), so differences between males and females could not be examined.
All adolescents had experience with children and a majority of adults were parents, which may have influenced how they perceived valuing health states for a child.
Possible differences in the values given to the health states by adolescents and adults were not investigated.

Video-interviewing over Zoom loses visual cues and makes a positive atmosphere harder to build, and weak internet connection was sometimes a challenge; the interview location may also affect the data.

Transferability to other settings and populations must be judged by the reader from the described context, sampling and procedures, although the questions are considered relevant wherever the EQ-5D-Y-3L is used.
Cognitive skill was measured only by the proxy of highest educational attainment, because the valuation protocol includes no explicit cognitive measure.
The experimental design covered main effects only, so interaction terms between dimensions and levels could not be identified or estimated.
The lead-time TTO approach cannot elicit values below -1, so worse-than-dead valuations had to be censored at -1.
The sample was not representative of the Hong Kong population for employment status.
Qualitative free-text feedback about the module was collected from only 71 participants, and some found the hypothetical health states unrealistic and hard to judge.

A student sample was used because of budget constraints; student preferences are more homogeneous than and differ from those of the general public, for example mobility was among the least important dimensions here but the most important in the Chinese value set.

Interview time (36.8 minutes) was shorter than in national valuation studies (58.3 minutes in the United States, 42.6 minutes in Italy), possibly because students are more engaged and interviewers were experienced.
The study assumed a main-effects specification is sufficient and did not test interaction effects, because the health-state selection was optimized for main-effects models.
Only vision was used as the added dimension, and its descriptors differed from those of established vision bolt-on studies, so the findings may not generalize to other bolt-on dimensions.

The design was smaller than the 86-state EQ-VT design, and a smaller design favors the CALE model because the 20-parameter conventional model overfits; a comparison with a larger design is still needed.

The dataset included only adult participants from Western, developed countries, so person and item ordering may not extend to other populations if item descriptions and response categories are interpreted differently.
Data were collected through online survey panels, whose participants may differ from the general population.
No data on children were available, although the level summary score may be especially relevant for the EQ-5D-Y; similar research in children is still needed.
Whether relationships between items are modified by other factors such as age or gender was not examined and needs future research.

Nonstandard terminology and frequent omission of bolt-on use from titles and abstracts made studies difficult to identify; despite a broad search, hand searching, and citation tracking, the review might not include all eligible studies.
Exact wording was confirmed for only about two thirds of studies, so some cognition bolt-on wordings can be absent from the review.
The quality checklist adapted criteria that were written as development guidance rather than for retrospective post-development assessment.
The review treated successful use of at least one translation as translatability evidence, but this is not a formal translatability assessment and none of the items had undergone such an assessment.

For the criterion on descriptors informed by qualitative language, the reviewers did not evaluate qualitative-study rigor, sample adequacy, or population diversity and relevance; qualitative work was rare and limited.
The direct method can be affected by sequence effects, heuristics, and life-stage beliefs, so the elicited pattern may not represent pure time preference.
The study did not perform validity checks for time-preference elicitation, including test-retest reliability.
Video interviews replaced physical interviews because of COVID-19 restrictions.
The 20-year cTTO had a higher minimum utility (-0.5) than the 10-year cTTO (-1.0), and the different lead-time-to-disease-time ratio might help explain the similar results.
The quantitative design gives only a partial explanation of the adult-child utility gap and cannot separate self-versus-other effects from adult-versus-child effects.
The English sample had a slight overrepresentation of highly educated respondents.
Maximum simulated likelihood can have difficulty estimating correlations in mixed-logit models and can produce biased estimates even when the model is correctly specified.
The analysis assumed only normally distributed random parameters; other distributional assumptions were not tested.
Computational limits restricted estimation to 250 Halton draws, although more draws can reduce simulation bias.

Only the two most recent HSE waves were used, so results may be affected by cohort effects and may not extrapolate to past or future cohorts, for example when calculating quality-adjusted life expectancy.
About 11% of participants had incomplete EQ-5D-5L responses and were excluded; men and residents of deprived neighbourhoods were more likely to be missing, and missing values were not imputed.
Findings for the EQ-5D-5L index (though not for dimension responses) depend on the chosen value set, and an ongoing UK EQ-5D-5L valuation study could change the results.
Dead people, who have a defined utility of zero, are not in the HSE, so inequality is measured conditional on being alive despite differential life expectancy by deprivation.
Reporting heterogeneity is possible: people of different socioeconomic backgrounds may report the same health differently on the EQ-5D, for example when interpreting limitations to usual activities.
The registry had limited information about factors that could explain socioeconomic differences, and the area-based postal-code indicator did not provide individual-level measures such as education.
The study used an indirect method to suggest reporting heterogeneity and could not separate true health differences from reporting effects.
The primary and secondary cohorts had some discrepant findings; the EQ-5D-5L cohort began during the COVID-19 pandemic, which affected orthopedic care and could explain subtle cohort differences.
The three methods were not randomized over all interviews, so the design may not have minimized ordering effects.
The sample size, guided by observations per state for value-set work, may have had insufficient power to detect small but important differences such as inconsistency-rate differences.
Quality control for nTTO and oTTO was less stringent than for cTTO because minimum times for examples and individual tasks were unknown; this may partly explain their shorter administration time.
The study could not confirm diagnosis, condition severity, or change in health with treating clinicians; it used caregiver reports and validated condition-specific measures instead.
The community sample had no dedicated clinical intervention, so responsiveness estimates may be conservative and health changes were small.
Small samples limited interpretation of test-retest reliability and responsiveness in several condition groups and for AQoL-6D, HUI3, and PROMIS-25.
The 4-week follow-up response rate was low, ranging from 28% to 50% across condition groups.

Head-to-head comparison required one total score per measure, although PROMIS-25 and the EQ-5D-Y instruments may be better suited to domain or utility scoring; the PROMIS-25 total score was exploratory and produced more favorable results than developer-recommended domain scoring.
Combining child self-reports and caregiver proxy reports prevented analysis of differences by reporter type; separate analyses would have lacked power, especially for responsiveness.
The study did not use think-aloud methods; retrospective debriefing could capture thoughts formed after completion of the cTTO tasks.
Zoom interviews made nonverbal communication less discernible and might have hindered positive and engaging interaction.
The Singapore setting limits generalizability because factors that lead to worse-than-dead valuation can differ across countries and cultures.

Recruiting a representative sample of about 350 people from a population of about 64,000 was difficult. Older women were overrepresented, and younger men and men in all age groups were underrepresented.
Some age-sex quota groups had too few observations for the preferred weighted models, so the investigators collapsed some quota groups.

Available Stata and R implementations did not support sampling weights for hybrid models. The study therefore used repeated representative subsamples and bootstrap estimation instead of a directly weighted hybrid model.
The online survey had a high refusal or early-termination rate, which the authors suggest could partly reflect overseas outreach in a small population.

The two repeated cross-sectional surveys included different participants at each administration, so there were no repeated measures on the same individuals and individual-level change in HRQL could not be examined.
The samples represent adults who seek emergency department or primary care services rather than the general population, so generalizability is limited to similar groups.
The surveys did not measure factors that may be associated with HRQL or the psychosocial impact of the pandemic.

Unmeasured characteristics such as number of comorbidities may explain the lack of change observed in the ED survey and may differ from the general Alberta population; the authors call this a key limitation.
The EQ-5D-5L may not capture aspects of HRQL important during the pandemic, such as social functioning and specific emotional aspects like distress, fear, or worry about the future.
Levels 4 and 5 had small sample sizes, so dimension levels had to be grouped for analysis.
The central assumption that the value of prolonging life is related to proximal defense is plausible but unproven and requires empirical testing.
The framework assumes that the proposed process operates within respondents.
Retrospective testing is susceptible to confirmation bias in study selection and in the terror-management interpretation of characteristics.
The literature search was only partly reproducible and was not systematic; the first three search strategies had no systematic records.

Studies were selected when characteristics significantly affected TTO, so some findings can be due to chance, negative results can be underreported, and significant determinant results were often absent from abstracts.
Study design, sample size, online versus face-to-face collection, TTO score distributions, and cultural variation can affect whether determinants are significant.
Fatigue was assessed with the RPQ fatigue item, which was developed for post-concussion symptoms and not specifically for assessing fatigue in the general population.
The recall timeframe differed between instruments: the EQ-5D-5L asks about health today while the fatigue item asks about the past 24 hours.
The survey was web-based, so the characteristics of non-respondents were unknown and respondents could not be compared with non-respondents.
A general population sample may not represent clinical or disease-specific groups, where bolt-on performance can differ.
The cross-sectional design could not assess responsiveness over time.

The study did not collect use of vision aids, so it could not compare the vision items among aid users and non-users; the small vision-problem subgroup and possible exclusion of corrected refractive errors also limited inference.

The age limit of 69 years, online-panel recruitment, and 30-minute completion limit may have excluded older adults, people with limited internet access, mild cognitive impairment, or low digital literacy. Representativeness by age and sex did not ensure socioeconomic or ethnic diversity.
The sole Hong Kong setting and Traditional Chinese translations may limit transfer to other Chinese and non-Chinese linguistic and cultural contexts.

With no validated bolt-on value sets, level sum scores were used. These scores assume equal dimension importance and equal intervals between levels, and different health profiles can have the same score.
PROMIS-29+2 appeared between the two randomized bolt-on groups and may have caused priming or order effects, although randomization balanced group order.
The fatigue bolt-on borrowed the PROMIS fatigue descriptor, which may have increased correlations with PROMIS fatigue items.
Recruitment from only three urban hospitals in Guizhou and Zhejiang may limit generalisability to the broader Chinese paediatric population, especially rural and less-resourced settings.
Cultural, linguistic, and health-system variation across China may affect the interpretation and relevance of the HRQoL instruments.
Health-status changes during the short test-retest interval can complicate reliability and responsiveness assessment.
The study does not assess effects of the HRQoL instruments on clinical decisions or long-term health outcomes.
Convenience sampling was used and most patients were connected to a patient association.
Self-selection bias may be present because patients volunteered, and willingness to participate or patient-association membership may not be independent of self-reported health or self-confidence.
Two modes of administration (face-to-face and video interviewing) were used, which could influence responses, although most patients used one mode and no differences across modes were observed.
Further bolt-ons that might be relevant in psoriasis, such as social relationships or sleep, were not included.
Minor semantic differences between the Hungarian and other language versions of the EQ-5D-5L and EQ-PSO may limit generalizability to other countries.

Results are difficult to generalise because the included data come from different studies, different population and patient samples, different language versions and value sets, and varying research designs such as order of administration and intervening questionnaires.
Differing methods, designs, analyses and potential cross-cultural differences in EQ-5D response patterns made summarising results difficult.

There are no established guidelines or standards, such as COSMIN, for preference-based measures, and the EuroQol Group could create a task force to develop reporting standards for more homogenous methods.
The search was restricted to publications in English and German, and confidence intervals for responsiveness were reported by only one of the three responsiveness studies.

Respondents who did not complete the T2 questionnaire were significantly younger and more often reported chronic conditions, so groups with potentially larger HRQoL and well-being changes may have been missed.
Although the T1 sample was representative by age and sex, more highly educated participants were over-represented, which may underestimate HRQoL and mental well-being changes.

Only two measurements were available, so changes over pandemic trajectories with varying incidence, restrictions and vaccination coverage may only have been partially captured; more frequent measurement would give a better picture.
Pre-COVID-19 HRQoL and mental well-being data were not available for the majority of respondents.
The study used online samples and had a relatively short observation period.
Health outcomes were self-reported.
The US Amazon MTurk sample had limited external validity to the general population, and the attempted longitudinal cohort had substantial attrition.
Treating EQ VAS scores as interval data has more limitations than other analytical approaches.

Only 2 of the 3 perspectives were randomised because participants always performed the tasks for themselves first, which may have influenced the results, for example through more frequent use of heuristics if the self perspective had come last.
The think-aloud protocol may have affected data quality: participants may not have verbalised all their thoughts or may have given their choices more thought than under other circumstances.
The results do not show the degree to which the identified thoughts influence the actual value of EQ-5D-Y-3L health states.

External validity may be limited because the study was conducted in The Netherlands, where the public may be more accustomed to discussing difficult topics such as the death of a child than in other countries.
Interviewer administration could have influenced responses through social-desirability or acquiescence bias, and Asian respondents might underreport physical and mental health problems.
All measures were administered in a fixed order, which could introduce order bias.
Respondent characteristics and medical conditions used in analyses were self-reported and therefore subject to reporting bias.
The patient sample contained only 50 respondents, split equally between diabetes and tuberculosis; the condition subgroups were not powered for direct comparison and limit subgroup interpretation.
The deliberately larger literate group created unequal group sizes that should be considered when interpreting between-group comparisons.
Hierarchical online-panel recruitment and online data collection limit generalisability; the general-population sample was healthier than Australian population norms.
Mandatory responses prevented assessment of item-level missing data as a possible indicator of relevance or acceptability.
The design could not assess feasibility in other common settings, such as routine clinical care.
EQ VAS was attached only to EQ-5D-Y-3L, so time and ease differences between EQ-5D-Y-3L and EQ-5D-Y-5L cannot be separated from the effect of EQ VAS.
The wide age quota bands resulted in a lower proportion of people aged 75 years and older than in the United Kingdom population.
The sample was more highly educated and had higher student and income representation than the general population for these non-quota characteristics.
Nation-specific sample sizes were too small to compare preferences or generate separate value sets for England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
A response rate could not be calculated because recruitment used a blended strategy that included postal mailout, social media, word of mouth, and posters.

The Tobit model violates some assumptions and can produce biased or unstable estimates; no assessed model could account simultaneously for censoring, repeated observations, heteroscedasticity, and preference heterogeneity.
Composite TTO censored values at -1, although some participants may have considered states worse than -1.
The 10-year and 20-year TTO horizons can be shorter than younger participants anticipated life expectancy and can affect their responses.
Time preferences can affect TTO responses, and there is no accepted method to adjust for this effect.
Arabic has a complex grammatical structure and rich vocabulary, and some English terms have no direct Arabic equivalent; translators therefore had to select terms carefully to preserve meaning.
Regional Arabic dialects can differ substantially across countries.
Use of this Standard Arabic version in other Arabic-speaking countries requires validation in the local context.
The DCE with duration tasks did not use the nonlinear DCE with duration format that EuroQol is testing for possible inclusion in the EQ-5D-Y-5L protocol.
Canadian findings may not generalize to adolescents in other countries because education, cultural norms, and social expectations can affect understanding and valuation.
Group-level analysis prevented linkage of individual questionnaire responses and behavior patterns to specific focus group comments.
The study focused on feasibility; examination of preference-data quality was outside its scope.
Completing the survey in the presence of others could have affected task completion and response quality, with some participants reporting that the group setting made them feel rushed or distracted.
The sample was too small to estimate a robust value set or assess whether the logical inconsistencies seen in the multicountry pilot were present.

The analysis used only about half of the 37,377 arthroplasty patients in the repository; attrition produced statistically higher presurgery WOMAC scores and more risk factors in the final samples, although the authors judge these differences clinically negligible.

No head-to-head comparison was possible because no patient completed both EQ-5D versions; propensity score matching may leave bias from observed imbalances such as preoperative risk factors and from unobserved sources.

The 3L and 5L samples came from different calendar periods (2010-2016 versus 2013-2017), so a time effect on how people perceive and rate their health may bias the comparison and needs further research.
Only cross-sectional measurement properties could be examined; data were insufficient to assess test-retest reliability, and responsiveness was not assessed.
Only preoperative data were used, so postsurgical performance of the EQ-5D-5L in this population remains unexplored.

The authors note that some readers may dispute direct comparability with the original study because the new approach does not require choices between children's lives or tradeoffs between HRQoL and life expectancy.
The derived values apply only to child HRQoL over one week and must not be multiplied by weeks or divided by seven to extrapolate to other durations.
The values must not be used to extrapolate quality-adjusted life expectancy for children with different life expectancies.
Because dying immediately is not positioned on the experience scale, the values cannot summarize the value of life extensions in children.
The sample had a larger proportion of respondents with post-secondary education than the Hong Kong population.
Values were based on adults preferences for the health states of an imagined child rather than on respondents preferences for themselves, which could affect the values.
The major limitation is the small sample size, which may have reduced the power to detect relationships.

The different methodology and engagement with the seven participants recruited at the information sharing session may have improved compliance and altered short-term HRQoL, possibly inflating their HRQoL reporting.
The sample was not randomly selected: respondents had taken part in earlier valuation research and had agreed to be recontacted, so the values generated do not represent the English population.
Thirteen sample I members had completed the identical standard questionnaire in 1998, which may have favourably biased version I's apparent performance relative to the modified versions.

The VAS used in versions II and III was inadvertently demarcated in twos rather than ones, which affected digit preference; there is no single official EuroQol valuation instrument, so results depend on the particular VAS used as comparator.
The redesigned questionnaire did not improve response rates, and questionnaire design alone does not determine survey response.
The explanations offered for version III's better performance are speculative; cognitive testing procedures would be needed to test the cognitive and mechanical mechanisms proposed.
Few participants selected severity levels 4 or 5, which limited psychometric evidence at the most severe response levels.
Although recruitment occurred at a specialized psychiatric hospital, the outpatient sample included more patients with mild conditions; this limits generalization to more unwell patients.
Interviewer administration might have introduced social-desirability bias, which could have influenced response patterns and limited the results' applicability to self-report contexts.
Age-target framing was not a pure manipulation of temporal distance because child framing can also change the contextual meaning of domains such as usual activities.
The evidence for the proposed theory was indirect: the study observed utility differences but did not directly measure or test psychological distance.
The within-person design could introduce anchoring or order effects that distort response distributions and reduce valuation variability.

Only four health states were included, which limits comparison with studies that use more states; some experimental perspectives, especially spatial location, also have limited practical relevance and add burden.
The six-step bisection procedure may increase cognitive burden and reduce accuracy, and its difference from the titration procedures used in most EQ-5D valuation studies limits generalizability.
Interviews were conducted online by video rather than in person, although the authors noted no clear evidence that online collection is less credible.
The test-retest sample of 25 was too small for accurate kappa estimates.
Five test-retest participants completed the interview between the two administrations and did not follow the protocol.
Only fluent English speakers were invited to qualitative interviews because interviewers fluent in other languages were not available, although interpreters were available for the survey.
Responsiveness to the Hub intervention was not assessed because implementation was only at an early stage at the six-month follow-up.
The level sum-score gives equal weight to dimensions and can represent very different profiles with the same total.
Only pilot United Kingdom preference weights were available; country-specific weights were not available.
The sample was generally well educated, which may limit interpretation for less educated caregivers, and migrant education did not necessarily correspond to comparable employment in Australia.
The study could not compare male and female caregivers because the gender groups were small and uneven.
The study did not directly compare EQ-HWB-S with specialist caregiver quality-of-life instruments such as CarerQoL, ASCOT, or the Carer Experience Scale.
The modest sample may have had insufficient power to detect a small EFT effect and limited analysis of heterogeneity in individual responses.
Online video interviews may have provided a less suitable environment for imagining future episodes than controlled in-person laboratory settings.
Using impaired health state 33333 for EFT might not evoke the positive emotions that can reduce discounting, and the largely healthy sample may have had little relevant lived experience.
The EFT scenes may not have been sufficiently vivid, health-specific, or directly relevant to later cTTO decisions, and the study had no evidence that the self-projection mechanism operated.
ERT was an active episodic-thinking control and may have engaged cognitive processes similar to EFT, which reduced the contrast between arms.

The direct time-preference method can be affected by preferences for improving or deteriorating health sequences, making it unclear whether the measured discounting pattern depends on elicitation method.

The empirical evidence was limited and formal EQ-5D-Y value sets had only recently become available, so it remained unclear whether and to what extent the proposed effects on valuation and incremental HRQoL gains would occur.
Data collection used videotelephony (Zoom) TTO interviews because of the COVID-19 lockdown, and formal equivalence of videotelephony and face-to-face valuation interviews has not been proven.
The sample was not representative: females and highly educated respondents were oversampled, and both characteristics may affect EQ-5D valuation.
Subjective life expectancy was measured after the TTO tasks, whereas earlier work measured it beforehand; respondent fatigue may have added noise to the life-expectancy estimates.
With a relatively small sample and possible added noise, the study may have been underpowered to detect a true effect.
Asking adults to think about life and death for a 10-year-old child is complex and can invoke negative emotions, which may have systematically influenced reported child subjective life expectancy.
The analyses were exploratory and no correction for multiple hypothesis testing was applied, so the scattered per-state significant coefficients should be interpreted with caution.

Cross-validation assumes that ability to predict a left-out part of the data proxies predictive ability outside the whole data set; if the 86 observed health states do not represent the full EQ-5D-5L state space, cross-validation is uninformative.
The data come from valuation studies conducted before recent strengthening of quality control in the EQ-VT system, so replication in data from more recently completed valuation studies is needed.

It is unknown whether the findings extend to DCE-based or hybrid models, since cross-validation of DCE data would need different leave-out procedures and hybrid models lack an apparent counterfactual.
The strict criterion that all participants be 65 years or older excluded studies in which only a minority of respondents were younger.
Included studies sampled only western, developed countries, so findings do not generalise to elderly populations in Asia, Africa or South America.

The elderly target population is heterogeneous, ranging from healthy independent to frail or cognitively impaired respondents, limiting generalisability, particularly for the EQ-5D-5L which appeared in only two studies.

Inconsistent feasibility terminology and differing database search engines may have caused relevant publications to be missed, especially where feasibility was only a secondary or descriptive analysis.
The DCE-with-duration method is not robust to poor-quality responses. It cannot distinguish strong longevity or quality-of-life preferences from inattentive flatlining in the B-versus-C choice.
The EQ-VT and DCE-with-duration samples differed in sex, education, and ethnicity, although the authors considered large effects on estimated values unlikely.
The methods were applied to different respondents rather than the same sample, and data collection periods were about six months apart.
This was one comparison in one country, so agreement must be tested in other language, cultural, and sampling settings.
All public-place recruitment data had to be discarded because of low validity. This caused a large loss of respondents, including some who were not classified as speeders.

The limited effect of the tested cTTO task modifications could reflect a diminished scope for further improvement after quality control had already been implemented, rather than the modifications being ineffective in principle.

A good interview could not be identified unambiguously, so flagged interviews could hold genuine responses and a lenient 40% threshold had to be used in the quality control process; the new requirements also increase study cost and may lead to removal of data.

Reliance on cTTO as the principal valuation method is a drawback of the current protocol because cTTO is costly and inherently difficult to implement for investigators with little valuation experience, which limits feasibility for smaller countries with fewer resources.
cTTO- and DCE-derived values cannot be expected to agree perfectly because the tasks, measurement models and axioms differ, raising concerns about the commensurability of the methods.

The common modelling assumption that the same proportional trade-offs are made regardless of remaining life expectancy may not hold, and violations are a bigger problem for DCE with duration than for cTTO because of the required extrapolation.
How often value sets should be updated is a question without any definite answer.

The sample comprised only 1296 participants from a few large cities, so preferences of people in less developed or remote areas are unknown and the results may not represent a true societal view on life and death.
The response rate was relatively low (68.4 %) because street and public place recruitment was challenging; 90 % of refusals were because people had no time.
The study sample had higher proportions of people with college or higher education, unemployed people and urban residents than the Chinese general population.
The 13 arguments were explicitly described as a non-exhaustive list.
The applicability assessment did not distinguish between children of different ages, although relevance can depend on age.
Only a small number of children are likely to be directly involved, so broader learning effects can be limited.
Qualitative and deliberative approaches can involve ethical concerns, cognitive demands, and difficulty reaching consensus on the value of child HRQoL.
It remains unclear whether conventional health-state valuation approaches are suitable for different child age groups or require modification, including for people aged 16 to 17 years.
Coding necessarily involved subjective judgement, so different researchers might have interpreted responses differently and theme frequencies should not be read directly as importance.
Only general public views were sought, most respondents were in good health, and patients and clinicians were not involved.
An ordering effect is possible because the follow-up tasks came after valuation tasks that familiarised respondents with the EQ-5D dimensions and the full health concept.
Respondent fatigue at the end of a long, cognitively demanding interview may have led some respondents to answer 'No', underestimating the number of missing health aspects.
The design did not allow probing or detailed questioning of the rationale behind responses, for example whose health respondents were considering.
Follow-up data were missing for 20 of the 456 respondents because of a recording error.

The included trials were mainly large phase 3 or phase 4 trials. Linear mixed-effects model robustness and agreement may be lower in small phase 1 or phase 2 trials and rare-disease trials, where ceiling effects and outliers can have more influence.

Missing-data assessment was limited to descriptive analysis and missing-completely-at-random tests. The study did not examine more complex missingness mechanisms, including missing not at random, which was especially important in two oncology trials with more than 60% missing EQ-5D data.
The study did not analyze the five EQ-5D dimensions separately because they are categorical and create modeling and interpretation problems for treatment-effect analyses.

Minimally important differences were used only as reference thresholds for comparing models. Their regulatory use remains debated, and thresholds should be disease-specific and meaningful to patients.

Covariates came from each trial's protocol and statistical analysis plan, but they may not have captured all important sources of heterogeneity; unmeasured heterogeneity could bias estimates, and its effect on model comparisons was unknown.

Only one included paper focused on tinnitus. The primary qualitative data criterion excluded other tinnitus and Meniere disease studies, so the synthesis may have missed physical symptoms such as sensations or dizziness and may not represent some diagnosis-specific effects.

The original search was conducted in August 2021. An update through August 2024 broadly supported the themes but found additional themes concerning access to medical or social services and financial issues.

Most included studies were from high-income countries. The synthesis is therefore unlikely to represent many people with hearing loss in low- and middle-income countries, especially people with untreated hearing loss.
The English-language restriction and the possible shortage of relevant qualitative studies in low- and middle-income countries may have contributed to limited geographic and cultural coverage.
Many source studies mixed groups defined by hearing-loss onset and use of hearing aids or cochlear implants, which made reliable comparisons between these groups difficult.

Wealth was based on self-reported household income, which can be under-reported because income is sensitive and informal employment is common in India. Such misreporting could distort the estimated socioeconomic gradient.
Test-retest reliability of the response scaling scores was not assessed for practical reasons.

Labels were initially rated independently with only the VAS anchors for context; ratings might have differed if labels had been rated in the context of other labels, for example in a paired-choice exercise.
Convenience samples that were not representative of national populations and were small in size may limit generalizability.

The proportion of participants with tertiary education was high in both phases, which may have produced more consistent results and greater acceptance of wording than a sample with lower educational levels.
Terms such as 'slight', 'moderate' and 'severe' can be open to intra- and inter-cultural variability in interpretation, and cross-cultural equivalence of the labels still requires investigation.
Caregivers reported mental health diagnoses and change at follow-up; diagnoses were not independently confirmed at either time point.
Only 28.0% completed follow-up, and too few children deteriorated to assess responsiveness to worsening health.
The approximately 4-week follow-up interval may have affected responsiveness and reliability estimates.
Findings may not generalize to mental health conditions other than ADHD, anxiety, or depression.
Online panel recruitment can cause sampling bias and self-selection, and the researchers could not verify whether child self-report was free from parental influence.
The author-constructed total performance score could be calculated and interpreted in other ways.
Small AQoL-6D and HUI3 samples prevented assessment of responsiveness and test-retest reliability and precluded direct comparison with the four main instruments.
Level sum scores give equal weight to items and can assign the same score to different response profiles; preference weights were not yet available for all instruments.
The small number of transgender, non-binary, gender-fluid, or undisclosed-gender participants prevented their inclusion in gender subgroup analyses.

Ethical concerns about identification prevented collection and reporting of detailed child condition, age, sex, race, income, and other participant characteristics, which limits interpretation and assessment of generalizability.
The qualitative study was conducted in one country with participants from Australia, so it is unknown whether the wording will remain suitable after translation or in other countries.
The adapted version was pilot tested with participants who had already contributed to the focus groups, so they may have been more likely to approve the final adaptation.
The focus-group approach was not fully open-ended because the study intended to retain and build on the existing EQ-5D-Y-3L structure.
Few datasets exist in which the same respondents completed both the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L, limiting the empirical comparison to two cross-sectional datasets.
No trial or longitudinal data were used, so observed change over time was not assessed directly.
Responsiveness was anchored only on the EQ VAS; other health anchors are needed to confirm the findings.
The EQ VAS was administered immediately after the 5L descriptive system, so an order effect may be present, and no 3L EQ VAS was available for sensitivity analysis.
Few severely ill respondents (EQ VAS below 50) were included, so measurement properties in very poor health could not be examined.
The study did not conduct age-stratified analyses because participant numbers within each age group were insufficient.
The analysis did not include disease-specific instruments, so it may omit domains important to specific conditions; including them could also bias results toward particular condition impacts.
The study excluded children younger than 5 years because HRQoL measurement in that age group is difficult and many available instruments remain experimental.

The distribution of a Stata example model by one of the organisers may have induced teams to drop out and led four of the eight submissions to use a similar analytical approach, reducing analytic diversity.
Selection of chi-square as the measure of fit was arbitrary, as any other goodness-of-fit measure would have been, and was a source of debate.

Teams predicted aggregate general-population preferences without access to respondent characteristics, so the competition says little about predicting individual preferences or preference heterogeneity.

Panel-based online surveys carry potential bias: low socioeconomic status is rare in online panels and was associated with dropout and non-trading behaviour, and responses of such participants may not reflect their actual preferences.
Exploratory and confirmatory data may differ because of seasonal or other unobservable changes in the panel.

Findings are scenario- and sample-dependent; different attributes, levels or scenario configurations could have led teams to approach the task differently, and choices in hypothetical tasks may concord poorly with real-life preferences.

It is difficult to state why the winning model won, because that would require adding and removing model elements and repeating the exploratory-confirmatory cycle to avoid hypothesising after the results are known; the confirmatory set also contained only a few immediate-death pairs.
Inferences about a respondent location from the internet connection type are limited; future studies should ask respondents directly where they are during the survey.
The samples of cell phone and tablet respondents were small, and a larger sample might have revealed greater differences between devices.
The effect of choice-task design features such as level overlap on inconsistent response behaviour across devices and locations was not examined.

Propensity score matching is not true randomization: respondents self-selected their device, so the higher number of logical inconsistencies among mobile and tablet groups may reflect uncontrolled population differences.
Within the modelling framework used, between-respondent variation from heterogeneous preferences cannot be separated from within-respondent randomness.
People from culturally and linguistically diverse communities were under-represented, and resource limits restricted eligibility to residents and proxies who could communicate in English.
All proxies completed the proxy-proxy version before the proxy-person version, so the nonrandomized sequence could have caused question-order bias.
Only family members served as proxies, and the sample was too small to stratify agreement by frequency of proxy contact.
The sample included only 63 dyads from 10 residential aged-care facilities in one Australian state, which limits generalizability.
Some proxy assessments occurred after the resident assessment, with delays of up to seven days, during which perceived quality of life could have changed.
The decision aid lacks PROM information for the option of not having total knee arthroplasty, because routine PROM systems generally follow only patients who had surgery.
Not all surgeons agreed to participate, and participating surgeons cannot be blinded because the summary report on the patient chart reveals the allocated arm, which may bias results.
Use of a research assistant to print the summary report limits the pragmatic nature and external validity of the trial.

Excluding participants who do not complete the routine questionnaires online before the surgical consultation limits generalizability, since non-completion may reflect lack of access to or comfort with a computer.
The control arm does not include a decision aid based on average values, so the trial cannot separate the effect of individualization from the effect of having any decision aid.
The trial is conducted at a single site in Alberta, Canada.
COVID-19 restrictions affected school recruitment in South Africa and may have caused nonresponse bias.
The researchers could not ensure that adolescents in the South African general-school and special-education samples completed the measures without influence from other people.
Different interviewers were used for Ethiopian school adolescents and adolescents with health conditions.
The cross-sectional data did not permit assessment of responsiveness or change over time.
The culturally adapted Amharic EQ-5D-Y-5L pain/discomfort wording limits generalization of Ethiopian findings to other EQ-5D-Y-5L versions.
Very few adolescents reported the most severe levels, so the study had little response variation for evaluating transitions at severe anchors.

Younger adults and females were overrepresented, and older adults were underrepresented; this could affect item interpretation, health-reporting patterns, captured condition severity, and discrimination across health states.
Medical conditions were self-reported without clinical verification or severity assessment.
The relatively small item pool could have affected the factor analysis; the EQ-HWB seeing item did not load on a factor.
The fixed instrument administration order could have caused order effects.
The cross-sectional study did not assess test-retest reliability or responsiveness to change.
Musculoskeletal pain was identified by self-report with PIP-Kids rather than by a medical diagnosis or ICD-11 classification, and its causes were heterogeneous.
Feasibility assessment used missing responses and completion rates but did not measure completion time or comprehensibility in the target population.
The randomized EQ-5D descriptive systems were answered consecutively without an intervening task, which could have caused confusion or recall bias.
Instrument comparisons were difficult because recall periods and response scales differed: PedsQL used the past month and a frequency scale, while EQ-5D-Y and CHU9D used today and severity scales.
The multi-item PedsQL domain scores might not align directly with the descriptive systems of the preference-based instruments.
The heterogeneous, self-reported pain condition and the prespecified hypothesis-testing approach could have influenced the construct-validity results.
The study did not assess redistribution properties or discriminatory power with the Shannon index.
No gold-standard HRQoL instrument exists for pediatric musculoskeletal pain, so criterion validity could not be assessed and the depth of validity assessment was limited.
The sample may not have been fully representative because people who could not read were excluded, although they form a substantial part of the Tunisian population.
The regional quota-sampling strategy did not adequately account for rural areas.
Technical problems with EQ-PVT corrupted and lost 97 DCE observations, approximately the data from 10 interviews.
Participants were recruited from the MTurk platform, which has shown mixed external validity relative to the general US population.
The sample was stratified only on age, gender and race; additional stratification measures could improve generalisability.
The wave 2 sample included wave 1 participants, who were more likely to respond again because they had already completed one follow-up.
The interval between wave 2 and wave 3 was longer than between wave 1 and wave 2, which could have increased the attrition rate.
The survey questions remained virtually unchanged across all three waves, which may have added respondent burden and raised attrition.
Findings may be partly specific to the COVID-19 pandemic, since the pandemic created conditions that differ substantially from pre-pandemic life.
Only 31 participants reported worsened health in the responsiveness analysis.
The single-center design and sociodemographic differences can limit generalizability to other settings.

Limited prior literature was available for comparison because this was the first study of measurement properties and agreement across these EQ-5D-Y-5L data-collection approaches in children and adolescents.
Self-complete and interviewer-administered versions were completed on the same day, which can cause recall bias despite a distracting activity between them.
The one-month follow-up can be too short to capture clinically meaningful HRQoL change, especially during recovery from acute injury or asthma exacerbation.
Completion times could not be collected for all versions.
No gold-standard test of true respondent validity exists, so the benchmark had to be simulated from mixed logit estimates rather than observed directly.

The benchmark assumes the standard mixed logit model with a unimodal multivariate normal mixing distribution correctly summarizes respondent preferences, and its population estimates are affected by the number of low-quality respondents in the data.
Only four case studies were included; a larger and more representative selection of DCEs would have given additional confirmation that the conclusions do not depend on the chosen case studies.

The performance of the RLH test depends on the model specification, the number of choice tasks per respondent, the efficiency of the experimental design and a sample large enough to fit a mixed logit model with correlated parameters.
The original data obtained from the corresponding authors did not contain the required repeated and dominant choice tasks and therefore could not be used for the convergent validity analysis.

Some participants considered several instrument dimensions poorly suited to 3-year-olds or interpreted age-typical limitations as health problems; the helping-look-after-themselves dimension was especially difficult for some non-parents, and participants may have overlooked the guidance notes.
The study did not examine methods for anchoring health-state preferences, which must be resolved if a value set is to support QALY estimation.
The small sample included no adults older than 60 and had limited representation of people with secondary education or less, which limits generalisability.
Self-reported ratings of task difficulty and understanding may not accurately indicate response quality.
Only 12 health states were tested, so the study may not have captured some interactions or differences between parents and non-parents.

The primary researcher’s non-parent status and personal perspectives may have influenced interview probes and interpretation, although reflexive practice, double coding, and wider-team review were used to reduce this risk.
The observational design does not support causal conclusions and remains vulnerable to confounding by indication.
Pulse width could change during a treatment series, but patients were classified only by pulse width at the first session.
Pulse width can be linked to other treatment parameters, including charge, so other ECT modalities could affect HRQoL outcomes.
Only 38% of the registry population had EQ-5D responses before and after ECT and entered the study sample, which creates a risk of selection bias despite broadly similar recorded characteristics.
The final regression samples were smaller because 39% of the study sample lacked data for one or more concurrent medications.
Loss to follow-up was substantial: six-month response rates were 12% for the EQ-5D index and 14% for EQ VAS.
Events and treatments during the six-month follow-up that could affect HRQoL were not included in the analysis.
The EQ-VT protocol was designed for literate populations and was difficult for illiterate participants; detailed verbal explanations enabled inclusion but did not achieve the planned quota.
Rural and low-literacy participants were underrepresented relative to Moroccan planning data despite efforts to obtain geographical diversity.
The mainly online survey could not reach people with limited internet access or technical skills, including some older people and residents of remote areas.
Because researchers had no face-to-face contact with online respondents, they could not directly assess understanding, engagement, or interest; quality-control procedures only reduced this concern.

The DCE sample was controlled only for age, sex, and region, while the cTTO sample was not representative; other respondent characteristics or a more balanced cTTO sample could change the preferences or anchor.
The fixed perspective of a hypothetical 10-year-old child may affect values because preferences may differ for children of other ages, one's own child, a known child, or a hypothetical child.
The cross-sectional design did not permit evaluation of responsiveness or test-retest reliability over time.
Small condition and known-group subgroups limited condition-specific inference and known-group analysis.
Use of an English instrument in a multilingual setting may have limited comprehension and interpretation.
High ceiling effects across EQ-TIPS dimensions limited interpretation of the Shannon indices.
Selecting conditions on the basis of burden of disease may have prioritised conditions with larger populations at the expense of smaller populations.
Measures were not identified or searched for systematically.
Not all identified studies were included and double extraction was not undertaken because of resource limitations.
The review only includes studies up to October 2017.
No formal assessment of the quality of included reviews was undertaken.
Important themes may have been missed despite the recurrence of themes across the targeted groups providing some support for the pragmatic approach.

The review focused primarily on a European or North American context and on English-language evidence, which may have missed themes important elsewhere or included themes not relevant in other cultures, for example individualistic conceptions of self-identity.
Stakeholder involvement included people from other countries but had a larger United Kingdom presence and focus, so cross-cultural issues need future work.
The final themes were not subjected to further primary qualitative work to confirm them.
Level overlap reduces the statistical efficiency of the DCE design, which requires additional respondents and can still be problematic in clinical research settings.

The highlighting-of-differences format inherently depends on some degree of overlap and therefore could not be combined with the design without level overlap, so only five of six factorial cells were tested.
138 respondents dropped out after completing the choice tasks because of browser compatibility problems with the final ranking task.
Not all DCE design generation software packages currently support imposing level overlap.
Only bolt-on levels 1, 3, and 5 were tested. Levels 2 and 4 require further testing to confirm the severity-dependent pattern.
The study used pairwise choices. Other methods, including ranking or tasks comparable with time trade-off, could give different evidence.
Question order within each block was not randomized, so order could have affected preferences.
Only three EQ-5D-5L health-state pairs were studied. The design was not powered for advanced econometric analyses such as interactions, and other pairs could produce different results.
Relevant information may have been missed because screening relied on titles and abstracts, while on this relatively unexplored topic arguments may appear only in full texts.
The review of books and PhD theses was limited by practical constraints, although the health economic handbooks examined provided no relevant arguments.

Individual-level classification depends on the information in each respondents choice tasks; neither dataset was designed to distinguish between utility functions, so more suitable designs or more tasks per respondent would reduce the uncertain category.
Respondents who used neither a multiplicative nor an additive utility function are still forced into one of the two latent classes, which may overstate the true class sizes.

Both datasets came from a single country (Australia) and used online panels, so these shared characteristics may be associated with a higher probability of additive choice behaviour; other modes and locations were not tested.
It is unclear whether the additive behaviour is inherent to the unrestricted DCE-duration format or could be reduced by adequate instructions and warm-up tasks.
Small samples within age groups and known groups limited interpretation.
The level sum score is a crude representation that ignores differences between health profiles with the same sum.
EQ-TIPS and EQ-5D-Y-3L have different content and numbers of dimensions, so the combined percentage level sum score provides only a basic overview across ages.
Very few caregivers completed PedsQL for children aged 8–12 and 13–18 years, which limited meaningful age-group comparisons.

The PPIE group was small, and a larger group with wider representation across different health conditions might have reached different decisions, particularly in the item-sorting exercise of session 3.

Members may have brought their own definitions of health and wellbeing that did not align with the domains and themes of the EQ-HWB, which could have affected the relative importance they gave to items.
Feedback after each session was relatively informal and the opportunity for a more formal evaluation of the PPIE process was not maximised.
Project delays led to periods of limited communication with PPIE members, which risks disengagement even though it did not occur here.
Sessions were intense and time-limited, and it was very challenging to cover everything in the scheduled time, so each session ended with a sense that more could have been achieved.
The quantitative analyses could not identify the concrete reasons for the preference differences; the authors called for qualitative research.
Urban-rural status was based on Hukou registration rather than actual residence, and some rural registrants lived in urban areas. This can underestimate urban-rural differences and inequalities.
Quota sampling was nonprobability sampling, and interviewers recruited from personal social networks. This created potential sampling bias and limited generalizability.
The source studies did not collect potentially important demographic and cultural variables such as marital status, religion, income, and occupation.
Most included studies used one hypothetical child age, usually 10 years, so the review could not determine the effect of child age on mean-value differences.
Most source studies did not report or justify a target sample size, which can reduce power to identify perspective effects.
More than half of the studies were European and only one reported Asian results, which limits geographic and cultural generalizability.
