Evidence about dimension ranking was mainly from EQ-5D-Y studies, so generalizability to other instruments is unknown.
Only four qualitative studies were identified, which limits explanation of why respondents make different choices.
Methods differed across disease-population proxy studies, including greater use of PedsQL and vignettes, which limited comparison.
There may have been an order effect in the stroke sample because EQ-5D-5L was always administered first.
Only one anchor (self-rated health) was available for the rehabilitation sample; multiple anchors, preferably including a clinical anchor, would be ideal.
Small sample sizes in the stroke improvement subsamples could have limited the number of significant results, especially for SES where many results were borderline significant.
Proxy assessments were used for 18.7% of the stroke sample, which could have affected responsiveness results.

Responsiveness was assessed in only two patient samples, so the results do not allow generalization to other disease areas, in particular regarding how the 3L bias manifests for condition-specific dimension problems.
Patient samples came from only two countries, so country-specific effects related to EQ-5D translations or response behaviour cannot be excluded.
Bias may also be present in EQ-5D-5L when compared with more refined classification systems, although such effects are expected to be substantially smaller.
The German EQ-5D-3L value set lacks several utility decrements (usual activities levels 2 and 3, anxiety/depression level 2), which might have affected the comparison with the German 5L value set.
Relative efficiency results for rehabilitation SES were rarely significant despite large absolute differences, because of large baseline standard deviations in the subsample.

The sample was a smallish convenience sample of young, healthy Polish students, whose disutilities are larger than those of the general population; the authors argue representativeness is not essential because the focus is methodological.

The results of some modelling approaches were probably influenced by the selection of health states: level 3 of self-care appeared in only three states and always with another dimension at level 3, which may explain degenerate (crisp) parameters in C3 and C5; a wider pool of states is needed in future studies.
Estimation error was neglected except where standard econometric techniques were used; bootstrap methods could be used in future research to assess the impact of sample randomness.

The elicited ranges were confined to either the TTO or the lead-time TTO scale, so epas/spas could not cross zero utility, and utilities were censored at -1, which may group answers and affect results.
The compatibility model (B2) was maximised numerically with the DEoptim package because the exact linear optimisation problem was overwhelmingly large, so the global optimum may not have been found.
It is paradoxical to ask respondents to report their imprecision as precise numbers; second-order (type-2 fuzzy) imprecision was not modelled because such questions would probably be unintelligible.
Only one type of imprecision was studied: other forms that respondents cannot access by introspection, such as framing or protocol effects on answers, were not addressed.
The paper does not attempt to determine the optimal way of modelling TTO data, for example how best to account for respondent heterogeneity, considering it beyond scope.
Only a single cTTO dataset (the Dutch EQ-5D-5L valuation study) was analysed, whereas previous studies combined datasets from several countries, which may give more generalizable results.
The study is a secondary data analysis used for hypothesis testing; qualitative studies would be needed to explore the reasoning behind respondents thresholds for considering states worse than dead.
41 respondents (about 4.2% of the sample) were excluded from the interaction-model analyses because they showed inconsistent large positive slopes for their positive values.
The small number of value-set pairs did not permit the authors to quantify the relative importance of time, mobility-level wording, and valuation method as drivers of the observed differences.
Individual-level classification with the garbage class model still requires the selection of statistical cutoff values, so some ambiguity in classifying respondents remains.

Neither the garbage class model nor the root likelihood statistic can distinguish respondents who answer honestly but care little about the attributes from unmotivated or dishonest respondents; excluding the former group is undesirable and can bias estimates and uptake predictions.

Both approaches depend on the quality of individual-level estimates, so they rely on correct model specification, an efficient design with informative non-zero priors, and enough choice tasks per respondent; neither is recommended when the number of choice tasks is considerably smaller than the number of parameters.

With only 2 classes the standard garbage class specification can be too parsimonious to represent the preference distribution of good-quality respondents, in which case a more flexible mixing distribution or multiple mixed logit classes would be needed, but such models require larger samples and more choice tasks.
Extending the specification with class membership predictor variables to examine determinants of garbage class membership was beyond the scope of the article.

The garbage class model does not capture intermediate attribute non-attendance behaviour explicitly; an attribute non-attendance extension would be needed if behavioural non-attendance estimates are of direct interest.

Generalizability is restricted to the study population sample; data came from telephone interviews with a high non-response rate (23.0% response), so subgroups such as people in poor health and the institutionalized population were probably not adequately represented.
The known-groups analysis relied on sociodemographic characteristics only, because variables reflecting objective physical and mental health were not available.
The analysis used cross-sectional data from a single survey cycle, so reliability and responsiveness of the two measures could not be compared.

The analyses used existing data sets that were not designed to collect respondents' feedback on the rationales behind their valuation responses; qualitative analysis would be needed to understand respondents' thought processes.
Recruitment from a volunteer pool may have selected participants in better health than non-volunteers and caused selection bias.
All data were collected through a web-based survey, and respondents unfamiliar with this mode may have given inappropriate answers, which may have caused information bias.
All data were caregiver self-reports, and no clinical information such as OI type was collected, which may limit generalizability.
Data were limited to one time point, so responsiveness to change and test-retest reliability could not be assessed.
The study lacked information on each parent's caregiving intensity, duration, share of burden, and other caregiving roles.
The study lacked a parent health-status variable, which could have reduced confounding in the regression analysis.
Participants who did not report female or male gender were excluded from the gender analysis because the group was very small.
The pilot United Kingdom preference weights might not represent Australian preferences and could produce different results from a future Australian value set.
The level sum-score gives equal weight to each dimension and can assign the same score to different profiles.
The study did not compare the EQ-HWB-S head to head with other caregiver measures.
The EQ-5D-3L vision bolt-on value set was experimental, was estimated from a relatively small general-population sample in one United Kingdom region, and was not an official value set.
The EQ-5D-5L vision bolt-on comparison used non-preference-based sum scores because no value set was available, so the results may not represent the performance of a preference-based index.
The sample was small and the study was not powered for multiple comparisons, so the results are preliminary.
Results may not generalize to other vision conditions or countries, where instrument translation could affect performance.
The analysis was limited to age, sex, education, and income; other relevant social and health variables were unavailable in a standardized form across datasets.
The analysis did not use an EQ-5D index because country-specific value sets would add cross-country differences in health-state preferences.
The study was not designed to rank countries or account for differences in demographic and other sample characteristics across countries.
The source surveys covered a large time interval and some data were old, which reduced direct policy relevance and required attention to possible changes in EQ-5D ratings over time.
Survey sample sizes and administration modes differed across countries.
Further research is needed to determine whether the binary no-problem versus any-problem method for EQ-5D-3L is comparable when applied to EQ-5D-5L data.
Immunization status was self-reported and the reliability of self-reported COVID-19 vaccine status has not been established, so acceptance may be over- or under-estimated.

Recruitment through internet advertising restricted the sample to people with internet access and may represent a selective subset of pregnant persons, so selection bias and limited generalizability cannot be excluded.

Data were collected in the six months after COVID-19 vaccines were introduced, and acceptance is likely to have changed since, given rising coverage and the emergence of more virulent SARS-CoV-2 variants.
Recruitment closed before the intended sample size of 280 was reached because recruitment was slower than expected given long surgical waiting times.
Only 21% of eligible patients participated, so included patients were probably more open-minded about education on treatment options, threatening generalizability.
Low uptake probably caused the imbalance in sex between arms; adjusting for sex may not capture its complex association with the outcomes.
The individualised decision aid could not be compared with a conventional decision aid using average information, because no such aid was available or routinely used in Canadian practice.
Describing numerical risks and levels of outcome improvement was challenging even with graphical displays, and patient feedback suggested the decision aid can be improved.
There is little information on outcomes of patients who do not have surgery, so the decision aid could not provide individualised results for the non-surgical option.
It is unclear if and how the decision aid and surgeon report influenced the consultation itself, since shared decision-making was only rated by patients after the consultation.
Surgeons and some staff could not be blinded to allocation because the surgeon report was placed in the patient file.

Fast median response times (4 s per question) and a high share of lexicographic responders suggest strategic behaviour or skimping on the task, so data quality in the unsupervised web-based setting is likely lower than in the previous interviewer-administered paper-based study.

Several differences between this study and the earlier one (interviewer presence, paper versus web administration, 15 versus 108 questions, closer adherence to the MVH protocol) are confounded, so the cause of the divergent findings cannot be isolated.
The restricted age range of 18-45 years may explain why age was not a determinant of preferences, unlike in other studies.
Significant differences between the randomized blocks existed in raw BTD preferences, gender, age and response times.
The child and adolescent samples were smaller than the adult sample, and the child sample contained a higher proportion of males.
Children were recruited through parents, so the study could not verify whether each child or a parent completed the child survey.
The small number of anchoring tasks could have reduced the statistical efficiency of the duration and immediate-death model estimates.

Online DCE collection can affect data quality, especially for children and adolescents; the applied quality checks might not have removed all problematic responses, and exclusion patterns differed across age groups.
Follow-up lasted only three months, and some patients were still receiving treatment, which could have limited estimation of minimal detectable change.
Excluding 46 patients who died and 5 patients lost to follow-up from the analysis could have introduced attrition bias and affected responsiveness and MCID estimates.
Responsiveness and MCID depend on interventions, patient characteristics, and setting, so the results may not generalize to other diseases.
Heterogeneity in patient characteristics and disease duration may have limited detection of meaningful individual-level change.

The results came from one simple full-factorial DCE with three alternatives, three attributes, 200 responses per choice set, and possible dominated alternatives, so other experimental designs can produce different patterns.
The random coefficients were normally distributed; asymmetric or discrete distributions such as latent classes were not examined.
The simulation addressed interpersonal heterogeneity but not intrapersonal variability in a person's parameters across choices.
The meta-analysis was exploratory and the list of study-level and country-level covariates was arbitrarily selected, neither exhaustive nor representative.
Countries that did not report standard errors of observed mean utilities, or whose data were a subset of studies already included, were excluded from the meta-regressions.
The review was restricted to English-language publications.
The BURQOL-RD database used was collected for other objectives and analyses, so the data were not designed for the present research question.
Caregiver age had a high rate of missing values and could not be included, although it is probably a relevant determinant of caregiver HRQOL.

The EQ-5D-Y was used for child patients in all countries except France, where the EQ-5D-5L was used for children because no French child version was available, which may influence the HRQOL ratings obtained.

Child utility values came from the Craig United States valuation of child HRQOL, produced with a methodology different from the usual TTO studies for the 3L version, so the values lie on a different scale, although they were used only as an explanatory variable.
The data are descriptive and cross-sectional, and the observed correlation between caregiver burden and HRQOL had a small effect size.

The examples used to populate the classification tables are probably biased towards value sets claiming to present experience-based values from the public perspective because of the snowball and citation search methods used, so condition-specific preference-based valuations are probably under-represented.

The framework trades comprehensiveness for practical simplicity and omits further nuances of experience such as the intensity, recency and duration of experience and its use as a reference point under loss aversion.

The classification omits other issues affecting values, including the elicitation method and its operationalisation, treatment of states worse than dead, and the modelling technique used to derive final values.
The classification is illustrative and is not intended as a definitive classification of the existing literature.

The reviewed study identifying an intermediate valuation group was limited by the small sample size of that group, and the question wording behind many VAS valuations was not specified, so time frames had to be assumed.

The adult EQ-5D-5L measure and adult disutility weights were applied to derive utilities for adolescents because an Amharic version was available; the EQ-5D-Y may have better content validity for this group.
No cognitive debriefing was done, so the suitability of the dimensions and the comprehensibility of the questionnaire were not tested.
Responsiveness to change was not examined because there was no intervention.
Different interviewers collected data for the school sample and for the patients with major mental health disorders, which may have affected the results.
PROTO was created for this study and was not properly validated; it had only face-validity testing and semi-structured interviews with a small patient sample.
ICIQ-LUTS is validated for lower urinary tract symptoms but not for measuring the effect of transurethral procedures on voiding symptoms.
The study lacked baseline LUTS data, which made it difficult to attribute postoperative symptoms directly to the procedure.
The study groups were heterogeneous in tumour characteristics and uneven in size because treatment allocation followed clinical practice in the observational design.
AQoL-6D and HUI3 samples were too small for robust test-retest reliability and responsiveness conclusions because these instruments were placed in randomized blocks to reduce respondent burden.
Online reporting provided no clinical tests, clinical reports, or other external indicator against which to compare participant responses.
Level sum scores are crude and can miss the complexity and relative importance of dimensions and levels that utility scores capture.
Not all instruments had value sets, which limits use of the results for economic evaluation and country-specific utility scoring.
The study included a selected set of common generic paediatric HRQoL instruments and did not cover all available instruments.
The evidence came from an Australian population, and generalizability to other countries is unknown.
Forty choice tasks in an approximately 18-minute survey can cause fatigue and inattentive or rushed responses despite randomization and interspersed demographic questions.
Religiousness correlates with characteristics such as ethnicity and socioeconomic status. Residual confounding can remain, and the study does not establish a causal effect of religiousness.
The online administration can help explain why irregular duration-response patterns were more common than in earlier paper-based studies.
The binary religious versus nonreligious grouping does not fully represent the spectrum of belief systems and cultural diversity.
The United Kingdom public sample was not nationally representative.
The inclusion of only one mild state and several severe states can limit variation in worse-than-dead preferences and reduce power to detect smaller or interaction effects.
The authors describe the publication samples as limited, so they do not establish the prevalence of nomenclature errors across all EQ-5D literature.

The analysis included people who responded after discharge and may be more likely to engage with follow-up; nonrespondents may differ in health literacy, socioeconomic status, and other unmeasured factors, so response bias is possible.
PROMs were collected weeks after discharge, so the landmark prediction horizons can miss early readmissions and do not support immediate discharge decisions.
PROMs were measured once and carried forward across landmarks; a time-dependent sensitivity analysis suggested that resulting bias was small.
External validation in other jurisdictions is needed before broader use.
The cross-sectional design cannot establish causal direction and cannot exclude reverse or bidirectional effects between physical limitations and anxiety/depression.
All data were self-reported, which can cause shared-method variance and social-desirability bias.
Unmeasured traits and experiences, such as neuroticism, chronic stress, and coping strategies, can confound mental and physical self-assessments despite DAG-based adjustment.
The single item for each EQ-5D-5L domain can capture less complexity than multidimensional measures.
Few participants reported severe or extreme anxiety/depression, which reduces precision and generalizability for the level 4/5 subgroup.
The study used a specific Chinese population. Cultural effects are possible, and generalizability to other populations is uncertain.
Recruitment overlapped the COVID-19 pandemic, but the study did not collect COVID-19 information.
The cohort had generally high health-status scores, which could have limited correlations and group discrimination.
Use of both self-administered and telephone formats could have caused mode-related score differences, including social-desirability bias by telephone.
PHQ-9 convergent validity should ideally have been assessed with another depression measure instead of only SF-36 components.
The response rate was low despite two reminders.
The cross-sectional study did not assess responsiveness.
Instruments were not administered in a controlled environment, so distractions could have affected responses.
Some comorbidity groups had small samples, which could explain nonsignificant known-groups comparisons.
The survey was administered only in English through an existing internet panel, so selection bias cannot be ruled out despite the representativeness measures taken.
Participants from New York City (n = 1045) and the rest of New York State (n = 1612) were combined although the two groups may differ in sociodemographic characteristics.
The analyses were cross-sectional.
COVID-19 exposure and symptoms, risk factors for COVID-19 complications, and chronic conditions were all self-reported.
A detailed analysis of non-responders was not possible because of the panel recruitment system used.
The cross-sectional design prevented assessment of responsiveness and test-retest reliability.
Convergent validity could be assessed only for EQ-5D-5L because head-to-head comparison data were not available for the other three measures.
Inaccurate and inadequate timing estimates prevented estimation of average measure-completion time.
Limited resident characteristics and unavailable PAS-Cog and Barthel Index data for some residents restricted sample description and known-groups analyses.

Some Powers of Attorney declined participation for residents with complex health needs or insufficient English proficiency. Some instruments had no translated version, and no interpreter was available. These factors limit generalizability to culturally and linguistically diverse residents.

Some family proxy reports were delayed. Staff roles, question explanations, assistance, and administration techniques also differed between facilities. These issues could affect interrater reliability.
The two facilities were selected by convenience, were not-for-profit, and belonged to the same provider. This limits transferability to private or government-owned facilities.
The study examined measures selected for the Australian context and did not assess other available measures, including ICECAP-O and WOOP.

The final sample was smaller than the target because renovations reduced bed numbers. The small sample was especially important for known-groups analyses and the randomly assigned second-measure subsamples.
Experts were limited to people known to the research group, which introduced selection bias, and social-work and education experts were not invited.
The identity and disciplinary mix of experts who participated at each Delphi stage were unknown because responses were anonymous, which limited interpretation of the final round.
The general-population commercial online panel can cause selection bias related to digital literacy and internet access, and results may not generalize to clinical populations.
Recruitment through Dynata can cause data-quality limitations despite the study quality-control measures.
Differences in sample size and unknown representativeness relative to the original PROMIS-16 item-testing survey may have affected distributional comparisons.
The comprehension quiz before EQ-5D-5L and the fixed instrument order may have affected responses, framing, cognitive burden, and response bias.
EQ VAS was administered directly after EQ-5D-5L, which may favor EQ-5D-5L in concordance comparisons and limits its independence as a comparator.
Data collection preceded the August 2024 PROMIS-16 erratum, so the survey used the original sleep-item wording and order, which may have affected performance.
The researchers did not return findings to participants for verification, which limited confirmation of the interpretations.
Participants recruited through a commercial panel might not represent the general population in interview experience or motivation.
Thinking aloud and responding to probes might change concentration and thought processes compared with independent and faster task completion.
The qualitative approach could not clearly identify time discounting; the effect might have been small or subconscious.
The fixed topic and task order might have influenced responses; the study did not randomize tasks because of ethical concerns about sensitive topics.
The second reviewer independently screened only a random 10% sample of records, rather than all records.
Data extraction was not fully independent, which may have increased the risk of extraction errors.
The review did not formally assess the methodological quality of included studies, which limits differentiation between more and less robust evidence.
The included studies were highly heterogeneous in research stage, EQ-5D version, wording, language, and population; the authors therefore used narrative synthesis and did not perform meta-analysis.
An English-language search strategy and restriction to Embase, PubMed, and Web of Science may have omitted relevant studies.

Unpublished data, conference abstracts, and grey literature were not searched systematically, which may have introduced publication bias, although EuroQol proceedings and citation searches supplemented the databases.
Some bolt-ons were developed in non-English languages and translated for publication, which creates uncertainty about exact wording.
EuroQol Group involvement in many included studies may increase the risk of positive-results orientation or publication bias.
Population categories were broad because evidence for more specific populations was scarce.
Administration mode was not accounted for in the synthesis because data were insufficient.
The review excluded non-English-language articles, which can limit generalizability to non-English-speaking populations.
The review did not cover all relevant instrument characteristics, including acceptability, feasibility, and inter-rater agreement between proxies and children.

Only 4 of the 7 instruments analysed were also present in the MIC dataset, and some MIC instruments (for example the SWLS) were absent from the OMS dataset, so the two measurement models cannot be compared perfectly.
The method identifies bolt-ons only for dimensions already covered by at least one instrument in the dataset; relevant dimensions absent from all included instruments cannot be found.
Data were collected in Australia, so cultural response heterogeneity may limit the generalisability of the identified measurement model.

The sample mixed healthy people and people with a variety of conditions, which suits generic bolt-on identification but not condition-specific bolt-ons, and differential item functioning by age, gender and condition has been reported.
The dimensionality identified by factor analysis depends on the measures included, so results may differ in datasets with different measures.

The samples of children with chronic disability (n = 35) and acquired chronic conditions (n = 32) were small, so results for these groups could be biased even though the overall target of 190 was exceeded.
The Composite Score is not ideal because it is derived from adult valuations of losses in a child's health and has not been formally endorsed by the EuroQol Research Foundation.
Discriminant validity between the two groups of children with chronic conditions was not demonstrated despite differences in their mobility.

Reliability of the Usual Activities dimension was limited, and further qualitative research with a larger sample is needed on how children understand Mobility, Usual Activities and Pain or Discomfort.
No official value set was available for EQ-5D-Y-5L, so only its level sum score was analyzed; this limits utility interpretation.

Severe heart disease was underrepresented, and recruitment was limited to stable outpatients with a relatively long time since diagnosis; these features may have constrained known-group validity and responsiveness.

The eligibility criteria excluded children with major developmental disabilities, significant intellectual impairment, and severe noncardiac comorbidities, which limits coverage of the broader pediatric heart-disease population.

The treatment-adherence domain applied only to participants taking heart-disease medication, producing a small sample and requiring cautious interpretation of its internal consistency and known-group validity.
The study was not prospectively registered.
The study data were not available in a public open-access database.
Chronic conditions were self-reported rather than clinically verified, which can introduce reporting bias.
General-population chronic-condition subgroups likely included milder cases, which limits generalizability to clinical populations.
The available item pool shaped the factor structure; more items related to physical-symptom bolt-ons could yield different factors.
The approximately one-month test-retest interval was longer than the usual five to seven days and can allow real changes or short-term fluctuations.
Responsiveness and test-retest groups were defined by general self-reported health change rather than change in specific bolt-on constructs.
COVID-19 pandemic conditions, restrictions, disease severity, and vaccine availability can have affected responses and bolt-on performance.
The wording of bolt-ons for Toolbox constructs differed from current proposed Toolbox versions, so direct interpretation for those versions requires caution.
All 15 bolt-ons appeared in a fixed order after EQ-5D-5L, unlike anticipated targeted use of a small number, and order or context can have affected responses.
Established cross-cultural adaptation procedures were not used for nonvalidated survey translations, which limits country comparisons.
The exploratory study occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic, and samples for individual variants were small and possibly underpowered to detect significant differences.

Despite interviewer training and instruction, patients could have processed recall periods, instructions, and response scales differently because of recall biases, mental heuristics, or reliance on semantic memory.
The 3-month SGRQ was used because no true gold-standard HRQoL instrument was available; its longer recall period could bias effect sizes in favor of longer-recall EQ-5D-5L variants.
The study did not use real-time symptom tracking because of resource limits and participant burden.
The follow-up interval was not standardized, which limited benchmarking of the five EQ-5D-5L versions, assessment of exacerbations, change-status assessment, and real-world generalizability.
Questionnaires were interviewer-administered, so results might not translate to routine busy-clinic use where EQ-5D-5L is more likely to be self-administered.
Results from this hospital sample might not apply to milder obstructive airway disease treated in the community or to other fluctuating health conditions.
The multiethnic Asian setting could have introduced cultural differences in concepts of time and well-being, although the authors also considered that the findings might transcend cultures.
The cross-sectional design does not permit temporal or causal inference; psychological factors and low HRQoL can have bidirectional relations.
The analyses did not consider lesion location, age at skin disease onset, or affected skin area; the authors omitted an affected-area measure to reduce participant burden.
Mean DLQI scores were in the moderate range and below the cutoff for severe effects.
The recruitment strategy may have caused self-selection bias, and the generalizability of the results is unclear.
The study used only self-report measures and did not include expert assessments.
The targeted search did not use all possible terms, including diary-related terms, and could have missed eligible studies.

The review excluded comparisons with longer recall periods and excluded ecological momentary assessment used to derive daily indices; the latter exclusion was a deviation from the registered protocol.
Heterogeneity in populations, instruments, collection methods, and analytical methods prevented meta-analysis and left the magnitude of the recall effect uncertain.
Many source studies inadequately controlled repeated questionnaire administration or recall-order effects, and small between-group samples often had limited statistical power.
Studies that used different instruments for the two recall periods could not isolate recall effects from other measurement artifacts.
Closed-ended probing in many qualitative studies could have restricted participants’ consideration of preferred recall duration.
There is no gold-standard marker of patient experience, so recall effects cannot be cleanly separated from response processes, reinterpretation of instructions, or selection and missing-data effects.
The sample differed from the Romanian general population in age, sex, and rural or urban residence; weights corrected these variables but not other differences such as education or income.
Survey weights used 2011 census data, and subsequent high migration could mean that the weights did not fully correct current population representativeness.
Data collection used more interviewers than optimal, and fieldwork barriers, interviewer fatigue, replacement, dropout, and variable performance reduced data quality.
The EQ-5D-3L valuation tasks followed ten EQ-5D-5L valuation tasks in the same interview, so respondent fatigue could have reduced attention and motivation.
The sensitivity analysis did not assess the effect of excluding respondents with inconsistent valuations.
Centralized face-to-face surveys in community centres required physical mobility and could have excluded residents whose health was most affected by heatwaves.
Suboptimal follow-up could have caused attrition bias because unwell participants might have been more likely to avoid travel to the survey site on hot days.
The timing of the first heatwave assessment could have captured strong adaptive behavior that reduced or reversed measured heatwave effects.
EQ-HWB-9 responses were derived from EQ-HWB items and not collected through standalone EQ-HWB-9 administration; the assumption of minimal administration effects needs empirical testing.
The study included only one Chinese city and two communities, which limits transfer to areas with different climates, urban layouts, or access to cooling.
The study included only older adults, so results might not apply to younger or working-age populations with occupational exposure or different adaptive behavior.
The included evidence focused mainly on chronic rhinosinusitis and allergic rhinitis, which limits generalizability to other upper respiratory tract diseases.
Convergent validity dominated the evidence; known-groups validity and responsiveness were assessed less often, and test-retest reliability was not assessed.
The source populations were mainly older than 40 years, so transferability to younger patients is uncertain.
The English-language eligibility criterion can have excluded evidence from non-English-speaking populations.
Most included studies used patient populations from the United States, which limits geographic generalizability.
The study was not designed to elicit a value set and used only 10 mostly severe EQ-5D states.

The baseline value of -4 assigned to respondents who exhausted the lead time came from a binary yes/no question without a visual aid and without iteration to indifference, so its reliability is questionable and it creates an artificial gap in the value distribution.
The method relies on the assumption of additive separability between the lead time in full health and the state being valued.
Time preference could not be measured, so results are not controlled for discounting even though lead time pushes the valued state further into the future.
Comparisons with MVH values are not straightforward because they involve either extreme negative numbers or artificially bounded ones.
One interviewer misapplied the batched ranking procedure, so 17 respondents were excluded from the ranking analysis.
The sample was recruited from areas dominated by mortgaged properties, giving a very high level of home ownership and limited representativeness.
Higher rescaled VAS values may reflect the set of mostly severe states valued, a potential violation of independence of irrelevant alternatives.
The sample size was relatively small, although consistent with most existing response scaling studies.
Persons of very poor socio-economic status were not included, because all participants were recruited from a shopping mall.
The main limitation was nonrandomized allocation between n-TTO and c-TTO: all c-TTO interviews were conducted first in Norway, and all n-TTO interviews were conducted first in Singapore.

Randomization between the two n-TTO route subgroups was not entirely successful; in Norway, participants assigned to bottom-up n-TTO were older than participants in the other groups, which could have biased comparisons because older respondents produced fewer unique values and more logical inconsistency.
Intrarespondent agreement could not be assessed because no health state was repeated within individuals.
True bias and prediction error cannot be assessed without simulation; only cross-validation was used.
Only two parametric and two nonparametric transforming functions were examined, and other functions might perform better.
Results apply to the particular set of TTO and DCE health states used in the study.
The assumption that better between-state variability in the UK was due to one-to-one interviewing cannot exclude other explanatory factors.
Only main effects models were fitted, because the pilot sample lacked power for interaction terms; larger studies with at least 1000 respondents per country were underway.
The analyses used existing data, and the desired variables were not collected in all countries.
Only a small number of sociodemographic variables could be analysed without losing too many countries.
Cultural data were available only at national level rather than respondent level, which reduces the chance of detecting a relation with Delta u.
Methods of data collection differ between 3L and 5L studies, and these differences had to be collapsed into a single 3L/5L dummy variable.
The valuation data were not cleaned, which might affect the findings, although removing inconsistent responses is reported to have little effect on preference-based valuations.
The assumption that each valuation study used a nationally representative sample is uncertain, since designs and sample sizes varied between 225 and 4043 respondents.
Correlation between the independent variables made the results harder to interpret.
Moderate health states were excluded, so the whole spectrum of EQ-5D health states was not analysed.

The existing datasets did not all contain comparator HRQoL measures or clinical measures for known groups, which prevented fuller age-specific psychometric comparisons and assessment of missing EQ-TIPS concepts.

The health conditions were heterogeneous and complex, acute versus chronic presentation was not recorded, and comorbid effects were not captured; this limited attribution of item-performance differences to health conditions.
Caregiver socioeconomic status, education, and caregiving experience were not collected, although these characteristics could have affected proxy reporting.
The sample was relatively small, young, and not representative of a defined general population; no formal hypotheses or sample-size calculation were specified for the novel exploratory method.

Only a limited set of health states was used, and Q1-Q3 were asked only when cTTO utility exceeded 0.1; few respondents therefore completed follow-ups for five or six states, limiting within-respondent consistency analysis.
The order of Q1-Q3 was not randomized, so ordering effects cannot be determined.
The simplified protocol had no standard EQ-5D-5L valuation feedback module and no test-retest check, and the many choice tasks could have tired or confused respondents.
The small amount of data per respondent and limited consistency prevented estimation of individual discount-function parameters, so the analysis used only ordinal response patterns.
The non-constant health profiles in Q2 and Q3 could have provoked complex behavior; if so, the findings have less relevance to tasks that use only constant profiles.
The rationale behind the children's EQ VAS scores was not explored, so the discrepancy between reported health profiles and VAS scores can only be explained speculatively.
The extensive cognitive debriefing appeared to cause response saturation or fatigue in some children, which may have limited the quality of their later answers.
An experimental version of the EQ-5D-Y-5L was translated because no official EuroQol version was available at the time, and the translation guideline used has since been revised.

The updated priors used data collected with the previous EQ-VT DCE design, which did not support random-parameter models; the meta-analysis therefore did not include within-country preference heterogeneity and assumed that between-country heterogeneity dominated it.
The priors did not yet represent the anticipated increase in choice consistency from attribute level overlap because data from the updated design were not yet available.

Increasing the number of tasks from 7 to 12 can increase respondent burden, fatigue, and completion time; these effects were not established in this study and will be monitored in future EQ-VT studies.
The study was not designed to separate the effects of the pandemic itself from the effects of non-pharmaceutical interventions.
The surveys used separate cohorts, so confounding can remain; regression adjustment was possible for EQ VAS but not for the aggregate EQ-5D-5L baseline comparison.
No individual-level pre-pandemic EQ-5D-5L data were available; the main analysis therefore relied on EQ VAS, and the EQ-5D-5L comparison used a 2017 aggregate baseline.
Monthly QALY losses were rough extrapolations from point estimates and assumed that measured HRQoL loss represented the entire month; the EQ-5D estimate depended partly on 2017 sample data.
Only two pandemic measurements were made, about one month and about ten months after the outbreak, so the results cannot be extrapolated directly to the full pandemic period.
The broad search and reference checks could still have missed some guidelines.
Some guidelines required online translation. Local experts validated the translations, but ambiguity could remain.
For some countries, it was unclear which guideline should be included.
The searches could not identify official guidelines that were unpublished or not publicly available, and they did not capture supplemental informal guidance from HTA authorities.
The HTA environment changes continuously, so the review can become outdated quickly and requires regular updates.
The model did not control for some factors that may determine health preferences, such as the respondent rate of time preference, marital status and urban household location.
Snowball sampling was used, so the samples were not representative of Polish migrants or of the native Irish, and the findings cannot be generalised.
Migrant samples are heterogeneous, which makes findings about migrants hard to generalise.
All survey questions were administered in English, so the sample may under-represent Polish migrants in Ireland who are not fluent in English.
The sample size was small, although the authors argue the Bayesian nonparametric model makes efficient use of few observations.

The two samples were unbalanced across sociodemographic characteristics; the authors state that data collection could have been quota-controlled by age group and sex, at the cost of a more complex process.
The Bayesian nonparametric results were not compared with parametric methods, which the authors propose for further research.
The Swedish and German VAS value sets were not anchored with dead at zero, which limits direct comparison with anchored value sets.
The value sets were developed with different statistical models and numbers of parameters, which may have affected the differences in calculated EQ-5D indices.

The valuation studies that produced the compared value sets occurred at different times, from 1997 through 2014, so temporal variation could not be separated from country, method, or perspective differences.

Different respondents completed each perspective arm. Therefore, differences between perspectives could reflect differences in underlying preferences between samples, although demographic characteristics were very similar.
The study used online self-completion. Prior cognitive debriefing of OPUF raised data-quality concerns and suggested that interviewer-led collection could be preferable.
The first publication-level clusters were heterogeneous because papers can share references even when their research questions and citation decisions differ.
The authors state that future work should use keywords and abstracts in network maps to support more granular interpretation of methodological topics over time.
The authors did not perform broader keyword searches such as trade-off because these required resources to exclude many unrelated publications.
The search was based on publications that cited Torrance (1970), Torrance et al. (1972), or Fanshel and Bush (1970), so it omitted relevant publications that did not cite those sources.
Included studies varied in quality, and some had small samples, low response rates, or incomplete data; this can affect pooled estimates and generalizability.
Inadequate or unclear source data prevented planned subgroup analyses for disease severity, complications, vaccination status, and access to COVID-19 testing.
When studies reported multiple time points, the review used only the final HRQoL assessment; this may bias estimates toward recovery because HRQoL tends to improve over time.
Means and standard deviations estimated from medians and ranges or interquartile ranges may be inaccurate for skewed data and reduce pooled-estimate precision.
The review included only English-language peer-reviewed publications and excluded gray literature, so it may have missed relevant evidence.
Extreme statistical heterogeneity limits the certainty and comparability of pooled EQ-5D utility and EQ VAS estimates.
The evaluation rests on a single cost-effectiveness analysis of dialysis treatments in Singapore, which limits generalisability.
EQ-5D values were not calculated with a value set from the country where the data were collected; applying UK and England value sets to Singaporean data may be a concern.
No primary EQ-5D-3L data were available, so mapped EQ-5D-3L values could not be compared with observed EQ-5D-3L values.
No mapping algorithm developed on dialysis patients exists, so the algorithms applied were derived from US samples that were much younger and healthier than the study sample.
Brachial procedures covered 2013-2020, while radial and femoral procedures covered 2019-2020.
Many femoral or brachial procedures were conversions from another access, most often radial access, which could bias access-change comparisons.
Quality-of-life impairments were assessed retrospectively by patients and could be subjective and affected by recall bias.
Follow-up physical-examination and laboratory records were not available.
The brachial-access group in the quality-of-life follow-up was small.
The cross-sectional dataset measured each respondent only once, so it could not assess responsiveness.
The psychometric analysis was sample-specific, and the general population survey included a relatively low proportion of participants with cardiorespiratory conditions.
Clinical breathing measurements such as FEV1 and clinical variables were unavailable, which limited comparison between clinical condition groups.
The analysis applied a Dutch valuation algorithm to Australian data because no Australian utility values were available for the respiratory bolt-ons.
Publications in languages other than English were excluded for practicality and because of limited resources.
Reports, conference papers, book chapters, reviews, theses and dissertations and opinion pieces were excluded, so only peer-reviewed studies were considered.

Because most included studies were cross-sectional and studies conducted over time did not necessarily reassess cognition, it was not possible to track the impact of cognitive decline on the ability of older people to self-report quality of life over time.
The wide variety of cognitive assessments and thresholds applied across the included studies made comparison between studies extremely challenging.

Inter-rater agreement statistics were not reported by all papers (only 26, 52%, reported ICC or kappa), and some reported statistics only for overall scores or only for dimensions, so mean scores had to be examined where no inter-rater statistics were available.
Meta-analysis could not be conducted, so findings were combined by narrative synthesis only.
The sample had higher education than the Ugandan general population, possibly because people with less education had difficulty understanding cTTO tasks.
The sample included more Baganda participants than the national population because collection occurred in the Central Region.
The authors note that collection during March to May 2021, during the COVID-19 pandemic, may have affected health valuations and warrants future research.
Data collection used only Luganda and was limited to the Central Region, because multilingual collection was not logistically possible and COVID-19 travel restrictions required a pragmatic design.
Females aged 35-44 and 55-64 years were slightly over-represented, and more educated people were over-represented relative to the 2011 census.
Some interviewer protocol-compliance problems persisted beyond the pilot and required correction during data collection.
Minor interviewer effects suggested possible differences in interview conduct, although respondent demographic differences could also have contributed.
The vignettes omitted some health consequences of beta-thalassemia severity and treatment to reduce respondent fatigue and protect data quality.
Some interviews had protocol-compliance issues, and possible interviewer effects must be considered despite training and quality review.
The quota-based UK general-population sample was reasonably similar in age and gender but was not fully nationally representative.
All interviews took place in one highly urbanized location in northwest England, so geographical bias cannot be ruled out.
Vignette-based TTO could not represent every issue and complication of beta-thalassemia and its treatment.
The extent to which these general-population utilities are comparable with utilities elicited from patients with beta-thalassemia is unknown.

Convenience, self-selecting sampling in all three countries produced samples that were not representative of any country and that differed in characteristics; respondents may have had a stronger interest in children than non-respondents.
The order of presentation was fixed and order effects were not controlled; reversing the order of the ADULT and CHILD sections would have been preferable.
A printing error meant that one health state in the English version did not match the standard set used in Germany and Spain.
Only a limited number of health states was used and values were elicited with VAS, so generalisation to other preference elicitation methods such as time trade-off is uncertain.
Without qualitative information the study cannot explain why values shift, for example whether framing effects or personal constructs are involved.
All participants came from one hospital in Shanghai and all patients had haematological malignancies, which limits generalizability to other regions and conditions.
Patients and caregivers were not separated during questionnaire completion and might have consulted each other despite instructions not to do so.
Official interviewer-administered Y-5L versions were unavailable, so the study used beta self-complete versions for patients and proxies; their wording could change before official approval.
The face-to-face interviewer-administered results might not generalize to self-administration.
The five-level self-rated-health question was a blunt stability criterion and might not detect small dimension-specific health changes captured by Y-5L.
The mapping depends on the relation between the two datasets and on methodological assumptions that can cause errors not present in directly elicited value sets.
The international sample used to estimate the crosswalk transition matrix did not include Slovenian respondents.
The study used diagnostic criteria that preceded newer multicenter criteria, so a few unilateral cases could have been misdiagnosed under the newer criteria.
New patients who had to pay for their own care might have declined botulinum toxin treatment because of financial limits, which created potential selection bias.
The study observed only one botulinum toxin A treatment cycle, so it could not assess progression or long-term effects.
The COVID-19 pandemic overlapped with follow-up and could have reduced reported post-treatment HRQoL below the level that would otherwise have occurred.

Convenience samples were used in all countries and in both phases, so the study populations are not representative of the national populations, although all age groups, both sexes and different school types were included.

The protocol adopted in the UK and in Spain deviated marginally from that used elsewhere; in the UK only the 5L version was developed and tested, in focus groups rather than individual cognitive interviews.
Children with current experience of illness could not be recruited in the UK because separate NHS ethical approval would have caused significant delay, so UK testing was limited to school children.
Only a self-report version was produced; proxy versions still have to be developed, and the psychometric properties of the EQ-5D-Y-5L remain untested.
Agreement analysis was exploratory because the instruments measure different quality-of-life components and use differently anchored utility scales.
Comparator instruments lacked conceptually overlapping items for exhaustion, daily activities, and control, which prevented a complete convergent-validity assessment of all EQ-HWB-9 items.

The dataset lacked diagnosed mental and physical health conditions for known-group validity analyses; SWEMWBS cutoffs indicate mental well-being problems but are not clinically validated to diagnose mental illness.
HUI3 disability categories are preference-confounded and classified many respondents as having severe disability; diagnosed or general-health data could have complemented these subjective categories.
The analysis used the experimental 2022 EQ-HWB-9, which can change after further validity assessment.
The final United Kingdom EQ-HWB-9 value set was not available, so the study used a provisional interim value set that provides only indicative utilities.
Further studies with different external anchors are needed to establish the minimally important change because improvement in the group reporting unchanged global health could be measurement noise.
The follow-up period was only three months.
The study did not use paper EQ-5D-5L as a gold-standard criterion for validity or concordance because that comparison would require a larger randomized controlled study.
Small response counts required grouping EQ-5D-5L levels 3 to 5, and the study lacked power for clinic-by-diagnosis subgroup analyses and for some deterioration analyses.
The sample was small.
Participants came from only two public outpatient clinics, which limits generalizability across clinical settings.
Validity and psychometric performance do not establish that electronic EQ-5D-5L data are clinically useful, acceptable, feasible, or resource-efficient in routine practice.
The trial evaluates only the 650 nm invasive laser acupuncture parameters from the pilot study and does not compare alternative wavelengths, energy doses, or acupoints.
The trial includes people with moderate non-specific chronic low back pain and excludes those with severe pain, which limits applicability to severe pain.
The practitioner cannot be blinded because the practitioner must operate the laser device according to group assignment; only patients and assessors are blinded.
The convenience sample was not representative of Norway and overrepresented young, female, and highly educated respondents.
Exclusion of 133 participants based on their TTO value sets could have caused selection bias because valuation patterns differ by demographic characteristics.
Each DCE task displayed four five-dimension EQ-5D-5L states and could have caused information overload.
Red shading used to aid comprehension might have influenced choices toward either the least-red final state or avoidance of the most-red initial state.
The DCE had no temporal dimension, did not directly assess QALYs, and did not directly test current QALY-shortfall severity criteria.
The study assumed that health-state values elicited from a self perspective also apply to choices concerning other people.
The tasks were designed to measure preference for the worse off, so the study could not quantify the apparent preference for the better off.
A coding error in the first application version caused five post-interview exclusions.
Rural residents, participants with no literacy, and adults aged 65 years or older were underrepresented, although geographical distribution was represented.
The visual-aid approach for participants with no literacy was not fully validated, so the investigators did not recruit to the exact national quota for this group.
COVID-19 interrupted data collection before the planned 1000 final interviews were reached.

The analyzed sample differed from the national population in marital status and health-insurance coverage, and the effect of weighting underrepresented characteristics on the value set was not assessed.
The cross-sectional design cannot establish temporal order or causality and is open to reverse causality.
The absence of pre-pandemic data prevents assessment of whether the inequalities worsened during COVID-19.

Income nonresponse caused exclusion of about 10% of survey completers and could bias income-related estimates; a unified imputation model was difficult because income reporting differed across countries.

Recruitment from voluntary online market-research panels can select younger, healthier, more digitally literate, and higher-SES respondents and can underrepresent older adults and people with limited internet access or literacy.

Combining employees, self-employed people, students, and retirees as employed, and combining several other statuses as unemployed, can obscure important distinctions and reduce cross-country comparability.
Using LSS instead of country-specific utility values limits comparison with standard EQ-5D utility studies and reduces use in economic evaluation.
Cultural differences in self-reporting EQ-5D-5L and EQ VAS may have affected the outcomes.
The pandemic may have temporarily changed socioeconomic conditions and HRQoL, and the analysis did not fully account for health-system, welfare-state, and national-response differences.
The many country, socioeconomic-indicator, and outcome tests had no formal multiple-testing correction, which can increase Type I error.

The analysis retained 93 respondents with inconsistent demographic answers between time points and/or questionnaire completion in less than one minute; this could have affected reliability, although their response distributions did not differ significantly.
Internet collection can cause sampling problems and response-rate problems.
The six-month interval could permit true health change and seasonal variation, which could affect reliability and country differences.
Monetary incentives could increase response bias if accepting an incentive is related to characteristics such as education or race.
The United Kingdom EQ-5D-5L value set was used for Italy because an Italian value set was not available; another value set could produce different results.
The reworded QOLIBRI-OS sum score gives equal weight to all items although their importance can differ across populations, and no value set was available.
Only 18 of the 120 tasks had differing durations between scenarios, giving a wide confidence interval on the duration coefficient that anchors the whole model.
An unrestricted design was used, so implausible EQ-5D-5L states were only checked manually rather than excluded by design.

The online panel methodology raises concerns about representativeness on unobservable characteristics, incentivised professional respondents, and limited information on respondent engagement beyond completion time.
Respondents aged over 65 were not recruited, so the sample is not fully representative of the adult population.
Duration was treated as continuous, assuming constant proportional time trade-off, which may have misspecified the indirect utility function.
The Harbin respondents were young, relatively healthy, and highly educated; including patients and older adults from Harbin could have broadened the observed perspectives.
All recruited patients were community based and most had chronic diseases, so hospitalized patients with severe illness and impaired independent living were not represented.
Some Chinese sub-themes and the mindset theme were difficult to translate accurately into English, including the term translated as positive or negative energy.
The study set no prospective criterion for saturation, so the final judgment of data saturation was subjective.
The 5L and 3L samples differed in size and in socio-demographic and health characteristics; the smaller 5L sample reduced statistical power and no adjustment was made for the sample differences.
There was a mismatch between the UK value sets used (3L tariff and crosswalk) and the English profile data, and a 5L-specific value set for England was not available at the time of analysis.
The categorisation of educational level was crude, and a more refined categorisation might have given more information about discriminatory power on that variable.
Restriction to English-language studies may have excluded relevant evidence and underrepresented some African regions.
The search covered five databases and supplementary sources but did not include dedicated gray-literature databases such as OpenGrey.
The exclusion of participants younger than 18 years limits conclusions about pediatric HRQoL measurement in Africa.
Heterogeneity in study designs, sample sizes, and reporting practices made definitive conclusions difficult.
The online DCE had possible low engagement and random responding; 58% of people who accepted the survey were excluded, mainly for noncompletion.

Adults may not validly represent preferences for children and adolescents when asked to consider a 10-year-old child; values may differ by the child age and by whether respondents imagine their own, a known, or another child.
The cTTO sample came from only three Brazilian states, which limits full geographic representation of a country with five regions.
The DCE and cTTO used different samples and different administration modes.
Online recruitment can select against people with low income, low education, or low digital literacy despite the use of quotas.
The preferred model predicted profile 33333 as -0.0059 compared with a mean observed cTTO value of -0.280, so users should use caution for severe youth health states.

The underlying survey data may be subject to selection bias favouring healthier and more independent respondents, so severely ill, institutionalised and dependent people may be under-represented and the demonstrated measurement properties may not generalise to them.
There is no information on whether respondents needed or received help when completing the EQ-5D, so this could not be controlled and feasibility may be overestimated.
The instructions of the EQ-5D used in SHARE differ from the original instrument instructions.
The sample size for the education (years of schooling) variable was below 30,000, which is why ISCED was additionally reported.
